solution: Read |x−2|+|x−5| as the total distance of x from the points 2 and 5 on the number line.Region A (2 ≤ x ≤ 5): the sum is exactly the gap 5−2 = 3, which is ≤ 7. So all of [2,5] works.Region B (x < 2): sum = (2−x)+(5−x) = 7−2x ≤ 7 ⇒ −2x ≤ 0 ⇒ x ≥ 0. So 0 ≤ x < 2 works.Region C (x > 5): sum = (x−2)+(x−5) = 2x−7 ≤ 7 ⇒ 2x ≤ 14 ⇒ x ≤ 7. So 5 < x ≤ 7 works.Combining all three: 0 ≤ x ≤ 7. The integers are 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 — that is 8 values. (A common error is to count only the interval [2,5] giving 4, or to forget that one endpoint of [0,7] is included.)The answer is A.
text: How many integer values of x satisfy the inequality|x − 2| + |x − 5| ≤ 7 ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Note the denominator x²−x+1 = (x−½)²+¾ > 0 for all real x, so f is defined everywhere. Set y = f(x) and clear the fraction:y(x² − x + 1) = x² + x + 1⇒ (y−1)x² − (y+1)x + (y−1) = 0.For real x this quadratic in x must have a real root, so its discriminant is ≥ 0:(y+1)² − 4(y−1)² ≥ 0.Expand: (y²+2y+1) − 4(y²−2y+1) = −3y² + 10y − 3 ≥ 0 ⇒ 3y² − 10y + 3 ≤ 0 ⇒ (3y−1)(y−3) ≤ 0.This holds for 1/3 ≤ y ≤ 3. So M = 3 and m = 1/3, giving M − m = 3 − 1/3 = 8/3. (Forgetting to handle the y=1 case or mis-expanding the discriminant typically yields 3 or 7/3.)The answer is C.
text: For real x, the functionf(x) = (x² + x + 1) ÷ (x² − x + 1)takes a maximum value M and a minimum value m over all real x. What is the value of M − m?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Use the Cauchy–Schwarz (Titu / Engel form) inequality:1/x + 9/y = 1²/x + 3²/y ≥ (1+3)² ÷ (x+y) = 16/10 = 8/5.Equality requires 1/x = 3/y, i.e. y = 3x. With x+y=10 that gives x=2.5, y=7.5, both positive, so the bound is attained. Hence the minimum is 8/5 = 1.6.(A frequent slip is to plug in x=y=5, getting 1/5+9/5 = 2, which is NOT the minimum — that distractor is option E. Another error mixes the equality condition and lands on 1.)The answer is D.
text: Positive real numbers x and y satisfy x + y = 10. What is the minimum possible value of1/x + 9/y ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Both sides are non-negative, so we may square without sign issues:(2x−3)² < (x+1)²⇒ 4x² − 12x + 9 < x² + 2x + 1⇒ 3x² − 14x + 8 < 0.Solve 3x² − 14x + 8 = 0: x = [14 ± √(196−96)]/6 = (14 ± 10)/6, giving x = 4 and x = 2/3. Since the parabola opens upward, the inequality holds strictly between the roots:2/3 < x < 4.The integers strictly inside are 1, 2, 3 — exactly 3 values. (Squaring an inequality with subtraction/addition errors, or including endpoint x=4, leads to 2 or 4.)The answer is B.
text: How many integer values of x satisfy|2x − 3| < |x + 1| ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Let s = a + b. Then s² = a² + b² + 2ab = 1 + 2ab, so ab = (s² − 1)/2. Since a,b are real with a²+b²=1, s ranges over [−√2, √2].The expression becomesE(s) = s + (s² − 1)/2 = ½s² + s − ½.This is an upward parabola in s, so on the interval [−√2, √2] its maximum occurs at the right endpoint s = √2:E(√2) = ½(2) + √2 − ½ = 1 + √2 − ½ = ½ + √2 ≈ 1.914.Check: s = √2 forces a = b = 1/√2, which satisfies a²+b²=1, so the value is achievable. (Maximizing only a+b gives √2; forgetting the −½ constant gives 1+√2.)The answer is E.
text: Real numbers a and b satisfy a² + b² = 1. What is the maximum possible value of(a + b) + ab ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: The set |x|+|y| ≤ n (for integer n) is a 'diamond' (rotated square) of lattice points centred at the origin. Count by the value of k = |x|+|y|:k = 0: just (0,0) → 1 point.k = 1: 4 points.k = 2: 8 points.k = 3: 12 points.In general each shell k ≥ 1 contains 4k lattice points. Total for |x|+|y| ≤ 3 is 1 + 4 + 8 + 12 = 25.(Equivalently the closed-form for |x|+|y| ≤ n is 2n²+2n+1 = 2·9+2·3+1 = 25.) A common error counts only the strict interior or forgets the axis points, giving 13 or 24.The answer is A.
text: How many ordered pairs of integers (x, y) satisfy|x| + |y| ≤ 3 ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: For a sum of absolute deviations from fixed points, the minimum is reached when x lies at the median of the points. With an even number of points (1, 2, 3, 10), any x in the middle interval [2, 3] minimizes the sum.Pair the outermost and innermost points: for any x in [2,3],|x−1| + |x−10| = (x−1) + (10−x) = 9 (the full span 10−1),|x−2| + |x−3| = (x−2) + (3−x) = 1 (the inner span 3−2).Total = 9 + 1 = 10, constant across [2,3]. So the minimum value is 10.(Plugging in the mean (16/4 = 4) instead of a median, or only spanning the extremes, are typical mistakes leading to 11 or 9.)The answer is E.
text: What is the minimum possible value, over all real x, of|x − 1| + |x − 2| + |x − 3| + |x − 10| ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Substitute t = x + 2. Since x > 0, we have t > 2, and x = t − 2. The expression becomes(t − 2) + 16/t = t + 16/t − 2.By AM–GM, t + 16/t ≥ 2√(t · 16/t) = 2√16 = 8, with equality when t = 16/t, i.e. t = 4. Since t = 4 > 2 is in the allowed range (it gives x = 2 > 0), the bound is attainable.Therefore the minimum is 8 − 2 = 6.(Forgetting to shift the variable and applying AM–GM directly to x + 16/(x+2) gives the wrong floor of 8; ignoring the −2 gives 8 as well.)The answer is C.
text: For x > 0, what is the minimum value ofx + 16 ÷ (x + 2) ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Since x² = |x|², let u = |x| (so u ≥ 0). The inequality becomesu² − 5u + 6 ≤ 0 ⇒ (u − 2)(u − 3) ≤ 0 ⇒ 2 ≤ u ≤ 3.So 2 ≤ |x| ≤ 3, meaning x lies in [−3, −2] ∪ [2, 3].The integers satisfying this are −3, −2, 2, 3 — exactly 4 values. (Treating the inequality as x²−5x+6≤0 and ignoring the modulus would give only 2 and 3, i.e. 2 values — a classic trap.)The answer is D.
text: How many integer values of x satisfyx² − 5|x| + 6 ≤ 0 ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Rewrite each factor using a + b + c = 1:1/a − 1 = (1 − a)/a = (b + c)/a, and similarly for the others. So the product is[(b+c)(a+c)(a+b)] ÷ (abc).By AM–GM, b + c ≥ 2√(bc), a + c ≥ 2√(ac), a + b ≥ 2√(ab). Multiplying:(b+c)(a+c)(a+b) ≥ 8√(bc · ac · ab) = 8√(a²b²c²) = 8abc.Dividing both sides by abc (positive): the product ≥ 8. Equality holds when a = b = c = 1/3, where each factor is (3 − 1) = 2, giving 2×2×2 = 8.So the minimum value is 8. (Mistaking the structure and computing 3×3×3 = 27, or stopping at a single factor's value, are the common errors.)The answer is B.
text: Positive real numbers a, b, c satisfy a + b + c = 1. What is the minimum possible value of(1/a − 1)(1/b − 1)(1/c − 1) ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Compute g(g(x)) first: g(x) = x/(1+x), so g(g(x)) = [x/(1+x)] / [1 + x/(1+x)] = [x/(1+x)] / [(1+2x)/(1+x)] = x/(1+2x). The pattern is g<sup>(n)</sup>(x) = x/(1+nx). Check by induction: g<sup>(n+1)</sup>(x) = g(x/(1+nx)) = [x/(1+nx)] / [1 + x/(1+nx)] = x/(1+(n+1)x). For n = 5: g<sup>(5)</sup>(x) = x/(1+5x). Substituting x = 2 gives 2/(1+10) = 2/11. (Applying g only once gives 2/3, the off-by-one trap.) The answer is 2/11.
text: Define the function g(x) = x / (1 + x) for all x ≠ −1. Let g<sup>(n)</sup>(x) denote g composed with itself n times (so g<sup>(2)</sup>(x) = g(g(x)), and so on). What is the value of g<sup>(5)</sup>(2)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Convert every term to base 2 using log<sub>b<sup>k</sup></sub>x = (1/k)·log<sub>2</sub>x. Since 4 = 2<sup>2</sup> and 16 = 2<sup>4</sup>: log<sub>4</sub>x = (1/2)log<sub>2</sub>x and log<sub>16</sub>x = (1/4)log<sub>2</sub>x. Let t = log<sub>2</sub>x. Then t + t/2 + t/4 = (4t + 2t + t)/4 = 7t/4 = 7, so t = 4. Therefore x = 2<sup>4</sup> = 16. (Mistakenly adding the bases' exponents as 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 forces t = 1 and the trap answer x = 2.) The answer is 16.
text: If log<sub>2</sub>x + log<sub>4</sub>x + log<sub>16</sub>x = 7, what is the value of x?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Factor the left side: 4<sup>x</sup> + 4<sup>x+1</sup> = 4<sup>x</sup>(1 + 4) = 5·4<sup>x</sup>. So 5·4<sup>x</sup> = 320, giving 4<sup>x</sup> = 64 = 4<sup>3</sup>, hence x = 3. Verification: 4<sup>3</sup> + 4<sup>4</sup> = 64 + 256 = 320. (Forgetting to factor and writing 4<sup>x</sup> = 320 leads to the non-integer log<sub>4</sub>320 trap; treating it as 4<sup>x</sup>·4<sup>x</sup> gives x = 2.5.) The answer is x = 3.
text: There is exactly one positive real value of x for which 4<sup>x</sup> + 4<sup>x+1</sup> = 320. What is that value of x?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Write f(x) = p(x) + 7, where p(x) = ax<sup>5</sup> + bx<sup>3</sup> + cx is an odd function, so p(−x) = −p(x). From f(−3) = p(−3) + 7 = 4 we get p(−3) = −3, hence p(3) = −p(−3) = 3. Therefore f(3) = p(3) + 7 = 3 + 7 = 10. (Treating the polynomial part as even and concluding f(3) = f(−3) = 4 is the classic trap.) The answer is 10.
text: A function is given by f(x) = ax<sup>5</sup> + bx<sup>3</sup> + cx + 7, where a, b, c are real constants. If f(−3) = 4, what is the value of f(3)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Use the chain rule for logs: log<sub>a</sub>c = log<sub>a</sub>b · log<sub>b</sub>c = 3 × 4 = 12. Express everything in base a: log<sub>a</sub>a = 1, log<sub>a</sub>b = 3, log<sub>a</sub>c = 12. By change of base, log<sub>abc</sub>c = log<sub>a</sub>c / log<sub>a</sub>(abc) = log<sub>a</sub>c / (log<sub>a</sub>a + log<sub>a</sub>b + log<sub>a</sub>c) = 12 / (1 + 3 + 12) = 12/16 = 3/4. (Dropping the log<sub>a</sub>a = 1 term gives 12/15 = 4/5; adding the original logs as 3 + 4 = 7 gives the 12/7 trap.) The answer is 3/4.
text: Suppose a, b, c are real numbers greater than 1 with log<sub>a</sub>b = 3 and log<sub>b</sub>c = 4. What is the value of log<sub>abc</sub>c?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: The domain requires 6 − x − x<sup>2</sup> ≥ 0, i.e. x<sup>2</sup> + x − 6 ≤ 0, i.e. (x + 3)(x − 2) ≤ 0, so −3 ≤ x ≤ 2. The expression under the root is a downward parabola in x with maximum at x = −1/2: value = 6 − (−1/2) − 1/4 = 6.25. So 6 − x − x<sup>2</sup> ranges over [0, 6.25], and f = √(that) ranges over [0, 2.5]. The integers in [0, 2.5] are 0, 1, 2 — exactly 3 of them. (Counting integers in the domain [−3, 2] gives 6, the common trap.) The answer is 3.
text: Consider the real-valued function f(x) = √(6 − x − x<sup>2</sup>), defined on its largest possible (real) domain. How many distinct integers lie in the range of f?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: The relation f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) with f(1) = 3 forces f(n) = 3<sup>n</sup> for positive integers (f(2) = f(1)f(1) = 9, f(3) = f(2)f(1) = 27, and so on). So the sum is 3 + 9 + 27 + 81 + 243. This is a geometric series with first term 3, ratio 3, five terms: 3(3<sup>5</sup> − 1)/(3 − 1) = 3(242)/2 = 363. (Stopping at f(5) = 243 alone, or summing 3+6+9+12+15 = 45 by treating f as linear, are the traps.) The answer is 363.
text: A function f defined on all real numbers satisfies f(x + y) = f(x)·f(y) for every pair of reals x and y, and f(1) = 3. What is the value of f(1) + f(2) + f(3) + f(4) + f(5)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Rewrite each nested surd as a perfect square. Note 7 + 4√3 = 4 + 4√3 + 3 = (2 + √3)<sup>2</sup>, and 7 − 4√3 = 4 − 4√3 + 3 = (2 − √3)<sup>2</sup>. Since 2 − √3 > 0, both square roots are positive: √(7 + 4√3) = 2 + √3 and √(7 − 4√3) = 2 − √3. Their difference is (2 + √3) − (2 − √3) = 2√3. (Adding the two surds instead of subtracting gives 4, the trap.) The answer is 2√3.
text: Evaluate the expression √(7 + 4√3) − √(7 − 4√3).
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Let t = log<sub>2</sub>x. Then log<sub>x</sub>2 = 1/t (reciprocal of a log), so the equation becomes t + 1/t = 5/2. Multiply by t: 2t<sup>2</sup> − 5t + 2 = 0, which factors as (2t − 1)(t − 2) = 0, giving t = 2 or t = 1/2. Then x = 2<sup>t</sup> = 2<sup>2</sup> = 4 or x = 2<sup>1/2</sup> = √2. The two solutions are 4 and √2; the integer one is 4. (Mistaking the t-value 2 for x itself yields the trap answer 2.) The answer is 4.
text: The equation log<sub>2</sub>x + log<sub>x</sub>2 = 5/2 has exactly two solutions for x (with x > 0 and x ≠ 1). Exactly one of these solutions is an integer. What is that integer?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Since g is the inverse of f, g(k) is the value of x for which f(x) = k; it is found by solving f(x) = k, not by evaluating f at k. For g(3): (x − 1)/(x + 2) = 3 ⇒ x − 1 = 3x + 6 ⇒ −7 = 2x ⇒ x = −7/2. For g(−1): (x − 1)/(x + 2) = −1 ⇒ x − 1 = −x − 2 ⇒ 2x = −1 ⇒ x = −1/2. So g(3) + g(−1) = −7/2 + (−1/2) = −8/2 = −4. (Evaluating f instead of its inverse gives f(3) + f(−1) = 2/5 + (−2) = −8/5, the trap; taking g(3) alone gives −7/2.) The answer is −4.
text: Let f(x) = (x − 1) / (x + 2), defined for x ≠ −2, and let g denote its inverse function. What is the value of g(3) + g(−1)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: The nth term equals S<sub>n</sub> − S<sub>n−1</sub>. So a<sub>12</sub> = S<sub>12</sub> − S<sub>11</sub>. S<sub>12</sub> = 3(144) + 5(12) = 432 + 60 = 492. S<sub>11</sub> = 3(121) + 5(11) = 363 + 55 = 418. Thus a<sub>12</sub> = 492 − 418 = 74. (Equivalently, a<sub>n</sub> = S<sub>n</sub> − S<sub>n−1</sub> = 6n + 2, so a<sub>12</sub> = 6(12) + 2 = 74.) A common error is to compute 6n = 72 (dropping the constant) or to use n = 13 giving 80. The answer is A.
text: The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression is given by Sn = 3n2 + 5n for every positive integer n. What is the value of the 12th term of this progression?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Let the first term be a and ratio r with 0 < r < 1. Then a/(1 − r) = 12 and a<sup>2</sup>/(1 − r<sup>2</sup>) = 48. Note a<sup>2</sup>/(1 − r<sup>2</sup>) = [a/(1 − r)] × [a/(1 + r)]. So 48 = 12 × a/(1 + r), giving a/(1 + r) = 4. Dividing the two relations: [a/(1 − r)] ÷ [a/(1 + r)] = 12/4 = 3, so (1 + r)/(1 − r) = 3, hence 1 + r = 3 − 3r, 4r = 2, r = 1/2. (Then a = 6; check: 6/(1/2) = 12 and 36/(3/4) = 48.) The answer is B.
text: An infinite geometric progression of positive terms has sum 12, and the sum of the squares of its terms is 48. What is the common ratio of the progression?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: This is an arithmetico-geometric series with general term (1 + 3k)·(1/3)<sup>k</sup> for k = 0, 1, 2, … — the arithmetic part has a = 1, d = 3 and the geometric part has r = 1/3. The sum to infinity of Σ(a + kd)r<sup>k</sup> is a/(1 − r) + d·r/(1 − r)<sup>2</sup>. Here a/(1 − r) = 1/(2/3) = 3/2, and d·r/(1 − r)<sup>2</sup> = 3·(1/3)/(2/3)<sup>2</sup> = 1/(4/9) = 9/4. Total = 3/2 + 9/4 = 6/4 + 9/4 = 15/4. A common slip is to use (1 − r) instead of (1 − r)<sup>2</sup> in the second term, which wrongly gives 3/2 + 3/2 = 3. The answer is C.
text: Evaluate the sum to infinity of the series1 + 4÷3 + 7÷9 + 10÷27 + 13÷81 + …where the numerators 1, 4, 7, 10, … increase by 3 and each denominator is 3 times the previous one.
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Let the three numbers be (a − d), a, (a + d). Their sum is 3a = 24, so a = 8. Their product is (8 − d)(8)(8 + d) = 8(64 − d<sup>2</sup>) = 440, so 64 − d<sup>2</sup> = 55, giving d<sup>2</sup> = 9 and d = 3. The three numbers are 5, 8, 11, and the largest is 11. (Choosing the middle term 8 is the trap for those who stop at a.) The answer is D.
text: Three numbers are in arithmetic progression. Their sum is 24 and their product is 440. What is the largest of the three numbers?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Pair the terms as (1<sup>2</sup> − 2<sup>2</sup>) + (3<sup>2</sup> − 4<sup>2</sup>) + … + (19<sup>2</sup> − 20<sup>2</sup>) + 21<sup>2</sup>. Each pair k<sup>2</sup> − (k+1)<sup>2</sup> = −(2k + 1) = −(sum of the two bases). The negative pairs sum to −(1+2) − (3+4) − … − (19+20) = −(1 + 2 + … + 20) = −(20·21/2) = −210. Adding the leftover 21<sup>2</sup> = 441 gives 441 − 210 = 231. (Equivalently, for an odd number of terms n, the sum is n(n+1)/2 = 21·22/2 = 231.) The answer is E.
text: What is the value of the sum1<sup>2</sup> − 2<sup>2</sup> + 3<sup>2</sup> − 4<sup>2</sup> + 5<sup>2</sup> − … + 21<sup>2</sup>(the signs alternate, beginning with + on 1<sup>2</sup> and ending with + on 21<sup>2</sup>)?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Let the first term be a and ratio r. Then ar = 6 and ar<sup>4</sup> = 48. Dividing, r<sup>3</sup> = 48/6 = 8, so r = 2, and a = 6/r = 3. The sum of the first 8 terms is a(r<sup>8</sup> − 1)/(r − 1) = 3(256 − 1)/(2 − 1) = 3(255) = 765. (Using 7 terms gives 3(127) = 381; using 9 terms gives 3(511) = 1533 — both off-by-one traps.) The answer is A.
text: In a geometric progression the 2nd term is 6 and the 5th term is 48. What is the sum of the first 8 terms?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: The sum of n terms is S<sub>n</sub> = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d] = (n/2)[10 + 4(n − 1)] = (n/2)(4n + 6) = n(2n + 3). Set n(2n + 3) = 495, i.e. 2n<sup>2</sup> + 3n − 495 = 0. The discriminant is 9 + 8·495 = 9 + 3960 = 3969 = 63<sup>2</sup>. So n = (−3 + 63)/4 = 60/4 = 15. (Check: S<sub>15</sub> = 15·33 = 495.) The answer is B.
text: An arithmetic progression has first term 5 and common difference 4. How many terms must be added, starting from the first, so that the sum of those terms is exactly 495?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Let the numbers be a and b. The arithmetic mean gives (a + b)/2 = 10, so a + b = 20. The geometric mean gives √(ab) = 8, so ab = 64. The harmonic mean is 2ab/(a + b) = 2(64)/20 = 128/20 = 6.4. (Equivalently, HM = GM<sup>2</sup>/AM = 64/10 = 6.4, since GM is the geometric mean of AM and HM.) A frequent error is to average AM and GM to get 9. The answer is C.
text: Two positive numbers have arithmetic mean 10 and geometric mean 8. What is their harmonic mean?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: S<sub>9</sub> = S<sub>17</sub> means the terms from the 10th through the 17th add to 0. Using S<sub>n</sub> = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d]: (9/2)(2a + 8d) = (17/2)(2a + 16d), so 9(a + 4d) = 17(a + 8d), giving 9a + 36d = 17a + 136d, hence −8a = 100d, i.e. 2a = −25d. Now S<sub>26</sub> = (26/2)[2a + 25d] = 13[2a + 25d] = 13[−25d + 25d] = 13·0 = 0. (General rule: if S<sub>m</sub> = S<sub>n</sub> with m ≠ n, then S<sub>m+n</sub> = 0; here m + n = 9 + 17 = 26.) The answer is D.
text: For a certain arithmetic progression, the sum of its first 9 terms equals the sum of its first 17 terms. What is the sum of its first 26 terms?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Here a<sub>k</sub> = 3k − 1 and the common difference is d = 3. Use the telescoping identity 1/(a<sub>k</sub>a<sub>k+1</sub>) = (1/d)[1/a<sub>k</sub> − 1/a<sub>k+1</sub>]. Summing from k = 1 to 20 telescopes to (1/d)[1/a<sub>1</sub> − 1/a<sub>21</sub>]. Now a<sub>1</sub> = 2 and a<sub>21</sub> = 3(21) − 1 = 62. So the sum = (1/3)[1/2 − 1/62] = (1/3)[(31 − 1)/62] = (1/3)(30/62) = (1/3)(15/31) = 5/31. Forgetting the 1/d factor wrongly gives 15/31. The answer is E.
text: Consider the arithmetic progression 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, … with kth term a<sub>k</sub>. Evaluate the sum1÷(a<sub>1</sub>a<sub>2</sub>) + 1÷(a<sub>2</sub>a<sub>3</sub>) + 1÷(a<sub>3</sub>a<sub>4</sub>) + … + 1÷(a<sub>20</sub>a<sub>21</sub>).
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Use Heron's formula. The semi-perimeter is s = (13+14+15)/2 = 21. Area = √(21×(21−13)×(21−14)×(21−15)) = √(21×8×7×6) = √7056 = 84. The altitude h to the side of length 14 satisfies Area = (1/2)(14)(h), so 84 = 7h, giving h = 12. (Distractor 11.2 is the altitude to side 15; 12 12/13 is the altitude to side 13.) The answer is D.
text: A triangle has sides of length 13, 14, and 15. A surveyor needs the length of the altitude drawn to the side of length 14. What is that altitude?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: By the Angle Bisector Theorem, the bisector from A divides the opposite side BC in the ratio of the adjacent sides: BD/DC = AB/AC = 12/18 = 2/3. So BD = BC × 2/(2+3) = 20 × 2/5 = 8. (Distractor 12 swaps the ratio and gives DC; distractor 10 is the naive midpoint.) The answer is B.
text: In triangle ABC, AB = 12, AC = 18, and BC = 20. The bisector of angle A meets side BC at point D. What is the length of segment BD (the part of BC nearer to B)?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: The median to side a (here a = BC = 14) has length m<sub>a</sub> = (1/2)√(2b² + 2c² − a²), where b = CA = 13 and c = AB = 15. So m<sub>a</sub> = (1/2)√(2×169 + 2×225 − 196) = (1/2)√(338 + 450 − 196) = (1/2)√592 = (1/2)(4√37) = 2√37. (Distractor 4√37 forgets to halve; distractor 7 is just half the base BC; distractor 12 is the altitude, not the median.) The answer is E.
text: In triangle ABC, side BC = 14, side CA = 13, and side AB = 15. M is the midpoint of BC. What is the length of the median AM?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: For similar figures, the ratio of areas equals the square of the ratio of corresponding linear measures (perimeters). So areas are in ratio 3² : 5² = 9 : 25. Let the areas be 9k and 25k. Their difference is 25k − 9k = 16k = 80, so k = 5. The larger area is 25k = 125. (Distractor 45 is the smaller area; distractor 200 wrongly uses the 3:5 ratio directly on the difference; distractor 128 mishandles 80 as the smaller area.) The answer is C.
text: Two triangles are similar. The ratio of their perimeters is 3 : 5. The area of the larger triangle exceeds the area of the smaller by 80 square units. What is the area of the larger triangle, in square units?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: The centroid is the average of the vertices: G = ((0+12+0)/3, (0+0+9)/3) = (4, 3). The distance GA = √(4² + 3²) = √(16 + 9) = √25 = 5. (Distractor 7.5 is the distance from A to the midpoint of BC, the full median length; the centroid is only 2/3 of the way along it, and here 2/3 × 7.5 = 5.) The answer is C.
text: A triangle has vertices A(0, 0), B(12, 0), and C(0, 9). G is the centroid of the triangle. What is the distance from G to vertex A?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: In a 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse 20, the legs are 20×sin30° = 10 and 20×sin60° = 10√3. For a right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c, the inradius is r = (a + b − c)/2 = (10 + 10√3 − 20)/2 = (10√3 − 10)/2 = 5(√3 − 1). (Distractor 5(√3 + 1) adds the hypotenuse instead of subtracting; 10(√3 − 1) forgets the factor of 1/2.) The answer is A.
text: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of length 20 and one acute angle of 30°. What is the radius of the circle inscribed in this triangle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: In a right triangle, the altitude to the hypotenuse creates similar sub-triangles. Each leg is the geometric mean of the whole hypotenuse and the adjacent segment: AC² = AD × AB = AD × (AD + DB) = 9 × 25 = 225, so AC = 15. (Distractor 12 is the altitude CD = √(9×16); distractor 20 is the other leg BC = √(16×25); distractor 25 is the hypotenuse.) The answer is C.
text: Triangle ABC has its right angle at C. The altitude from C meets the hypotenuse AB at point D, splitting it so that AD = 9 and DB = 16. What is the length of leg AC?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Since DE ∥ BC, triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC with ratio AD/AB = 2/(2+3) = 2/5. The area ratio is (2/5)² = 4/25, so area(ADE) = (4/25)×175 = 28. The trapezoid is the remainder: area(DBCE) = 175 − 28 = 147. (Distractor 28 is the small triangle, not the trapezoid; distractor 105 wrongly uses the linear ratio 2/5 directly; distractor 70 uses 3/5 linearly.) The answer is E.
text: In triangle ABC, point D lies on AB and point E lies on AC with DE parallel to BC. The point D divides AB so that AD : DB = 2 : 3. The area of triangle ABC is 175 square units. What is the area of trapezoid DBCE (the region between DE and BC), in square units?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: For an equilateral triangle of side s, area = (√3/4)s². Setting (√3/4)s² = 36√3 gives s² = 144, so s = 12. The altitude is h = (s√3)/2 = (12√3)/2 = 6√3. (Distractor 12 is the side length itself; distractor 6 forgets the √3 factor in the height.) The answer is A.
text: An equilateral triangle has area 36√3 square units. What is the length of its altitude (height)?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: By the Law of Cosines, QR² = PQ² + PR² − 2·PQ·PR·cos(60°) = 64 + 144 − 2×8×12×(1/2) = 208 − 96 = 112. So QR = √112 = √(16×7) = 4√7. (Distractor √208 = 4√13 forgets the cosine term entirely; distractor 20 just adds 8 + 12; 2√19 uses cos = +1/2 with a sign slip giving 76.) The answer is A.
text: In triangle PQR, PQ = 8, PR = 12, and the angle at P equals 60°. What is the length of side QR?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: With the square's corner at the right angle and sides along the legs a = 20 and b = 21, similar triangles give the square side s = ab/(a + b) = (20×21)/(20 + 21) = 420/41 ≈ 10.24. (This is the standard formula for a square sharing the right-angle vertex. Distractor 210/41 halves it incorrectly; distractor 10.5 is half the leg; the hypotenuse-based formula s = abc/(ab + c²) applies only when a side of the square lies on the hypotenuse, a different configuration.) The answer is D.
text: A right triangle has legs of length 20 and 21. A square is inscribed in the triangle so that one of its corners sits at the right angle and two of its sides lie along the two legs. What is the side length of the square?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Apply Stewart's Theorem to cevian AD on side BC (= 12), with BD = 9 and DC = 3. Stewart's relation: AB²·DC + AC²·BD = BC·(AD² + BD·DC). Substitute: 10²×3 + 6²×9 = 12×(AD² + 9×3), so 300 + 324 = 12×(AD² + 27), giving 624 = 12·AD² + 324, hence 12·AD² = 300, AD² = 25, AD = 5. (Distractor √57 swaps BD and DC in the formula; 2√6 = √24 forgets to subtract the BD·DC term.) The answer is C.
text: In triangle ABC, AB = 10, AC = 6, and BC = 12. Point D lies on side BC with BD = 9 and DC = 3. What is the length of the cevian AD?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: By the intersecting-chords (power of a point) theorem, AP × PB = CP × PD. So CP × PD = 9 × 4 = 36. Since P is the midpoint of CD, we have CP = PD = x, giving x² = 36, so x = 6. Therefore CD = CP + PD = 6 + 6 = 12. (Choosing 6 stops at the half-chord; 13 just adds 9 + 4; 18 mishandles the doubling.) The answer is A.
text: In a circle, two chords AB and CD intersect at an interior point P. Along the first chord, AP = 9 and PB = 4. The point P happens to be the exact midpoint of chord CD. What is the length of CD?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: By the tangent-secant (power of a point) theorem, PT² = PA × PB, where PB is the WHOLE secant length from P, not just the chord AB. Here PB = PA + AB = 4 + 12 = 16. So PT² = 4 × 16 = 64, giving PT = 8. (The trap √48 comes from using PT² = PA × AB = 4 × 12 = 48; choosing 16 takes PB itself; 12 takes AB.) The answer is C.
text: From an external point P, a tangent line touches a circle at T, and a secant line from P passes through the circle hitting it first at A and then at B, with A between P and B. Given PA = 4 and AB = 12, find the length of the tangent segment PT.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: The two angles at vertex A on either side of diagonal AC combine to give the full interior angle: ∠BAD = ∠BAC + ∠CAD = 40° + 30° = 70°. In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles are supplementary, so ∠BCD = 180° − ∠BAD = 180° − 70° = 110°. (Choosing 70° reports ∠BAD itself; 40° uses only one sub-angle; 140° doubles instead of complementing.) The answer is C.
text: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle (a cyclic quadrilateral). Diagonal AC is drawn. It is given that ∠BAC = 40° and ∠CAD = 30°. Find the measure of ∠BCD.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: For a regular n-gon, each interior angle is (n − 2) × 180° / n. The fastest route uses the exterior angle: each exterior angle = 180° − 156° = 24°, and exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360°, so n = 360° / 24° = 15. Check: (15 − 2) × 180 / 15 = 13 × 12 = 156°. (Choosing 24 mistakenly reports the exterior angle as the count.) The answer is D.
text: A regular convex polygon has each interior angle equal to 156°. How many sides does the polygon have?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency, so ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°. Quadrilateral OAPB has interior angles summing to 360°: ∠OAP + ∠OBP + ∠APB + ∠AOB = 360°. Thus 90° + 90° + 40° + ∠AOB = 360°, giving ∠AOB = 140°. (Choosing 40° just echoes ∠APB; 220° takes the reflex angle; 50° uses 90 − 40.) The answer is D.
text: From an external point P, two tangent lines are drawn to a circle with center O, touching it at points A and B. The angle between the two tangents, ∠APB, is 40°. Find the measure of the central angle ∠AOB (the angle at O subtended by the two tangent points, on the side facing P).
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: First find the central angle. With radii perpendicular to the tangents, quadrilateral OAPB gives 90° + 90° + 50° + ∠AOB = 360°, so the central angle ∠AOB = 130°, subtending the MINOR arc AB (the short arc near P). A point C on the MAJOR arc subtends that same minor arc, so by the inscribed-angle theorem ∠ACB = (1/2) × 130° = 65°. (If C were on the minor arc the answer would be 115°, the supplement; choosing 130° forgets to halve; 50° echoes ∠APB.) The answer is B.
text: From an external point P, two tangents PA and PB touch a circle at A and B, with ∠APB = 50°. A point C lies on the circle, on the MAJOR arc AB (the longer arc, on the far side from P). Find the measure of the inscribed angle ∠ACB.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: Since ABCD is cyclic, apply Ptolemy's theorem: (product of diagonals) = (sum of products of opposite sides). For quadrilateral ABCD with diagonals AC and BD: AC × BD = AB × CD + BC × AD. Because the triangle is equilateral, AB = BC = AC = s, so s × BD = s × CD + s × AD, and dividing by s gives the elegant result BD = AD + CD = 7 + 8 = 15. (This is the classic 'Van Schooten' relation; a coordinate check with the circumradius forced by AD = 7, CD = 8 gives BD = 15.000 exactly. Choosing 13 = √(49+64+56) computes the triangle side s, not BD; √113 forgets the cosine cross-term; choosing 1 takes a difference.) The answer is C.
text: Triangle ABC is equilateral and inscribed in a circle. A point D lies on the minor arc AC (the arc not containing B). The chords from D satisfy AD = 7 and CD = 8. Find the length of chord BD.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: At each vertex the interior and exterior angles are supplementary, summing to 180°. Splitting 180° in the ratio 7 : 2 (total 9 parts) gives interior = 180 × 7/9 = 140° and exterior = 180 × 2/9 = 40°. The number of sides is n = 360° / (exterior angle) = 360 / 40 = 9. The number of diagonals of an n-gon is n(n − 3)/2 = 9 × 6 / 2 = 27. (Choosing 9 stops at the side count; 35 corresponds to n = 10; 18 forgets the division by 2.) The answer is A.
text: In a certain regular convex polygon, the ratio of each interior angle to each exterior angle is 7 : 2. How many diagonals does this polygon have?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: The line joining the centers is the perpendicular bisector of the common chord. Let x be the distance from the radius-13 center to the chord. Then x² + h² = 13² and (14 − x)² + h² = 15², where h is the half-chord. Subtracting: x² − (14 − x)² = 169 − 225, so 28x − 196 = −56, giving 28x = 140, x = 5. Then h² = 169 − 25 = 144, so h = 12 and the full chord = 2h = 24. (Since |13 − 15| < 14 < 13 + 15, the circles do meet at two points. Choosing 12 reports only the half-chord; 26 uses the diameter of the smaller circle.) The answer is B.
text: Two circles intersect at two points. One circle has radius 13 and the other has radius 15, and the distance between their centers is 14. Find the length of their common chord.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle (Thales' theorem), so ∠ACB = 90° and triangle ABC is right-angled at C with hypotenuse AB = 26. By the Pythagorean theorem, BC = √(AB² − AC²) = √(26² − 10²) = √(676 − 100) = √576 = 24. (This is a 10-24-26 right triangle. Choosing √69 mistakenly uses the radius 13 instead of the diameter; 12 halves the result; 16 = 26 − 10.) The answer is E.
text: Points A, B, and C lie on a circle, and AB is a diameter of length 26. The chord AC has length 10. Find the length of chord BC.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: Write the line as ax + by + c = 0 with a = 1, b = −2, c = 4, so a² + b² = 5.Compute t = (a·5 + b·2 + c)/(a² + b²) = (5 − 4 + 4)/5 = 5/5 = 1.The reflection is P′ = (5 − 2·a·t, 2 − 2·b·t) = (5 − 2(1)(1), 2 − 2(−2)(1)) = (3, 6).Check: the midpoint (4, 4) satisfies 4 − 2(4) + 4 = 0, and PP′ has slope (6−2)/(3−5) = −2, perpendicular to the line's slope 1/2. Good.Sum = 3 + 6 = 9. (A common error is to move only to the foot of the perpendicular (4, 4), giving sum 8.)The answer is C.
text: The point P(5, 2) is reflected across the line x − 2y + 4 = 0 to give its mirror image P′. What is the sum of the coordinates of P′?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Let P divide AB in ratio k : 1 from A, so the x-coordinate is (k·9 + 1·(−3))/(k + 1) = 1.Then 9k − 3 = k + 1, giving 8k = 4, so k = 1/2.Thus AP : PB = k : 1 = 1/2 : 1 = 1 : 2.Verify with the y-coordinate: ((1/2)(−8) + 4)/(3/2) = (−4 + 4)/(3/2) = 0. Correct.(Swapping the section-formula weights gives the trap 2 : 1.)The answer is A.
text: The point P(1, 0) lies on the segment joining A(−3, 4) and B(9, −8). In what ratio does P divide AB, measured as AP : PB (from A to B)?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Area of triangle ABC by the shoelace formula = ½|0(0 − 6) + 9(6 − 0) + 3(0 − 0)| = ½|54| = 27.D divides AB 2 : 1, so D = (6, 0). E divides AC 2 : 1, so E = (2, 4).Triangle ADE shares angle A with ABC and has AD/AB = AE/AC = 2/3, so it is similar with ratio 2/3; its area = (2/3)² · 27 = 4/9 · 27 = 12.Quadrilateral DBCE = area(ABC) − area(ADE) = 27 − 12 = 15.(Choosing 12 reports the small triangle ADE itself; 18 = 2/3 of the whole; 9 = 1/3 of the whole.)The answer is D.
text: In triangle ABC, A = (0, 0), B = (9, 0), and C = (3, 6). Point D lies on AB with AD : DB = 2 : 1, and point E lies on AC with AE : EC = 2 : 1. What is the area of quadrilateral DBCE?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Slope of the line through (2, 5) and (6, −3) = (−3 − 5)/(6 − 2) = −8/4 = −2.Point-slope: y − 5 = −2(x − 2), i.e. 2x + y − 9 = 0.Distance from (7, 1) = |2(7) + 1 − 9| / √(2² + 1²) = |14 + 1 − 9| / √5 = 6/√5.Rationalize: 6/√5 = 6√5/5 ≈ 2.68.(Forgetting to take the square root of 5 in the denominator gives the trap 6/5.)The answer is B.
text: What is the perpendicular distance from the point (7, 1) to the line passing through (2, 5) and (6, −3)?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Side AB is vertical (from (2,−1) to (2,7)) with length 8; side AC is horizontal (from (2,−1) to (10,−1)) with length 8. These meet at right angles at A, so triangle ABC is right-angled at A.For a right triangle, the circumcenter is the midpoint of the hypotenuse BC, and the circumradius is half the hypotenuse.Hypotenuse BC = √((10 − 2)² + (−1 − 7)²) = √(64 + 64) = √128 = 8√2.Radius = ½ · 8√2 = 4√2 ≈ 5.66.(Using the full hypotenuse gives 8√2; treating a leg as the diameter gives traps like 4 or 8.)The answer is C.
text: Triangle ABC has vertices A(2, −1), B(2, 7), and C(10, −1). A circle passes through all three vertices. What is the radius of this circle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: From 4x − y = 5 we get y = 4x − 5. Substitute into 2x + 3y = 13:2x + 3(4x − 5) = 13 ⇒ 2x + 12x − 15 = 13 ⇒ 14x = 28 ⇒ x = 2, so y = 4(2) − 5 = 3.Thus P = (2, 3).Distance from origin = √(2² + 3²) = √(4 + 9) = √13 ≈ 3.61.(Adding the coordinates gives the trap 5; forgetting the square root gives 13.)The answer is B.
text: The lines 2x + 3y = 13 and 4x − y = 5 intersect at point P. What is the distance from P to the origin?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Side vector AB = (5 − 1, 5 − 2) = (4, 3), with length √(16 + 9) = 5.The next side BC must be perpendicular to AB with the same length. Rotating (4, 3) by 90° gives either (−3, 4) or (3, −4).Going around ABCD, D = A + (perpendicular) and C = B + (perpendicular). For D to have a larger y than A we need the +y option, the vector (−3, 4).Then C = B + (−3, 4) = (5 − 3, 5 + 4) = (2, 9), and D = A + (−3, 4) = (−2, 6) (whose y = 6 > 2, as required).Check all sides equal 5 and diagonals equal 5√2 — it is a square.Sum of C's coordinates = 2 + 9 = 11. (The opposite orientation gives C = (8, 1), sum 9.)The answer is B.
text: A(1, 2) and B(5, 5) are two adjacent vertices of a square ABCD (labeled in order). The square is positioned so that vertex D has a larger y-coordinate than vertex A. What is the sum of the coordinates of vertex C?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Reflecting across y = x swaps the coordinates, so P′ = (2, 6).Triangle with vertices O(0, 0), P(6, 2), P′(2, 6). Using the shoelace formula:Area = ½|x_P · y_{P′} − x_{P′} · y_P| = ½|6·6 − 2·2| = ½|36 − 4| = ½(32) = 16.(Omitting the factor of ½ gives the trap 32.)The answer is B.
text: The point P(6, 2) is reflected across the line y = x to produce point P′. What is the area of the triangle formed by P, P′, and the origin O(0, 0)?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Original volume = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(12²)(24) = (1/3)π(144)(24) = 1152π cm³. The top cone is similar to the whole cone, and its volume is 1/8 of the original, so the linear scale factor is (1/8)^(1/3) = 1/2 (half the radius and half the height give 1/8 the volume). The small cone's volume = (1/8)(1152π) = 144π. The frustum is what remains: 1152π − 144π = 1008π cm³. (Choosing 144π forgets that the question asks for the frustum, not the slice; 1152π forgets to subtract at all.) The answer is C.
text: A solid right circular cone has base radius 12 cm and height 24 cm. A cut is made by a plane parallel to the base such that the small cone sliced off the top has a volume equal to one-eighth of the original cone's volume. Find the volume of the remaining frustum.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Volume of sphere = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π(9³) = (4/3)π(729) = 972π cm³. Volume of one cone = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(3²)(9) = (1/3)π(9)(9) = 27π cm³. Number of cones = 972π / 27π = 36. (A common error is to use πr²h = 81π for the cone, forgetting the 1/3, which gives 972/81 = 12.) The answer is D.
text: A solid metal sphere of radius 9 cm is melted down (no metal lost) and recast entirely into identical small solid cones, each having base radius 3 cm and height 9 cm. How many complete cones are produced?
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Cubes with exactly two painted faces are the ones lying along the edges of the big cube but not at the corners. A cube has 12 edges. Along each edge of length 10, the two end positions are corners (3 faces painted), leaving 10 − 2 = 8 edge-only cubes per edge. Total = 12 × 8 = 96. (Using 12 × 9 = 108 mistakenly subtracts only one corner; 384 = 6 × 8² is the count of exactly-one-face cubes.) The answer is C.
text: A large wooden cube of edge 10 cm is painted red on all six outer faces. It is then sliced by cuts parallel to its faces into 1000 unit cubes, each of edge 1 cm. How many of these unit cubes have paint on exactly two of their faces?
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: The cylinder contributes πr²h = π(3²)(8) = 72π mm³. The two hemispheres together form one complete sphere of radius 3: volume = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π(27) = 36π mm³. Total = 72π + 36π = 108π mm³. (Choosing 72π forgets the rounded ends; 90π counts only one hemisphere of 18π; 144π mistakenly adds a full sphere at each end.) The answer is A.
text: A medicine capsule is shaped like a cylinder with a hemisphere stuck on each flat end (a "capsule" solid). The common radius is 3 mm and the cylindrical middle section is 8 mm long. Find the total volume of the capsule.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Place A = (0,0), B = (14,0), C = (14,14), D = (0,14). The two quarter-circles are x²+y² ≤ 14² (centre A) and (x−14)²+(y−14)² ≤ 14² (centre C). The overlap of two quarter-circles whose centres are opposite corners of a square of side s (radius = s) has area (π/2 − 1)s²: by symmetry the lens is twice a circular segment, and combining the two quarter sectors and removing the jointly covered square reduces to (π/2 − 1)s². With s = 14: (π/2 − 1)(196) = (22/14 − 1)(196) = (11/7 − 1)(196) = (4/7)(196) = 112 cm². (154 is one whole quarter-circle; 196 is the square; 308 is two quarter-circles.) The answer is B.
text: ABCD is a square of side 14 cm with A, B, C, D taken in order around the square. Two quarter-circle arcs, each of radius 14 cm, are drawn inside the square: one centred at corner A, the other centred at the opposite corner C. Find the area of the region lying inside both quarter-circles. (Take π = 22/7.)
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Frustum volume = (1/3)πh(R² + Rr + r²) with R = 10, r = 4, h = 21. Compute R² + Rr + r² = 100 + 40 + 16 = 156. Volume = (1/3)(22/7)(21)(156) = (22/7)(7)(156) = 22 × 156 = 3432 cm³. (Dropping the cross term Rr gives (1/3)(22/7)(21)(116) = 2552; averaging the radii to a cylinder gives π(7²)(21) = 3234; treating it as the full big cylinder π(10²)(21) gives 6600.) The answer is E.
text: A bucket is in the shape of a frustum of a cone. Its circular top has radius 10 cm, its circular base has radius 4 cm, and its vertical depth is 21 cm. Find the capacity (volume) of the bucket. (Take π = 22/7.)
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Volume of sphere = (4/3)π(6³) = (4/3)π(216) = 288π cm³. The wire is a cylinder of radius = 0.4/2 = 0.2 cm, so its cross-sectional area = π(0.2)² = 0.04π cm². Setting volumes equal: 0.04π × L = 288π ⇒ L = 288 / 0.04 = 7200 cm. (Using the diameter 0.4 as the radius gives π(0.16)L = 288π ⇒ L = 1800, a classic radius-vs-diameter error.) The answer is A.
text: A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and drawn out into a single long cylindrical wire of uniform diameter 0.4 cm. Assuming no metal is lost, find the length of the wire.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Volume of water = cone volume = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(6²)(24) = (1/3)π(36)(24) = 288π cm³. In the cylinder, volume = πR²H = π(8²)H = 64πH. Setting 64πH = 288π gives H = 288/64 = 4.5 cm. (Forgetting the 1/3 in the cone volume gives 864π/64π = 13.5 cm.) The answer is B.
text: A conical vessel of base radius 6 cm and height 24 cm is completely filled with water. All of this water is then poured into an empty cylindrical jar of base radius 8 cm. Assuming nothing spills, find the height to which the water rises in the cylinder.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: The water forms a smaller cone similar to the full cone. At depth 12 cm the surface radius scales with height: r = 12 × (12/18) = 12 × (2/3) = 8 cm. Water volume = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(8²)(12) = (1/3)π(64)(12) = 256π cm³. (Using the full top radius 12 instead of the scaled 8 gives (1/3)π(144)(12) = 576π, and other distractors come from mis-scaling the radius.) The answer is D.
text: An inverted cone (vertex pointing straight down) has a top opening of radius 12 cm and a height of 18 cm. Water is poured in until its depth, measured vertically from the vertex, is 12 cm. Find the volume of the water.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Volume of hemisphere = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π(8³) = (2/3)π(512) = 1024π/3 cm³. Cone volume = (1/3)πR²h = (1/3)π(4²)h = (16/3)πh. Setting equal: (16/3)πh = (1024/3)π ⇒ 16h = 1024 ⇒ h = 64 cm. (Using a full sphere (4/3)πr³ instead of a hemisphere gives a value of 128 then mishalved; forgetting the cone's 1/3 gives 21.33.) The answer is E.
text: A solid metal hemisphere of radius 8 cm is melted down and recast, with no loss of metal, into a single solid right circular cone whose base radius is 4 cm. Find the height of the cone.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: We need 7^2024 mod 100. The powers of 7 mod 100 cycle with period 4: 7^1 = 07, 7^2 = 49, 7^3 = 343 -> 43, 7^4 = 2401 -> 01, then it repeats. So the cycle is (07, 49, 43, 01) for exponents congruent to (1, 2, 3, 0) mod 4. Compute 2024 mod 4 = 0, which corresponds to the 4th term in the cycle, i.e. 7^4 -> 01. Therefore the last two digits of 7^2024 are 01. (Common traps: 49 comes from misreading the cycle position, 43 from off-by-one.) The answer is A.
text: What are the last two digits of 7<sup>2024</sup>?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Since 17 is prime, Wilson's theorem gives 16! ≡ −1 (mod 17). Now 16! = 16 × 15!, and 16 ≡ −1 (mod 17), so (−1) × 15! ≡ −1 (mod 17). Multiplying both sides by −1 gives 15! ≡ 1 (mod 17). Therefore the remainder is 1. (Trap: 16 comes from stopping at 16! ≡ −1 and forgetting to strip off the factor 16; 0 wrongly assumes 17 divides 15!, but 17 is prime and larger than every factor in 15!.) The answer is B.
text: What is the remainder when 15! is divided by 17?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: We need the smallest positive N with N ≡ 2 (mod 3), N ≡ 3 (mod 5), N ≡ 5 (mod 7). From N ≡ 3 (mod 5), write N = 5k + 3. Substitute into N ≡ 5 (mod 7): 5k + 3 ≡ 5 (mod 7) -> 5k ≡ 2 (mod 7); since 5 × 3 = 15 ≡ 1, the inverse of 5 mod 7 is 3, so k ≡ 6 (mod 7), i.e. k = 7m + 6, giving N = 35m + 33. Now apply N ≡ 2 (mod 3): 35m + 33 ≡ 2m + 0 ≡ 2 (mod 3) -> m ≡ 1 (mod 3), so the smallest is m = 1, giving N = 35 + 33 = 68. Check: 68 = 3×22 + 2, 5×13 + 3, 7×9 + 5. (Trap: 173 is the next valid solution, 68 + 105; 53 satisfies only two of the three conditions.) The answer is D.
text: A pile of coins is counted three ways. When grouped in 3s, 2 coins are left over; in 5s, 3 are left over; and in 7s, 5 are left over. What is the smallest possible number of coins in the pile?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Units digits cycle with period 4. For 2: (2, 4, 8, 6) for exponents ≡ (1, 2, 3, 0) mod 4. Since 2024 ≡ 0 (mod 4), 2^2024 ends in 6. For 3: (3, 9, 7, 1) for exponents ≡ (1, 2, 3, 0) mod 4. Since 2024 ≡ 0 (mod 4), 3^2024 ends in 1. Sum of units digits: 6 + 1 = 7. Therefore the units digit of the total is 7. (Trap: treating exponent ≡ 0 as the 'zeroth' power gives 1 + 1 = 2; misaligning the cycle by one gives 8 + 7 = 5 or 4 + 9 = 3.) The answer is D.
text: What is the units digit of 2<sup>2024</sup> + 3<sup>2024</sup>?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Here 89 is prime. Fermat's little theorem states that for a prime p and any integer a not divisible by p, a^p ≡ a (mod p). With a = 2 and p = 89: 2^89 ≡ 2 (mod 89). Therefore the remainder is 2. (Trap: 1 comes from misremembering Fermat as a^p ≡ 1, which is actually a^(p−1) ≡ 1; that would apply to 2^88, not 2^89. 88 ≡ −1 is a sign-error distractor.) The answer is A.
text: What is the remainder when 2<sup>89</sup> is divided by 89?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Chinese Remainder Theorem: since 7 and 11 are coprime, the two conditions pin N uniquely mod 77. Scan numbers ≡ 5 (mod 11): 5, 16, 27, 38 — and 38 ≡ 3 (mod 7). ✓ So N ≡ 38 (mod 77). Every N satisfying the conditions (38, 115, 192, …) leaves the same remainder.
text: A positive integer N leaves remainder 3 when divided by 7 and remainder 5 when divided by 11. What remainder does N leave when divided by 77?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: First reduce the base: 32 ≡ 5 (mod 9). The multiplicative order of 5 mod 9 is 6 (5, 7, 8, 4, 2, 1), so we need the exponent E = 32^32 modulo 6. Mod 6: 32 ≡ 2, so E ≡ 2^32 (mod 6). Powers of 2 mod 6 cycle (2, 4, 2, 4, ...) for exponents 1, 2, 3, 4, ...; since 32 is even, 2^32 ≡ 4 (mod 6). So E ≡ 4 (mod 6), and 32^(32^32) ≡ 5^4 (mod 9). Now 5^4 = 625 = 9×69 + 4, so 5^4 ≡ 4 (mod 9). Therefore the remainder is 4. (Trap: reducing the exponent mod φ(9)=6 but mishandling 2^32 mod 6 as 2 gives 5^2 = 25 ≡ 7; ignoring the tower and using 5^2 also lands on 7.) The answer is C.
text: What is the remainder when 32<sup>(32<sup>32</sup>)</sup> is divided by 9?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Note 15 = 3 × 5. For any n ≥ 5, n! contains both factors 3 and 5, so n! is divisible by 15 and contributes remainder 0. Thus only 1! + 2! + 3! + 4! matters: 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33. Then 33 mod 15 = 3 (since 33 = 2×15 + 3). Therefore the remainder is 3. (Trap: 9 comes from including 5! whose remainder is actually 0; 0 wrongly assumes the whole sum is divisible by 15.) The answer is E.
text: What is the remainder when the sum 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 100! is divided by 15?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: The tower is 3^(3^3) = 3^27. We need 3^27 mod 100. The powers of 3 mod 100 repeat with period 20 (since φ(100) = 40 but the order of 3 is 20: 3^20 ≡ 1 mod 100). So 3^27 ≡ 3^7 (mod 100) because 27 = 20 + 7. Now 3^7 = 2187, and 2187 mod 100 = 87. Therefore the last two digits are 87. (Trap: reading the tower as (3^3)^3 = 3^9 gives 3^9 = 19683 -> 83, a wrong-association distractor; 27 comes from stopping at 3^3 = 27.) The answer is E.
text: What are the last two digits of 3<sup>(3<sup>3</sup>)</sup>?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: n^2 ≡ 1 (mod 24) means 24 | (n−1)(n+1). Checking residues mod 24, the solutions are exactly n ≡ 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 (mod 24) — that is, all n coprime to 24 (8 residues per block of 24), since for every odd n not divisible by 3, n^2 ≡ 1 mod 8 and mod 3, hence mod 24. So in each complete block of 24 consecutive integers there are 8 valid values, a density of 8/24 = 1/3. From 1 to 984 there are 41 complete blocks (41 × 24 = 984) giving 41 × 8 = 328 solutions. The remaining integers 985 to 1000 correspond to residues 1 through 16 mod 24; the valid residues in {1,...,16} are 1, 5, 7, 11, 13 — that is 5 more. Total = 328 + 5 = 333. (Trap: 334 is an off-by-one from miscounting the tail; 250 = 1000/4 over-counts by assuming all odd n work.) The answer is C.
text: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000 satisfy n<sup>2</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 24)?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: A divisor 2<sup>a</sup>3<sup>b</sup>5<sup>c</sup>7<sup>d</sup> (with 0 ≤ a ≤ 3, 0 ≤ b ≤ 4, 0 ≤ c ≤ 2, 0 ≤ d ≤ 1) is a perfect square exactly when every exponent is even. For 2: a may be 0 or 2 (2 choices). For 3: b may be 0, 2, or 4 (3 choices). For 5: c may be 0 or 2 (2 choices). For 7: only d = 0 is even and allowed (1 choice). Total = 2 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 12. (The trap 120 is the total number of divisors 4×5×3×2.) The answer is B.
text: Let N = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>4</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup> × 7. How many of the positive divisors of N are perfect squares?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Trailing zeros are governed by the number of factors of 5 (factors of 2 are far more plentiful). Count multiples of powers of 5 up to 250: ⌊250/5⌋ = 50, ⌊250/25⌋ = 10, ⌊250/125⌋ = 2, ⌊250/625⌋ = 0. Sum = 50 + 10 + 2 = 62. (The trap 50 stops after the first term.) The answer is D.
text: How many consecutive zeros are there at the end of 250! (the product of all integers from 1 to 250)?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: The number must contain 2<sup>2</sup> × 3 (to be divisible by 12) and have divisor count (e<sub>1</sub>+1)(e<sub>2</sub>+1)… = 18. Useful factorizations of 18: 6×3 and 3×3×2. The two-prime form 2<sup>a</sup>3<sup>b</sup> with (a,b) = (5,2) gives 2<sup>5</sup>3<sup>2</sup> = 288. The three-prime form with exponents (2,2,1) gives 2<sup>2</sup>·3<sup>2</sup>·5 = 180, which is divisible by 12 and has (3)(3)(2) = 18 divisors. Checking smaller multiples of 12 (120 has 16 divisors, 144 has 15 divisors) shows none below 180 works. So the smallest is 180. The answer is C.
text: What is the smallest positive integer that is divisible by 12 and has exactly 18 positive divisors?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Write 12 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3, so 12<sup>k</sup> = 2<sup>2k</sup> × 3<sup>k</sup>. Exponent of 2 in 50!: ⌊50/2⌋+⌊50/4⌋+⌊50/8⌋+⌊50/16⌋+⌊50/32⌋ = 25+12+6+3+1 = 47. Exponent of 3: ⌊50/3⌋+⌊50/9⌋+⌊50/27⌋ = 16+5+1 = 22. We need 2k ≤ 47 (so k ≤ 23) and k ≤ 22. The binding constraint is k ≤ 22. (The trap 23 forgets that 12 also needs the prime 3.) The answer is E.
text: What is the largest integer k such that 12<sup>k</sup> divides 50! exactly (i.e., 12<sup>k</sup> is a factor of 50!)?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Factor: 360 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5. The sum-of-divisors function is multiplicative: σ(360) = (1+2+4+8)(1+3+9)(1+5) = 15 × 13 × 6. Compute 15 × 13 = 195, then 195 × 6 = 1170. (The trap 24 is the number of divisors, 4×3×2.) The answer is A.
text: What is the sum of all the positive divisors of 360?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Write the numbers as 12m and 12n where gcd(m, n) = 1. Then LCM = 12·m·n = 72, so m·n = 6. The coprime ordered factorizations of 6 are (1, 6) and (2, 3). The pair (1, 6) gives numbers (12, 72); the pair (2, 3) gives (24, 36). As unordered pairs, that is 2 distinct pairs. (The trap 4 counts ordered pairs.) The answer is B.
text: Two positive integers have an HCF (greatest common divisor) of 12 and an LCM of 72. How many distinct unordered pairs of such integers are possible?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: For any two positive integers, HCF × LCM = product. So HCF = 2160 ÷ 360 = 6. Write the numbers as 6a and 6b with gcd(a, b) = 1; then LCM = 6·a·b = 360, giving a·b = 60. The coprime unordered factorizations of 60 = 2<sup>2</sup>·3·5 send each prime-power block (4, 3, 5) entirely to one side, giving 4 unordered pairs: {1,60}, {3,20}, {4,15}, {5,12}. These map to (6, 360), (18, 120), (24, 90), (30, 72). So there are 4 pairs. The answer is D.
text: The product of two positive integers is 2160 and their LCM is 360. How many distinct unordered pairs of integers satisfy both conditions?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Trailing zeros in base 6 count the highest power of 6 = 2 × 3 dividing 60!, which is min(exponent of 2, exponent of 3). Exponent of 2 in 60!: ⌊60/2⌋+⌊60/4⌋+⌊60/8⌋+⌊60/16⌋+⌊60/32⌋ = 30+15+7+3+1 = 56. Exponent of 3: ⌊60/3⌋+⌊60/9⌋+⌊60/27⌋ = 20+6+2 = 28. So min(56, 28) = 28. (The trap 56 mistakenly uses the power of 2.) The answer is A.
text: If 60! (the product of all integers from 1 to 60) is written out in base 6, how many consecutive zeros appear at its right-hand end?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Base 12 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3, so each trailing zero needs two factors of 2 together with one factor of 3. Exponent of 2 in 90!: ⌊90/2⌋+⌊90/4⌋+⌊90/8⌋+⌊90/16⌋+⌊90/32⌋+⌊90/64⌋ = 45+22+11+5+2+1 = 86. Exponent of 3: ⌊90/3⌋+⌊90/9⌋+⌊90/27⌋+⌊90/81⌋ = 30+10+3+1 = 44. The number of 12s = min(⌊86/2⌋, 44) = min(43, 44) = 43. (The trap 44 forgets that each 12 needs two 2's.) The answer is C.
text: If 90! (the product of all integers from 1 to 90) is written in base 12, how many consecutive zeros appear at its right-hand end?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: First find the LCM of 1 through 12: the needed prime powers are 2<sup>3</sup> (from 8), 3<sup>2</sup> (from 9), 5, 7, 11, so LCM = 2<sup>3</sup>·3<sup>2</sup>·5·7·11 = 27720. A perfect square needs every prime exponent even, so round each odd exponent up: 2<sup>3</sup>→2<sup>4</sup>, 3<sup>2</sup> stays, 5→5<sup>2</sup>, 7→7<sup>2</sup>, 11→11<sup>2</sup>. The smallest such square = 2<sup>4</sup>·3<sup>2</sup>·5<sup>2</sup>·7<sup>2</sup>·11<sup>2</sup> = (2<sup>2</sup>·3·5·7·11)<sup>2</sup> = 4620<sup>2</sup> = 21344400. (The trap 27720 is the LCM itself, not a perfect square.) The answer is E.
text: What is the smallest perfect square that is divisible by every integer from 1 to 12 inclusive?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: First seat the 5 ordinary delegates around the table: circular arrangements of 5 = (5−1)! = 24. These 5 people create 5 gaps between consecutive delegates. The chair, vice-chair, and secretary must each go into a distinct gap so that no two are adjacent: choose and order 3 of the 5 gaps = P(5,3) = 5×4×3 = 60. Total = 24 × 60 = 1440. (Common error: using 7! and naive subtraction, or treating gaps as 5! ÷ something.) The answer is C.
text: Eight delegates are to be seated around a circular conference table (seats distinguished only by who sits next to whom). Three of them — the chair, the vice-chair, and the secretary — insist that no two of these three sit next to each other. In how many distinct ways can all eight delegates be seated?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: This counts surjective (onto) functions from 10 books to 3 shelves. By inclusion-exclusion: 3<sup>10</sup> − C(3,1)·2<sup>10</sup> + C(3,2)·1<sup>10</sup> = 59049 − 3·1024 + 3·1 = 59049 − 3072 + 3 = 55980. (Common error: forgetting to subtract the empty-shelf cases gives 3<sup>10</sup> = 59049, the distractor B.) The answer is A.
text: A librarian must place 10 distinct books onto 3 distinguishable shelves so that no shelf is left empty. Only which books sit on which shelf matters (the left-to-right order on a shelf is irrelevant). In how many ways can this be done?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Let each child get x<sub>i</sub> with 2 ≤ x<sub>i</sub> ≤ 8 and ∑x<sub>i</sub> = 20. Substitute y<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> − 2, so 0 ≤ y<sub>i</sub> ≤ 6 and ∑y<sub>i</sub> = 12. Unrestricted nonnegative solutions: C(12+3, 3) = C(15,3) = 455. Subtract cases where some y<sub>i</sub> ≥ 7: pick the child (4 ways), set y' = y − 7, then ∑ = 5, giving C(5+3,3) = C(8,3) = 56 each, so 4·56 = 224. Two children both ≥ 7 would need ∑ ≥ 14 > 12, impossible. Total = 455 − 224 = 231. (Common error: forgetting the upper-bound subtraction gives 455, distractor A.) The answer is C.
text: Twenty identical chocolates are to be distributed among 4 children so that each child receives at least 2 and at most 8 chocolates. In how many ways can this be done?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: "Exactly one card in its original box" means exactly one fixed point. Choose which single card stays fixed: C(6,1) = 6 ways. The remaining 5 cards must form a derangement of 5 (none in its original box): D(5) = 44. Total = 6 × 44 = 264. (Recall D(5) = 5!(1 − 1 + 1/2 − 1/6 + 1/24 − 1/120) = 44. Common error: using D(4)=9 with C(6,1) gives 54, or miscounting which set is deranged; 265 is the total derangements D(6), distractor C.) The answer is E.
text: Six gift boxes labeled 1 through 6 each contain a unique card numbered 1 through 6 (initially card k in box k). The cards are taken out and redistributed back into the six boxes, one card per box. In how many of these redistributions does exactly one card return to its original box?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: BALLOON has letters B, A, L, L, O, O, N. Total distinct arrangements = 7! ÷ (2!·2!) = 5040 ÷ 4 = 1260. Let X = arrangements with the L's together (glue LL into one block): 6! ÷ 2! = 360. Let Y = arrangements with the O's together: 6! ÷ 2! = 360. Both together (LL block and OO block): 5! = 120. By inclusion-exclusion, arrangements with L's apart AND O's apart = 1260 − 360 − 360 + 120 = 660. (Common error: 1260 − 360 − 360 = 540 forgets to add back the overlap, distractor A.) The answer is D.
text: How many distinct arrangements of all 7 letters of the word BALLOON are there in which the two L's are NOT adjacent and the two O's are also NOT adjacent?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Total people = 12. Need at least 2 women and at least 1 man, so the number of women can be 2, 3, or 4 (5 women would leave no man). Women = 2: C(5,2)·C(7,3) = 10·35 = 350. Women = 3: C(5,3)·C(7,2) = 10·21 = 210. Women = 4: C(5,4)·C(7,1) = 5·7 = 35. Total = 350 + 210 + 35 = 595. (Common error: including women = 5 case C(5,5)·C(7,0)=1 violates the man condition; or computing 'at least 2 women' as C(12,5) − (0 or 1 woman) = 792 − ... and forgetting the man constraint.) The answer is B.
text: A committee of 5 is to be chosen from 7 men and 5 women. The committee must contain at least 2 women and at least 1 man. How many such committees are possible?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: If the digits strictly increase left to right, each choice of 5 distinct digits corresponds to exactly one valid number (just write them in increasing order). The digit 0 can never appear, because in any strictly increasing number 0 would have to be the leftmost digit, which is not allowed for a 5-digit number (and 0 cannot follow a larger digit). So we choose 5 distinct digits from {1,2,...,9}: C(9,5) = 126. (Common error: using digits 0–9 gives C(10,5)=252, distractor A; multiplying by 5! to 'order' them double-counts.) The answer is B.
text: How many 5-digit positive integers have all five of their digits in strictly increasing order from left to right (for example, 13579)?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Place the rings one at a time. Think of arranging all 6 rings in a sequence and inserting 3 'finger dividers'. Equivalently, the number of ways = (number of fingers + number of rings − 1)! ÷ (number of fingers − 1)! = (4+6−1)! ÷ (4−1)! = 9! ÷ 3! = 362880 ÷ 6 = 60480. Constructively: the first ring has 4 finger-positions; the second has 5 possible slots (4 fingers, and it can go above/below the placed ring), the third 6, ... giving 4·5·6·7·8·9 = 60480. (Common error: 4<sup>6</sup> = 4096 ignores the order on each finger, distractor A; 6! = 720 ignores finger choice.) The answer is C.
text: Six distinct rings are to be worn on the 4 fingers of one hand (the thumb is not used). Any finger may hold any number of rings (including none), and on each finger the vertical order of the rings is significant. In how many ways can the 6 rings be arranged on the 4 fingers?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Total monotone (east/north) paths from (0,0) to (4,4) require 4 easts and 4 norths in some order: C(8,4) = 70. Paths passing through (2,2): from (0,0) to (2,2) it is C(4,2) = 6, and from (2,2) to (4,4) it is C(4,2) = 6, giving 6×6 = 36. Routes avoiding (2,2) = 70 − 36 = 34. (Common error: reporting the blocked count 36, distractor C, or forgetting to subtract and giving 70.) The answer is B.
text: On a square street grid, a courier starts at the southwest corner (0,0) and must reach the northeast corner (4,4), moving only one block east or one block north at each step. Due to construction, the central intersection at (2,2) is closed and cannot be used. How many distinct routes can the courier take?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Treat each couple as a single block, so there are 4 blocks to arrange in a row: 4! = 24 ways. Within each block the two partners can swap seats: 2 ways per couple, and there are 4 couples, giving 2<sup>4</sup> = 16. Total = 24 × 16 = 384. (Common error: 4! = 24 alone forgets the internal swaps; 8! = 40320 ignores the togetherness constraint, distractor A; using 2·4 = 8 instead of 2<sup>4</sup> gives 192.) The answer is B.
text: Four married couples (8 people total) are to be seated in a single row of 8 chairs so that the two members of every couple sit next to each other. In how many distinct seating arrangements is this possible?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Use Bayes' theorem. P(defective and B) = 0.40 × 0.06 = 0.024. P(defective and A) = 0.60 × 0.03 = 0.018. Total P(defective) = 0.024 + 0.018 = 0.042. So P(B | defective) = 0.024 / 0.042 = 24/42 = 4/7. (The trap 3/7 is P(A | defective), the complement of the requested value.) The answer is A.
text: A small electronics plant has two assembly lines. Line A produces 60% of all units, of which 3% are defective; Line B produces the remaining 40%, of which 6% are defective. A finished unit is pulled from the combined output and found to be defective. What is the probability that it came from Line B?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Choose 2 of the 5 red: C(5,2) = 10. Choose 1 of the 7 non-red: C(7,1) = 7. Favorable outcomes = 10 × 7 = 70. Total ways to choose any 3 of 12: C(12,3) = 220. Probability = 70/220 = 7/22. The answer is B.
text: An urn contains 5 red, 4 blue, and 3 green marbles (12 total). Three marbles are drawn at once, without replacement. What is the probability that exactly 2 of the 3 drawn are red?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Each face has probability 1/6. The even outcomes pay their face value, contributing 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 in winnings. The odd outcomes (1, 3, 5) each lose $2, contributing 3 × (−2) = −6. Expected value = (12 − 6)/6 = 6/6 = $1. The answer is C.
text: A single fair six-sided die is rolled once. If the result is an even number, you win that many dollars (so a 4 wins $4). If the result is odd, you lose $2 regardless of the value. What is your expected net gain from one roll?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Condition on the event B = 'at least one heart'. P(no heart) = C(39,2)/C(52,2) = 741/1326, so P(at least one heart) = 1 − 741/1326 = 585/1326. The only way to have two cards of the same suit while including a heart is for BOTH cards to be hearts: C(13,2) = 78 such pairs. So P(same suit and at least one heart) = 78/1326. The conditional probability = 78/585 = 2/15. (The distractor 4/17 is the unconditional P(same suit); 1/17 = P(both hearts) appears in the work.) The answer is D.
text: Two cards are drawn together (without replacement) from a standard 52-card deck. Given that at least one of the two cards is a heart, what is the probability that both cards belong to the same suit?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: P(has and positive) = 0.02 × 0.90 = 0.018. P(healthy and positive) = 0.98 × 0.05 = 0.049. P(positive) = 0.018 + 0.049 = 0.067. By Bayes, P(has | positive) = 0.018/0.067 = 18/67 ≈ 0.269. (The trap 9/10 mistakes sensitivity for the answer; 18/100 forgets to divide by the total positive rate.) The answer is E.
text: A condition is present in 2% of a population. A screening test detects it correctly in 90% of people who have it (sensitivity), and gives a false positive in 5% of people who do not have it. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability the person actually has the condition?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: The first two draws must be black and the third white: (6/10) × (5/9) × (4/8). Numerator = 6 × 5 × 4 = 120; denominator = 10 × 9 × 8 = 720. So 120/720 = 1/6. (The distractor 1/30 corresponds to a with-replacement style computation or drops a factor.) The answer is A.
text: A bag holds 4 white chips and 6 black chips. Chips are drawn one at a time, without replacement, and you stop as soon as a white chip appears. What is the probability that the first white chip appears on exactly the third draw?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Condition on the colour of the transferred ball. P(red moved) = 3/5; then Y holds 2 red of 6, giving P(red drawn) = 2/6 = 1/3, contribution (3/5)(1/3) = 1/5. P(green moved) = 2/5; then Y holds 1 red of 6, P(red drawn) = 1/6, contribution (2/5)(1/6) = 1/15. Total = 1/5 + 1/15 = 3/15 + 1/15 = 4/15. (The trap 2/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 mishandles the green-transfer case.) The answer is D.
text: Bag X contains 3 red and 2 green balls. Bag Y contains 1 red and 4 green balls. One ball is chosen at random from Bag X and moved into Bag Y. Then one ball is drawn at random from Bag Y. What is the probability that the ball drawn from Bag Y is red?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: The maximum equals k exactly when one ball is k and the other two are chosen from {1,...,k−1}: P(max = k) = C(k−1, 2)/C(10,3), valid for k = 3 to 10, with C(10,3) = 120. Then E[max] = Σ k·C(k−1,2)/120 = (3·1 + 4·3 + 5·6 + 6·10 + 7·15 + 8·21 + 9·28 + 10·36)/120 = (3+12+30+60+105+168+252+360)/120 = 990/120 = 33/4 = 8.25. This matches the general formula E[max] = (n+1)m/(m+1) = 11·3/4. (The trap 11/2 is the mean of a single draw, not the max of three.) The answer is C.
text: A box contains 10 balls numbered 1 through 10. Three balls are drawn at once, without replacement. What is the expected value of the largest number among the three drawn?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: First find the total number of students using inclusion-exclusion. Total = 70 + 65 + 55 − 40 − 30 − 25 + 15 = 190 − 95 + 15 = 110.The 'all three' region holds 15. The three 'exactly two' regions are each a pairwise overlap minus the triple overlap: (40 − 15) + (30 − 15) + (25 − 15) = 25 + 15 + 10 = 50.Exactly one = Total − (exactly two) − (all three) = 110 − 50 − 15 = 45.(Check via the direct formula: A + B + C − 2(sum of pairwise) + 3(triple) = 190 − 2(95) + 3(15) = 190 − 190 + 45 = 45.) The distractor 95 comes from forgetting to add back the triple overlap when finding the total. The answer is C.
text: In a school enrichment program, every one of a group of students signed up for at least one of three workshops: Algebra, Geometry, or Calculus.• 70 chose Algebra, 65 chose Geometry, 55 chose Calculus.• 40 chose both Algebra and Geometry, 30 chose both Geometry and Calculus, 25 chose both Algebra and Calculus.• 15 chose all three workshops.How many students chose exactly one workshop?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: The overlap is minimized when the union of the two sets is as large as possible. The union can be at most the universe of 800 people. So the smallest the intersection can be is (smartphone owners) + (laptop owners) − (universe) = 540 + 420 − 800 = 960 − 800 = 160.If the overlap were any smaller, the union would exceed 800, which is impossible. So the minimum is 160. The distractor 420 is the maximum overlap (the smaller set entirely inside the larger), and 260 is the spread between max and min. The answer is A.
text: Among 800 commuters surveyed, 540 own a smartphone and 420 own a laptop. A commuter may own both, one, or neither device.What is the minimum possible number of commuters who own both a smartphone and a laptop?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: The percentage with at least one of the two = 62% + 48% − 35% = 110% − 35% = 75%. So the percentage with neither = 100% − 75% = 25%.Number of households = 25% of 5,000 = 0.25 × 5,000 = 1,250.The distractor 1,750 = 35% of 5,000 (mistaking 'both' for 'neither'), and 2,750 = 55% of 5,000 (forgetting to subtract the overlap properly). The answer is E.
text: In a town with 5,000 households, 62% subscribe to a streaming service and 48% own a gaming console. It is known that 35% of all households have both.How many households have neither a streaming subscription nor a gaming console?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: Work with the employees who did NOT complete each training: 15 missed Safety, 25 missed Ethics, 35 missed Compliance. At most 15 + 25 + 35 = 75 distinct employees could have missed at least one training.Therefore at least 100 − 75 = 25 employees missed none of them, i.e., completed all three. This minimum is achievable when the three 'missed' groups are entirely disjoint.Equivalently, minimum all-three = 85 + 75 + 65 − 2(100) = 225 − 200 = 25. The distractor 65 is the smallest single set (the MAXIMUM possible all-three, not the minimum), and 125 comes from using a + b + c − N instead of a + b + c − 2N. The answer is C.
text: A company has 100 employees. By year-end, 85 had completed Safety training, 75 had completed Ethics training, and 65 had completed Compliance training.What is the minimum possible number of employees who completed all three trainings?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: The number of people using at least one app = 200 − 30 = 170.This union splits into three disjoint groups: those using exactly one, those using exactly two, and those using all three. So:exactly one = 170 − (exactly two) − (all three) = 170 − 20 − 12 = 138.The distractor 168 comes from forgetting the 30 'none' people and using 200 as the union (200 − 20 − 12), and 170 is the entire union before removing the multi-app users. The answer is D.
text: A survey of 200 people asked which of three news apps they use: X, Y, or Z.• 30 people use none of the three apps.• Exactly 20 people use exactly two of the apps.• 12 people use all three apps.How many people use exactly one of the apps?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: To minimize the all-three overlap, spread the solvers as much as possible. The minimum forced overlap of three sets in a universe of N is max(0, a + b + c − 2N).Here a + b + c = 38 + 35 + 28 = 101, and 2N = 100. So minimum all-three = 101 − 100 = 1.Intuition via complements: 12 missed Puzzle 1, 15 missed Puzzle 2, 22 missed Puzzle 3; that is at most 12 + 15 + 22 = 49 contestants who failed at least one puzzle. Since there are 50 contestants, at least 50 − 49 = 1 contestant solved all three. The distractor 0 ignores the forced overlap, 28 is the maximum (not minimum) possible all-three, and 51 comes from using a + b + c − N. The answer is B.
text: In a competition, 50 contestants each attempted three puzzles. Exactly 38 solved Puzzle 1, exactly 35 solved Puzzle 2, and exactly 28 solved Puzzle 3.What is the minimum possible number of contestants who solved all three puzzles?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: Let the meeting occur after time t (both trains run for the same time t until they meet). Let the faster speed be 3v and the slower 2v. Before meeting, the faster covers 3v·t and the slower covers 2v·t. After meeting, the faster must cover the slower train's pre-meeting distance (2v·t) at speed 3v, so its remaining time is t₁ = 2v·t / 3v = (2/3)t. The slower must cover the faster's pre-meeting distance (3v·t) at speed 2v, so t₂ = 3v·t / 2v = (3/2)t. Multiplying: t₁·t₂ = (2/3)t × (3/2)t = t², i.e. t = √(t₁·t₂), the standard meeting relation. We are given t₁ = 3 h 20 min = 10/3 h. From t₁ = (2/3)t we get t = (3/2)(10/3) = 5 h. Then t₂ = (3/2)t = (3/2)(5) = 7.5 h. (Reporting the faster train's 10/3 h as if it were the slower's is the trap, option A.) The answer is C.
text: Two trains start at the same instant from stations P and Q, which are 600 km apart, and travel toward each other at constant speeds in the ratio 3 : 2 (the faster one leaves from P). They meet at some point and each continues, without stopping, to the other's starting station. After the moment they meet, the faster train takes exactly 3 hours 20 minutes to reach station Q. How long, after the meeting, does the slower train take to reach station P?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Anaya's rate = 1/24 per day. Together rate = 1/15, so Bilal = 1/15 − 1/24 = (8−5)/120 = 3/120 = 1/40. In 5 days together they finish 5×(1/15) = 1/3, leaving 2/3. Anaya's reduced rate = (1/24)×0.8 = (1/24)×(4/5) = 1/30 per day. Time = (2/3) ÷ (1/30) = (2/3)×30 = 20 days. (Forgetting the 20% drop gives (2/3)÷(1/24) = 16 days, a trap.) The answer is D.
text: Working together, Anaya and Bilal can finish a job in 15 days; Anaya alone would take 24 days. They work together for 5 days, after which Bilal leaves. From that point Anaya's efficiency drops by 20% (fatigue) for the remainder of the job. How many more days does Anaya need to finish the job?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: After each draw-and-replace, the milk fraction is multiplied by (80 − drawn)/80. Start 80 L. Step 1: 80×(64/80) = 64. Step 2: 64×(60/80) = 64×0.75 = 48. Step 3: 48×(72/80) = 48×0.9 = 43.2 L. (Subtracting the drawn amounts directly, 80−(16+20+8)=36, is the classic error.) The answer is C.
text: A vessel holds 80 litres of pure milk. The following is done three times in sequence: a quantity is drawn off and replaced with the SAME quantity of water (the mixture is stirred uniformly each time). The amounts drawn in the three steps are 16 L, then 20 L, then 8 L. How much pure milk remains in the vessel at the end?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Net price after discounts = 2500×0.90×0.80 = 2500×0.72 = ₹1800. The 8% GST (=₹144) is collected for the government, so it is NOT store revenue. Store's profit = net selling price − cost = 1800 − 1500 = ₹300. (Adding GST into profit gives 1800×1.08−1500 = ₹444; treating the two discounts as a single 30% gives 1750−1500 = ₹250 — both traps.) The answer is B.
text: A jacket is marked at ₹2500. The store offers two successive discounts of 10% and 20% on the marked price. At the till an 8% GST is added on the net (post-discount) price, which the customer pays. The store's cost price for the jacket is ₹1500, and the GST collected is passed on in full to the government. What is the store's profit on this sale?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Capital-months (in thousands): Anil = 50×4 (months 1–4) + 40×8 (months 5–12) = 200 + 320 = 520. Bina (months 3–12): 60 for months 3–8 (6 months) then 40 for months 9–12 (4 months) = 60×6 + 40×4 = 360 + 160 = 520. Chetan (months 6–12, 7 months): 80×7 = 560. Total = 520 + 520 + 560 = 1600. Ratio 520 : 520 : 560 = 13 : 13 : 14, sum 40. Profit ₹40,000 ÷ 40 = ₹1000 per part. Anil = 13×1000 = ₹13,000; Chetan = 14×1000 = ₹14,000. Difference = 14,000 − 13,000 = ₹1,000. The answer is B.
text: Three people run a business for one year (12 months). Anil starts with ₹50,000 and at the start of month 5 withdraws ₹10,000. Bina joins at the start of month 3 with ₹60,000 and withdraws ₹20,000 at the start of month 9. Chetan joins at the start of month 6 with ₹80,000. The year-end profit is ₹40,000, shared in proportion to each person's capital-months. By how much does Chetan's share exceed Anil's share?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Downstream speed = 36/2 = 18 km/h. Upstream speed = 24/4 = 6 km/h. Still-water speed = (downstream + upstream)/2 = (18 + 6)/2 = 12 km/h (and current = (18−6)/2 = 6 km/h). Time for 60 km in still water = 60/12 = 5 hours. (Using downstream speed gives 60/18 = 3⅓ h; using current speed gives 60/6 = 10 h — both traps.) The answer is C.
text: A motorboat covers 36 km downstream in 2 hours and 24 km upstream in 4 hours, the river current being constant. At the boat's speed in still water, how long would it take to travel 60 km across a still lake?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Rates per hour: A = 1/10, B = 1/15, leak = 1/30 (draining). First 3 hours both inlets: (1/10 + 1/15)×3 = (3/30 + 2/30)×3 = (5/30)×3 = 1/2 filled. Remaining = 1/2. After A is shut, net rate = B − leak = 1/15 − 1/30 = 2/30 − 1/30 = 1/30 per hour. Time for remaining half = (1/2) ÷ (1/30) = 15 hours. Total = 3 + 15 = 18 hours. (Ignoring the leak gives (1/2)÷(1/15)=7.5, total 10.5 h, a trap.) The answer is D.
text: An empty tank is connected to inlet pipe A (fills the tank in 10 hours) and inlet pipe B (fills it in 15 hours). Both pipes are opened together. After exactly 3 hours, pipe A is shut and at that same moment a leak develops that, on its own, would empty a full tank in 30 hours. Pipe B and the leak then continue until the tank is full. What is the TOTAL time taken to fill the tank from empty?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Let x kg of X and y kg of Y. Then x + y = 50. Gold contributed: (3/5)x + (1/5)y. Target gold = (2/5)×50 = 20 kg. So (3/5)x + (1/5)y = 20, i.e. 3x + y = 100. Subtract x + y = 50: 2x = 50, x = 25 kg (and y = 25 kg). Check: gold = (3/5)(25) + (1/5)(25) = 15 + 5 = 20 kg, copper = 30 kg, ratio 2 : 3. The answer is C.
