text: Alloy X contains gold and copper in the ratio 3 : 2; alloy Y contains gold and copper in the ratio 1 : 4. The two alloys are melted together to form exactly 50 kg of a new alloy in which gold and copper are in the ratio 2 : 3. How many kilograms of alloy X are used?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Let cost be ₹1 per gram. The customer pays for 1000 g at the marked-and-discounted price: selling price = 1000×1.50×0.90 = ₹1350. But the grocer actually gives only 900 g, whose cost to him is 900×₹1 = ₹900. Profit = 1350 − 900 = ₹450 on a cost of ₹900, so profit % = 450/900 = 50%. (Ignoring the false weight gives 1.5×0.9 = 1.35 → 35%, the trap.) The answer is D.
text: A dishonest grocer marks his price 50% above cost and then gives the buyer a 10% discount on the marked price. On top of this, he cheats on weight, handing over only 900 grams when the customer pays for 1 kilogram. What is his overall percentage profit?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Running in opposite directions, their relative speed = 5 + 3 = 8 m/s. They meet each time their combined distance equals one lap, 600 m, i.e. every 600/8 = 75 s. The 4th meeting occurs at 4×75 = 300 s. (Using same-direction relative speed 5−3 = 2 m/s gives 600/2 = 300 s per meeting → 1200 s for the 4th — a trap.) The answer is C.
text: On a circular track 600 m long, Anu and Vikram start together from the same point and run in opposite directions at constant speeds of 5 m/s and 3 m/s respectively. After how many seconds will they meet for the 4th time (anywhere on the track)?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Successive multipliers: 1.20, then 0.75, then 1.60. Combined factor = 1.20×0.75×1.60 = 0.90×1.60 = 1.44. So original × 1.44 = 144, giving original = 144/1.44 = 100. (Adding the percentages, +20 −25 +60 = +55%, and dividing 144/1.55 ≈ 92.9 is the classic error.) The answer is B.
text: A certain number is first increased by 20%, the result is then decreased by 25%, and that result is finally increased by 60%. The final value is 144. What was the original number?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Rates per day: A = 1/12, B = 1/15, C = 1/20. Combined rate of all three = 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/20 = (5 + 4 + 3)/60 = 12/60 = 1/5. Let the total duration be T days; Aarav and Bhavna work all T days, Chirag works T − 4 days. Total work = (all three for T) − (Chirag's missing 4 days) = (1/5)T − (1/20)(4) = (1/5)T − 1/5 = 1. So (1/5)T = 1 + 1/5 = 6/5, giving T = 6 days. Chirag's work = (1/20)×(6 − 4) = (1/20)×2 = 1/10 of the job. Since wages are proportional to work done and total work = 1, Chirag's wage = (1/10)×9000 = ₹900. (Check: Aarav does (1/12)×6 = 1/2, Bhavna (1/15)×6 = 2/5, Chirag 1/10; sum = 1/2 + 2/5 + 1/10 = 1.) The answer is C.
text: Aarav, Bhavna and Chirag can individually finish a job in 12, 15 and 20 days respectively. They begin working together, but Chirag leaves exactly 4 days before the work is completed; Aarav and Bhavna continue to the end. The total wages of ₹9,000 are split in proportion to the actual amount of work each person does. What is Chirag's wage?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: For a cubic t³ − 9t² + 23t − 15 = 0 with roots a, b, c, Vieta's formulas give a + b + c = 9, ab + bc + ca = 23, and abc = 15. The required sum of reciprocals is (1/a) + (1/b) + (1/c) = (bc + ac + ab)/(abc) = 23/15. (You never even need to find the actual roots, which happen to be 1, 3, and 5.) The answer is B.
text: Three real numbers a, b, and c are the roots of the cubic equation t³ − 9t² + 23t − 15 = 0. What is the value of (1/a) + (1/b) + (1/c)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Let s = x + 1/x = 4. Build the power sums using the recurrence pₙ = s·pₙ₋₁ − pₙ₋₂, where pₙ = xⁿ + 1/xⁿ. We have p₁ = 4. Then x² + 1/x² = s² − 2 = 14. Next x³ + 1/x³ = s·14 − s = 56 − 4 = 52. Then x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = 14² − 2 = 194. Finally x⁵ + 1/x⁵ = s·194 − (x³ + 1/x³) = 4·194 − 52 = 776 − 52 = 724. (Stopping at 4·194 = 776 forgets to subtract the lower term.) The answer is D.
text: A real number x satisfies x + (1/x) = 4. What is the value of x<sup>5</sup> + (1/x<sup>5</sup>)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: We need 5x + 8y = 149 with x, y both positive integers. For x to be a positive integer, 149 − 8y must be a positive multiple of 5, i.e. 8y ≡ 149 (mod 5) → 3y ≡ 4 (mod 5) → y ≡ 3 (mod 5). So y = 3, 8, 13, 18, giving x = 25, 17, 9, 1, and pairs (25,3), (17,8), (9,13), (1,18). Their sums are 28, 25, 22, 19. The greatest is x + y = 28. (Note x + y grows when y is smallest, since x carries the larger coefficient weight per unit.) The answer is D.
text: Positive integers x and y satisfy 5x + 8y = 149. Over all such pairs, what is the greatest possible value of x + y?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: From (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y²: 49 = 29 + 2xy, so 2xy = 20 and xy = 10. Then x⁴ + y⁴ = (x² + y²)² − 2(xy)² = 29² − 2·10² = 841 − 200 = 641. (Using just (x²+y²)² = 841 forgets the correction term; subtracting only 2xy = 20 gives the wrong 741.) The answer is B.
text: Two real numbers x and y satisfy x + y = 7 and x² + y² = 29. What is the value of x⁴ + y⁴?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Let the numerator be n; then the denominator is n + 7, so the fraction is n/(n + 7). Subtracting 4 from each: (n − 4)/(n + 3) = 2/3. Cross-multiplying: 3(n − 4) = 2(n + 3) → 3n − 12 = 2n + 6 → n = 18. So the original fraction is 18/(18 + 7) = 18/25. (Check: (18−4)/(25−4) = 14/21 = 2/3. Choice C is that reduced check value, not the original; choice D inverts it.) The answer is A.
text: In a certain fraction, the denominator is 7 more than the numerator. If 4 is subtracted from both the numerator and the denominator, the resulting fraction equals 2/3. What is the original fraction?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: If the roots are positive integers p and q, then p + q = 13 and pq = k. The unordered pairs of positive integers summing to 13 are (1,12), (2,11), (3,10), (4,9), (5,8), (6,7), giving k = 12, 22, 30, 36, 40, 42. Summing these distinct k-values: 12 + 22 + 30 + 36 + 40 + 42 = 182. (Counting ordered pairs would double-count to 364; 42 is only the largest single value.) The answer is C.
text: The equation x² − 13x + k = 0 has two roots that are both positive integers. What is the sum of all possible values of k?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: From x² + 1/x² = 7 we get (x − 1/x)² = x² − 2 + 1/x² = 7 − 2 = 5, so x − 1/x = √5 (positive since x > 1). Now use x³ − 1/x³ = (x − 1/x)(x² + 1 + 1/x²) = √5 · (7 + 1) = 8√5. (Choice A, 18, is x³ + 1/x³; choice D, 3√5, is x² − 1/x².) The answer is C.
text: A real number x > 1 satisfies x² + (1/x²) = 7. What is the value of x³ − (1/x³)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Let n be the number of nickels. Then dimes = n + 3 and quarters = 2n. Total value in cents: 5n + 10(n + 3) + 25(2n) = 420 → 5n + 10n + 30 + 50n = 420 → 65n = 390 → n = 6. So nickels = 6, dimes = 9, quarters = 12, giving a total of 6 + 9 + 12 = 27 coins. (Check value: 30 + 90 + 300 = 420 cents.) The answer is B.
text: A collection of coins consists of nickels (5 cents), dimes (10 cents), and quarters (25 cents) and is worth $4.20 in total. There are 3 more dimes than nickels, and the number of quarters is twice the number of nickels. How many coins are there in all?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Since x² − y² = (x − y)(x + y) = 45 and x − y = 3, we get x + y = 15. Combined with x − y = 3, this gives x = 9, y = 6. Then x³ − y³ = 9³ − 6³ = 729 − 216 = 513. (Choice A, 945, is x³ + y³; choice B, 117, is x² + y².) The answer is C.
text: Two numbers x and y satisfy x − y = 3 and x² − y² = 45. What is the value of x³ − y³?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Let the roots be r and s with r + s = 15 (sum) and rs = c (product). We are told r − s = 7. Solving r + s = 15 and r − s = 7 gives r = 11 and s = 4. Therefore c = rs = 11 × 4 = 44. (Equivalently, (r − s)² = (r + s)² − 4rs → 49 = 225 − 4c → 4c = 176 → c = 44.) The answer is B.
text: The two roots of the equation x² − 15x + c = 0 differ by 7. What is the value of c?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: A linear system has no solution when the coefficient ratios are equal but the constant ratio differs: (a − 1)/3 = 2/(a − 2) ≠ 4/a. From (a − 1)(a − 2) = 6: a² − 3a + 2 = 6 → a² − 3a − 4 = 0 → (a − 4)(a + 1) = 0, so a = 4 or a = −1. Check the constant ratio. For a = 4: (a−1)/3 = 1, 2/(a−2) = 1, and 4/a = 1 too — all three equal, so the lines coincide (infinitely many solutions), not no solution. For a = −1: (a−1)/3 = −2/3, 2/(a−2) = −2/3, but 4/a = −4 ≠ −2/3, giving no solution. Thus a = −1. The answer is C.
text: For the system of linear equations(a − 1)x + 2y = 43x + (a − 2)y = ato have NO solution, what is the required value of a?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Let u = x/(x − 3). Then the equation becomes u + 1/u = 5/2, so 2u² − 5u + 2 = 0 → (2u − 1)(u − 2) = 0, giving u = 2 or u = 1/2. Case u = 2: x/(x − 3) = 2 → x = 2x − 6 → x = 6. Case u = 1/2: 2x = x − 3 → x = −3. Both are valid (neither makes a denominator zero). The sum of all solutions is 6 + (−3) = 3. The answer is B.
text: Find the sum of all real values of x that satisfy the equationx/(x − 3) + (x − 3)/x = 5/2.
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: First condition: (L + 3)(W − 2) = LW → LW − 2L + 3W − 6 = LW → 3W − 2L = 6. Second condition: (L − 3)(W + 4) = LW → LW + 4L − 3W − 12 = LW → 4L − 3W = 12. Adding 3W − 2L = 6 and 4L − 3W = 12 gives 2L = 18, so L = 9. Then 3W = 6 + 2(9) = 24 → W = 8. The area is LW = 9 × 8 = 72. The answer is B.
text: A rectangular plot has length L and width W. If the length is increased by 3 and the width decreased by 2, the area is unchanged. If instead the length is decreased by 3 and the width increased by 4, the area is again unchanged. What is the area of the original plot?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Use wavy-curve sign analysis. The critical points are x = −1 and x = 4 (excluded, denominator zero), and x = 1, 2, 3 (zeros of numerator). Note x = 2 is a double root (even multiplicity, sign does NOT change) and x = 3 is a triple root (odd multiplicity, sign changes); x = 1 is simple.Order the points: −1, 1, 2, 3, 4. Test the rightmost interval x > 4: all factors positive, expression > 0. Moving left, the sign flips at each odd-multiplicity point (4, 3, 1, −1) and stays the same across x = 2.From the right: (4,∞) +, (3,4) −, (2,3) +, (1,2) +, (−1,1) −, (−∞,−1) +.So expression ≥ 0 on: x < −1, plus 1 ≤ x ≤ 3 (including the zeros at 1, 2, 3 where it equals 0), plus x > 4.Count integers in −10 ≤ x ≤ 10:• x < −1: x = −10,…,−2 → 9 values (x = −1 excluded).• 1 ≤ x ≤ 3: x = 1, 2, 3 → 3 values.• x > 4: x = 5,6,7,8,9,10 → 6 values (x = 4 excluded).Total = 9 + 3 + 6 = 18.The answer is A.
text: For how many integer values of x in the interval −10 ≤ x ≤ 10 does[(x − 1)(x − 2)²(x − 3)³] ÷ [(x + 1)(x − 4)] ≥ 0 ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: A quadratic ax² + bx + c with a > 0 is positive for ALL real x exactly when its discriminant is negative. Here a = 1 > 0, so require:(−2k)² − 4(1)(k + 6) < 04k² − 4k − 24 < 0k² − k − 6 < 0(k − 3)(k + 2) < 0.This holds when −2 < k < 3. The integer values strictly between −2 and 3 are k = −1, 0, 1, 2 → 4 values.(Common error: using ≤ 0, which would wrongly include k = −2 and k = 3, giving 6.)The answer is E.
text: The inequalityx² − 2kx + (k + 6) > 0holds for every real number x. How many integer values of k satisfy this condition?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Group the constraint into three terms with equal coefficients and apply AM−GM to 2a, 3b, 6c:(2a + 3b + 6c) / 3 ≥ (2a · 3b · 6c)^(1/3)18 / 3 ≥ (36 abc)^(1/3)6 ≥ (36 abc)^(1/3)Cube both sides: 216 ≥ 36 abcabc ≤ 6.Equality in AM−GM requires 2a = 3b = 6c. With their sum 18, each equals 6, so a = 3, b = 2, c = 1, giving abc = 6, which is achievable.The answer is B.
text: Positive real numbers a, b, c satisfy2a + 3b + 6c = 18.What is the maximum possible value of the product abc?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Let y = (2x² + 4x + 5)/(x² + 1). The denominator x² + 1 is always positive, so y is defined everywhere. Cross-multiply:y x² + y = 2x² + 4x + 5(y − 2)x² − 4x + (y − 5) = 0.For a real x, the discriminant must be ≥ 0:(−4)² − 4(y − 2)(y − 5) ≥ 016 − 4(y² − 7y + 10) ≥ 0Divide by 4: 4 − (y² − 7y + 10) ≥ 0−y² + 7y − 6 ≥ 0y² − 7y + 6 ≤ 0(y − 1)(y − 6) ≤ 0.So 1 ≤ y ≤ 6, giving m = 1 and M = 6. (The case y = 2 makes the equation linear, −4x + (−3) = 0, which has a real root, so it is also attainable and lies inside the range.)M − m = 6 − 1 = 5.The answer is D.
text: Over all real numbers x, the expression(2x² + 4x + 5) ÷ (x² + 1)takes a maximum value M and a minimum value m. What is M − m?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Expand using a + b = 1:(1 + 1/a)(1 + 1/b) = 1 + 1/a + 1/b + 1/(ab).Since 1/a + 1/b = (a + b)/(ab) = 1/(ab), this becomes:1 + 1/(ab) + 1/(ab) = 1 + 2/(ab).To minimize the expression we must maximize ab subject to a + b = 1. By AM−GM, ab ≤ ((a+b)/2)² = 1/4, with equality at a = b = 1/2.So the maximum of ab is 1/4, and the minimum value is:1 + 2/(1/4) = 1 + 8 = 9.The answer is C.
text: Positive real numbers a and b satisfy a + b = 1. What is the minimum possible value of(1 + 1/a)(1 + 1/b) ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: By the Cauchy−Schwarz inequality:(x + 2y + 3z)² ≤ (1² + 2² + 3²)(x² + y² + z²)= (1 + 4 + 9)(14) = 14 × 14 = 196.Therefore x + 2y + 3z ≤ √196 = 14.Equality holds when (x, y, z) is proportional to (1, 2, 3): take x = t, y = 2t, z = 3t. Then x² + y² + z² = 14t² = 14, so t = 1, giving (1, 2, 3) and x + 2y + 3z = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14, which is attainable.The answer is A.
text: Real numbers x, y, z satisfyx² + y² + z² = 14.What is the maximum possible value of x + 2y + 3z?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Bring everything to one side:(x − 1)/(x − 2) − (x − 3)/(x − 4) ≤ 0.Combine over the common denominator (x − 2)(x − 4):Numerator = (x − 1)(x − 4) − (x − 3)(x − 2)= (x² − 5x + 4) − (x² − 5x + 6) = −2.So the inequality is −2 / [(x − 2)(x − 4)] ≤ 0, i.e. 2 / [(x − 2)(x − 4)] ≥ 0, i.e. (x − 2)(x − 4) > 0 (strict, since x = 2, 4 are excluded). This holds when x < 2 or x > 4.Integers with 0 ≤ x ≤ 10 satisfying x < 2 or x > 4: {0, 1} and {5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10} = 2 + 6 = 8 values.The answer is E.
text: For how many integer values of x with 0 ≤ x ≤ 10 does(x − 1)/(x − 2) ≤ (x − 3)/(x − 4) ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: By the Cauchy−Schwarz inequality:(3x + 4y)² ≤ (3² + 4²)(x² + y²)25² ≤ 25 · (x² + y²)625 ≤ 25 · (x² + y²)x² + y² ≥ 25.Geometrically, x² + y² is the squared distance from the origin to a point on the line 3x + 4y = 25; its minimum equals the squared perpendicular distance = (25 / √(9 + 16))² = (25/5)² = 25.Equality is achieved at the foot of the perpendicular (x, y) = (3, 4), where 3(3) + 4(4) = 25 and x² + y² = 9 + 16 = 25.(Common error: computing the distance 5 and forgetting to square it.)The answer is B.
text: Real numbers x and y satisfy3x + 4y = 25.What is the minimum possible value of x² + y²?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Substitute t = √(x² + 1). Since x² ≥ 0, we have t ≥ 1, and t² = x² + 1, so x² + 2 = t² + 1.The expression becomes:(t² + 1) / t = t + 1/t.For t ≥ 1, the function g(t) = t + 1/t is increasing (its derivative 1 − 1/t² ≥ 0 for t ≥ 1), so its minimum on t ≥ 1 occurs at t = 1, giving g(1) = 1 + 1 = 2.(AM−GM gives t + 1/t ≥ 2 with equality at t = 1, which is allowed here since t = 1 corresponds to x = 0.) At x = 0 the original expression is (0 + 2)/√1 = 2.The answer is A.
text: Over all real numbers x, what is the minimum value of(x² + 2) ÷ √(x² + 1) ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Substitute x = 2: f(2) + 2·f(1/2) = 6. Substitute x = 1/2: f(1/2) + 2·f(2) = 3/2. Let a = f(2) and b = f(1/2). Then a + 2b = 6 and 2a + b = 3/2. From the first, a = 6 − 2b; substituting: 2(6 − 2b) + b = 3/2, so 12 − 3b = 3/2, giving 3b = 21/2, b = 7/2. Then a = 6 − 2(7/2) = 6 − 7 = −1. The answer is A.
text: A function f, defined for all non-zero real numbers, satisfiesf(x) + 2·f(1/x) = 3x for every x ≠ 0.What is the value of f(2)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Work with base-2 and base-3 logs. Let t = log<sub>2</sub>3. Then log<sub>12</sub>27 = log(3<sup>3</sup>)/log(2<sup>2</sup>·3) = 3·log3 / (2·log2 + log3). Dividing top and bottom by log2: a = 3t / (2 + t). Solve for t: a(2 + t) = 3t ⇒ 2a + at = 3t ⇒ 2a = t(3 − a) ⇒ t = 2a/(3 − a). Now log<sub>6</sub>16 = log(2<sup>4</sup>)/log(2·3) = 4·log2/(log2 + log3) = 4/(1 + t). Substitute t: 1 + t = 1 + 2a/(3 − a) = (3 − a + 2a)/(3 − a) = (3 + a)/(3 − a). Therefore log<sub>6</sub>16 = 4(3 − a)/(3 + a). The answer is B.
text: Suppose log<sub>12</sub>27 = a. Express log<sub>6</sub>16 in terms of a.
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Notice that (2 + √2)<sup>3</sup> = 8 + 3·4·√2 + 3·2·2 + 2√2 = 8 + 12√2 + 12 + 2√2 = 20 + 14√2. So ∛(20 + 14√2) = 2 + √2. Similarly (2 − √2)<sup>3</sup> = 20 − 14√2, so ∛(20 − 14√2) = 2 − √2. Their sum is (2 + √2) + (2 − √2) = 4. (Check: let S be the sum; S<sup>3</sup> = 40 + 3·(∛((20)<sup>2</sup> − (14√2)<sup>2</sup>))·S = 40 + 3·∛(400 − 392)·S = 40 + 3·2·S = 40 + 6S, giving S<sup>3</sup> − 6S − 40 = 0, whose real root is S = 4.) The answer is C.
text: What is the value of∛(20 + 14√2) + ∛(20 − 14√2)?(Here ∛ denotes the real cube root.)
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: The number of digits of a positive integer N is ⌊log<sub>10</sub>N⌋ + 1. Here log<sub>10</sub>(6<sup>20</sup>) = 20·log<sub>10</sub>6 = 20·(log<sub>10</sub>2 + log<sub>10</sub>3) = 20·(0.3010 + 0.4771) = 20·0.7781 = 15.562. The characteristic is ⌊15.562⌋ = 15, so the number of digits is 15 + 1 = 16. (The common slip is to answer 15, forgetting the ‘+1’.) The answer is B.
text: Using log<sub>10</sub>2 = 0.3010 and log<sub>10</sub>3 = 0.4771, how many digits are in the integer 6<sup>20</sup> when written in ordinary decimal notation?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Apply the rule repeatedly to find the period. Let A = f(x). Then f(x+5) = (1+A)/(1−A). Applying again, f(x+10) = (1 + (1+A)/(1−A)) / (1 − (1+A)/(1−A)) = ((1−A)+(1+A)) / ((1−A)−(1+A)) = 2 / (−2A) = −1/A. So f(x+10) = −1/f(x), and therefore f(x+20) = −1/f(x+10) = −1/(−1/f(x)) = f(x). The function has period 20. Now 2023 − 3 = 2020 = 101·20, a multiple of 20, so f(2023) = f(3) = 2. The answer is A.
text: A function f, defined for all real x, satisfiesf(x + 5) = (1 + f(x)) / (1 − f(x)) for every real x.Given that f(3) = 2, what is f(2023)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Compute the first few compositions. f(x) = 1/(1−x). f<sup>(2)</sup>(x) = f(1/(1−x)) = 1 / (1 − 1/(1−x)) = (1−x) / ((1−x) − 1) = (1−x)/(−x) = (x−1)/x. f<sup>(3)</sup>(x) = f((x−1)/x) = 1 / (1 − (x−1)/x) = x / (x − (x−1)) = x/1 = x. So f has period 3 under composition. Since 100 = 3·33 + 1, f<sup>(100)</sup> = f<sup>(1)</sup> = f. Thus f<sup>(100)</sup>(3) = f(3) = 1/(1 − 3) = −1/2. The answer is A.
text: Let f(x) = 1 / (1 − x), and let f<sup>(n)</sup> denote f composed with itself n times, so f<sup>(2)</sup>(x) = f(f(x)), etc. What is the value of f<sup>(100)</sup>(3)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Unwind from the outside. log<sub>4</sub>(·) = 1/2 means the inner quantity equals 4<sup>1/2</sup> = 2, so log<sub>2</sub>(log<sub>3</sub>x) = 2. That means log<sub>3</sub>x = 2<sup>2</sup> = 4, so x = 3<sup>4</sup> = 81. (Check: log<sub>3</sub>81 = 4, log<sub>2</sub>4 = 2, log<sub>4</sub>2 = 1/2.) The answer is D.
text: Find the value of x that satisfieslog<sub>4</sub>(log<sub>2</sub>(log<sub>3</sub>x)) = 1/2.
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Take the base-10 log: log<sub>10</sub>((1/3)<sup>50</sup>) = −50·log<sub>10</sub>3 = −50·0.4771 = −23.855. For a number between 0 and 1, the characteristic is the floor: ⌊−23.855⌋ = −24. The mantissa is −23.855 − (−24) = 0.145 (positive), so the value is 10<sup>0.145</sup> × 10<sup>−24</sup> ≈ 1.40 × 10<sup>−24</sup>. A value of the form (first non-zero digit)×10<sup>−24</sup> has its first significant digit in the 24th decimal place, so there are 24 − 1 = 23 zeros immediately after the decimal point. The answer is B.
text: Using log<sub>10</sub>3 = 0.4771, how many zeros immediately follow the decimal point before the first non-zero digit in the decimal expansion of (1/3)<sup>50</sup>?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Let the common value be k (with k > 0, k ≠ 1). Then 2<sup>x</sup> = k gives x = log<sub>2</sub>k, so 1/x = log<sub>k</sub>2. Likewise 3<sup>y</sup> = k gives 1/y = log<sub>k</sub>3, and 6<sup>−z</sup> = k gives −z = log<sub>6</sub>k, so 1/(−z) = log<sub>k</sub>6, i.e. 1/z = −log<sub>k</sub>6. Adding: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = log<sub>k</sub>2 + log<sub>k</sub>3 − log<sub>k</sub>6 = log<sub>k</sub>(2·3/6) = log<sub>k</sub>1 = 0. The answer is A.
text: Real numbers x, y, z (all non-zero) satisfy2<sup>x</sup> = 3<sup>y</sup> = 6<sup>−z</sup>.What is the value of 1/x + 1/y + 1/z?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: First f(2) = 8 − 6 = 2. Solve x<sup>3</sup> − 3x = 2, i.e. x<sup>3</sup> − 3x − 2 = 0. Since x = 2 is a root, factor: x<sup>3</sup> − 3x − 2 = (x − 2)(x<sup>2</sup> + 2x + 1) = (x − 2)(x + 1)<sup>2</sup>. The roots are x = 2 and x = −1 (a double root). The distinct values are 2 and −1, whose sum is 2 + (−1) = 1. (Counting the double root twice would wrongly give 0.) The answer is A.
text: Let f(x) = x<sup>3</sup> − 3x. Consider all real numbers x for which f(x) = f(2). What is the sum of the distinct such values of x?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: In a harmonic progression (HP), the reciprocals of the terms form an arithmetic progression (AP). Let the reciprocal AP have first term A and common difference D, so the kth reciprocal is A + (k−1)D.The 3rd term of the HP is 1÷12, so its reciprocal is 12: A + 2D = 12.The 7th term is 1÷28, so its reciprocal is 28: A + 6D = 28.Subtracting: 4D = 16, so D = 4, and then A = 12 − 2(4) = 4.The reciprocal of the nth term is 4 + (n−1)(4) = 4n. For n = 15, the reciprocal is 4(15) = 60.Therefore the 15th term of the HP is 1÷60. (Note: 60 itself is the reciprocal, a common trap; 1÷64 comes from using 4 + 15×4 = 64 without subtracting 1.)The answer is C.
text: In a harmonic progression, the 3rd term is 1÷12 and the 7th term is 1÷28. What is the 15th term of this harmonic progression?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: The kth term is k(k+2) = k<sup>2</sup> + 2k, so the sum is Σk<sup>2</sup> + 2Σk for k = 1 to 20.Σk<sup>2</sup> = n(n+1)(2n+1)÷6 = 20×21×41÷6 = 2870.Σk = n(n+1)÷2 = 20×21÷2 = 210, so 2Σk = 420.Total = 2870 + 420 = 3290. (Using only Σk<sup>2</sup> = 2870 forgets the +2k part; treating each term as k(k+3) gives 3500.)The answer is A.
text: What is the value of the sum1×3 + 2×4 + 3×5 + 4×6 + … + 20×22,where the kth term is k(k+2)?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Let S = Σ k·2<sup>k</sup> for k = 1 to 6. Multiply by the ratio 2:2S = Σ k·2<sup>k+1</sup> = 1·2<sup>2</sup> + 2·2<sup>3</sup> + … + 6·2<sup>7</sup>.Subtract S from 2S, aligning powers of 2:2S − S = 6·2<sup>7</sup> − (2<sup>1</sup> + 2<sup>2</sup> + 2<sup>3</sup> + 2<sup>4</sup> + 2<sup>5</sup> + 2<sup>6</sup>).The geometric part 2 + 4 + … + 64 = 2(2<sup>6</sup> − 1) = 126.So S = 6·128 − 126 = 768 − 126 = 642.(Equivalently the closed form is (n−1)2<sup>n+1</sup> + 2 = 5·128 + 2 = 642. Dropping the final +2 gives the trap 640; using n·2<sup>n+1</sup> gives 768.)The answer is D.
text: What is the value of the finite arithmetico-geometric sum1×2 + 2×2<sup>2</sup> + 3×2<sup>3</sup> + 4×2<sup>4</sup> + 5×2<sup>5</sup> + 6×2<sup>6</sup>,i.e. Σ k×2<sup>k</sup> for k = 1 to 6?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: The first descent is 27 m. After that, every up-and-down pair occurs at successive bounce heights forming a geometric progression with ratio 2÷3.The rebound heights are 27×(2÷3) = 18, then 12, then 8, … Each such height is travelled twice (up then down).Total = 27 + 2×(18 + 12 + 8 + …).The bracket is an infinite GP with first term 18 and ratio 2÷3: sum = 18÷(1 − 2÷3) = 18÷(1÷3) = 54.Total = 27 + 2×54 = 27 + 108 = 135 metres.(Counting only the descents, 27÷(1÷3) = 81, ignores the upward travel; this is the common trap.)The answer is B.
text: A ball is dropped from a height of 27 metres onto a hard floor. After each impact it rebounds to two-thirds of the height from which it last fell, and on the next descent falls from that lower height, continuing forever. What is the total distance (in metres) the ball travels before coming to rest?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Suppose n means are inserted between 7 and 71. Then there are n + 2 terms in all and n + 1 equal gaps, each of size d = (71 − 7)÷(n + 1) = 64÷(n + 1).The kth inserted mean is 7 + k·d. The 5th mean is 7 + 5d = 27, so 5d = 20 and d = 4.Then 64÷(n + 1) = 4, giving n + 1 = 16, so n = 15.Check: the progression is 7, 11, 15, … with d = 4; the 5th mean is 7 + 5×4 = 27. Correct.(Using d = 64÷n instead of 64÷(n+1) wrongly gives n = 16.)The answer is E.
text: A number of arithmetic means are inserted between 7 and 71 so that, together with 7 and 71, all the numbers form a single arithmetic progression. If the 5th of the inserted means (counting from the 7 end) equals 27, how many arithmetic means were inserted?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Compute directly: 1 + 27 + 125 + 343 + 729.1 + 27 = 28; 28 + 125 = 153; 153 + 343 = 496; 496 + 729 = 1225.This matches the standard identity for the sum of the first n odd cubes: n<sup>2</sup>(2n<sup>2</sup> − 1). For n = 5 that is 25×(50 − 1) = 25×49 = 1225.(Squaring the sum of the odds, (1+3+5+7+9)<sup>2</sup> = 25<sup>2</sup> = 625, is a tempting but wrong shortcut; misremembering the identity as n<sup>2</sup>(2n<sup>2</sup>+1) gives 1275.)The answer is A.
text: What is the value of the sum of the cubes of the first five odd positive integers, namely1<sup>3</sup> + 3<sup>3</sup> + 5<sup>3</sup> + 7<sup>3</sup> + 9<sup>3</sup>?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Let the first term be a and the common ratio be r (with 0 < r < 1). The full sum is a÷(1 − r) = 162.The even-position terms are ar, ar<sup>3</sup>, ar<sup>5</sup>, …, themselves an infinite GP with first term ar and ratio r<sup>2</sup>:even sum = ar÷(1 − r<sup>2</sup>) = ar÷[(1 − r)(1 + r)].Dividing the even sum by the total sum: [ar÷((1−r)(1+r))] ÷ [a÷(1−r)] = r÷(1 + r) = 54÷162 = 1÷3.So 3r = 1 + r, giving r = 1÷2. Then a = 162×(1 − r) = 162×(1÷2) = 81.Check: even sum = 81×(1÷2)÷(1 − 1÷4) = 40.5÷0.75 = 54. Correct.The answer is C.
text: An infinite geometric progression of positive terms has sum 162. The sum of the terms occupying the even positions (the 2nd, 4th, 6th, … terms) is 54. What is the first term of the progression?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: The numbers of logs per row form an arithmetic progression: 20, 19, 18, …, 5, decreasing by 1.Number of rows = (20 − 5) + 1 = 16 (inclusive count of integers from 5 to 20).Sum of an AP = (number of terms)×(first + last)÷2 = 16×(20 + 5)÷2 = 16×25÷2 = 8×25 = 200.(Taking 20 − 5 = 15 rows forgets to add 1 and gives the non-integer 25×15÷2 = 187.5; counting all rows 1 to 20 as 20 terms gives 210.)The answer is D.
text: Logs are stacked so that the bottom row has 20 logs and each row above it has exactly one fewer log than the row below, with the top row containing 5 logs. How many logs are in the entire stack?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Let the first term be a and common ratio r. The first three terms sum to a(1 + r + r<sup>2</sup>) = 7.The 4th, 5th, 6th terms are ar<sup>3</sup>, ar<sup>4</sup>, ar<sup>5</sup>, whose sum is ar<sup>3</sup>(1 + r + r<sup>2</sup>) = 56.Dividing the second equation by the first: r<sup>3</sup> = 56÷7 = 8, so r = 2.Then a(1 + 2 + 4) = 7, i.e. 7a = 7, so a = 1.The 7th term is ar<sup>6</sup> = 1×2<sup>6</sup> = 64.(Stopping at the 6th term ar<sup>5</sup> = 32 is the common slip; the 8th term would be 128.)The answer is C.
text: In a geometric progression with positive terms, the sum of the first three terms is 7, and the sum of the next three terms (the 4th, 5th and 6th) is 56. What is the 7th term of the progression?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: The semiperimeter is s = (13 + 13 + 10)÷2 = 18. By Heron, the area K = √(18 × 5 × 5 × 8) = √3600 = 60. The circumradius satisfies R = abc÷(4K) = (13 × 13 × 10)÷(4 × 60) = 1690÷240 = 169⁄24. (The value 10⁄3 is the inradius K⁄s, a common confusion.) The answer is D.
text: An isosceles triangle has two sides of length 13 and a base of length 10. The triangle is inscribed in a circle. What is the radius of that circle (the circumradius)?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: The semiperimeter is s = (9 + 10 + 17)÷2 = 18. By Heron, the area K = √(18 × (18−9) × (18−10) × (18−17)) = √(18 × 9 × 8 × 1) = √1296 = 36. The inradius is r = K⁄s = 36÷18 = 2. (Dividing the area by the full perimeter 36 gives the trap value 1.) The answer is B.
text: A triangle has sides of length 9, 10, and 17. What is the radius of the circle inscribed in this triangle (its inradius)?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Geometric-mean relation: the altitude to the hypotenuse satisfies h² = (4.5)(8) = 36, so h = 6. The hypotenuse is 4.5 + 8 = 12.5, and the area = ½ × 12.5 × 6 = 37.5. No need to find the legs at all — that is the long way.
text: In a right triangle, the altitude drawn to the hypotenuse divides the hypotenuse into segments of lengths 4.5 and 8. What is the area of the triangle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Use mass points. On BC, BD : DC = 2 : 3 requires mass(B) : mass(C) = 3 : 2. On AC, AE : EC = 3 : 1 requires mass(A) : mass(C) = 1 : 3. Set mass(C) = 6: then mass(B) = 9 (from 3:2 scaled) and mass(A) = 2 (from 1:3). Point D carries mass(B) + mass(C) = 9 + 6 = 15. On cevian AD, the ratio AP : PD equals mass(D) : mass(A) = 15 : 2. (Reversing the two given ratios yields the trap 5 : 1.) The answer is B.
text: In triangle ABC, point D lies on side BC with BD : DC = 2 : 3, and point E lies on side AC with AE : EC = 3 : 1. Cevians AD and BE intersect at point P. In what ratio does P divide AD, that is, what is AP : PD?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Let H be the foot of the altitude from A, with AH = h. In right triangle ABH, angle B = 45°, so AB = h√2; since AB = 10√2, h = 10 and BH = h = 10. In right triangle ACH, angle C = 30°, so HC = h÷tan30° = h√3 = 10√3. Then BC = BH + HC = 10 + 10√3 = 10(1 + √3). Area = ½ × BC × AH = ½ × 10(1 + √3) × 10 = 50(1 + √3). The answer is D.
text: In triangle ABC, angle B = 45° and angle C = 30°. The foot of the altitude from A lands on side BC. If AB = 10√2, what is the area of triangle ABC?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Because DE is parallel to BC, triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC, so AD÷AB = DE÷BC. Thus 8÷AB = 6÷15 = 2⁄5, giving AB = 8 × 5÷2 = 20. Therefore DB = AB − AD = 20 − 8 = 12. (Using AD÷DB = DE÷BC instead of AD÷AB gives the trap 20.) The answer is C.
text: In triangle ABC, a line through point D on AB and point E on AC is drawn parallel to BC. Segment DE has length 6 and BC has length 15. If AD = 8, what is the length of DB?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: The semiperimeter is s = (25 + 29 + 36)÷2 = 45. By Heron, the area K = √(45 × (45−25) × (45−29) × (45−36)) = √(45 × 20 × 16 × 9) = √129600 = 360. The inradius is r = K⁄s = 360÷45 = 8. The answer is C.
text: A triangle has sides of length 25, 29, and 36. What is the radius of its inscribed circle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: In any right triangle the median to the hypotenuse equals half the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse = 2 × 12.5 = 25. With one leg 7, the other leg = √(25<sup>2</sup> − 7<sup>2</sup>) = √(625 − 49) = √576 = 24. (Treating 12.5 as a leg, or 12.5 as half a leg, leads to the wrong options.) The answer is C.
text: In a right triangle, the median drawn from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse has length 12.5, and one of the legs has length 7. What is the length of the other leg?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: The external bisector of angle A divides side BC externally in the ratio AB : AC = 6 : 4 = 3 : 2, so BD : DC = 3 : 2 with D outside segment BC. Since AB > AC, D lies beyond C, giving BD = BC + CD. Let CD = 2k and BD = 3k; then 3k = 5 + 2k, so k = 5. Therefore CD = 2k = 10. (Dividing internally would give CD = 2, and BD = 15 is the other segment.) The answer is B.
text: In triangle ABC, AB = 6 and AC = 4. The external bisector of angle A meets line BC, extended beyond C, at point D. If BC = 5, what is the length of CD?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Use mass points to locate P on AD. D is the midpoint of BC, so mass(B) = mass(C) = 1 and mass(D) = 2. On AC, AE : EC = 1 : 2 requires mass(A) : mass(C) = 2 : 1, so mass(A) = 2. On cevian AD, AP : PD = mass(D) : mass(A) = 2 : 2 = 1 : 1, so P is the midpoint of AD. Now [ABD] = ½[ABC] since D is the midpoint of BC, and because P is the midpoint of AD, [ABP] = ½[ABD] = ¼[ABC]. The answer is C.
text: In triangle ABC, D is the midpoint of BC and E lies on AC with AE : EC = 1 : 2. Cevians AD and BE intersect at point P. What fraction of the area of triangle ABC is the area of triangle ABP?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: The semiperimeter is s = (17 + 25 + 28)÷2 = 35. By Heron, the area K = √(35 × (35−17) × (35−25) × (35−28)) = √(35 × 18 × 10 × 7) = √44100 = 210. Each altitude equals 2K÷(its base) = 420÷(side), so the shortest altitude corresponds to the longest side, 28: altitude = 420÷28 = 15. The answer is A.
text: A triangle has sides of length 17, 25, and 28. What is the length of the shortest of its three altitudes?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: First find QR by the Law of Cosines: QR<sup>2</sup> = 5<sup>2</sup> + 8<sup>2</sup> − 2 × 5 × 8 × cos60° = 25 + 64 − 80 × ½ = 89 − 40 = 49, so QR = 7. The median from P to QR satisfies PM<sup>2</sup> = (2 × PQ<sup>2</sup> + 2 × PR<sup>2</sup> − QR<sup>2</sup>)÷4 = (2 × 25 + 2 × 64 − 49)÷4 = (50 + 128 − 49)÷4 = 129÷4. Thus PM = √129 ÷ 2. (Forgetting to halve QR or mis-signing the cosine term gives the other options.) The answer is C.
text: In triangle PQR, angle P = 60°, PQ = 5, and PR = 8. A point M is the midpoint of QR. What is the length of the median PM?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: By the power of a point P with respect to the circle, the products of the two distances along each secant from P are equal: PA × PB = PC × PD.So 6 × 16 = 8 × PD, giving 96 = 8 × PD, so PD = 12.The chord CD is the part of the second secant inside the circle: CD = PD − PC = 12 − 8 = 4.(A common error is to stop at PD = 12, or to confuse CD with PC = 8.)The answer is A.
text: From an external point P, two secant lines are drawn to a circle. The first secant passes through the circle, meeting it first at A and then at B, with PA = 6 and PB = 16. The second secant from P meets the circle first at C and then at D, with PC = 8. Find the length of the chord CD.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: For any cyclic quadrilateral, Ptolemy's theorem states that the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of the two pairs of opposite sides:AC × BD = (AB × CD) + (BC × AD).Substitute the known values: 12 × 10 = (9 × 8) + (6 × AD).120 = 72 + 6 × AD, so 6 × AD = 48 and AD = 8.(A common error is adding instead of pairing opposite sides, e.g. computing (120 + 72)/6 = 32, or pairing the wrong sides.)The answer is B.
text: Quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle. Its sides are AB = 9, BC = 6, CD = 8, and the two diagonals are AC = 12 and BD = 10. Find the length of side AD.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: By the tangent−chord angle theorem, the angle between the tangent and the chord AB equals half the intercepted arc AB cut off on that side. So that minor arc AB = 2 × 58° = 116°.The point C lies on this minor arc, so the inscribed angle ∠ACB subtends the OTHER arc — the major arc AB — which measures 360° − 116° = 244°.An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc: ∠ACB = 244° / 2 = 122°.(By the alternate segment theorem, a point on the major arc would give 58° — the common trap; a point on the minor arc gives the supplement, 122°.)The answer is D.
text: A line is tangent to a circle at point A. A chord AB is drawn, and the acute angle between the tangent and this chord measures 58°. A point C lies on the circle on the minor arc AB (the arc cut off on the same side of the chord as the tangent direction that makes the acute angle). Find the measure of the inscribed angle ∠ACB.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: A convex polygon with n sides has n(n − 3)/2 diagonals.Set this equal to 5 times the number of sides: n(n − 3)/2 = 5n.Since n ≠ 0, divide both sides by n: (n − 3)/2 = 5, so n − 3 = 10, giving n = 13.Check: a 13-gon has 13 × 10 / 2 = 65 diagonals, and 5 × 13 = 65. Confirmed.The answer is D.
text: In a certain regular convex polygon, the total number of diagonals is exactly 5 times the number of sides. How many sides does the polygon have?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: Let the circle have radius R.A regular hexagon inscribed in the circle has side length equal to R, and its area is 6 small equilateral triangles of side R: Area = 6 × (√3/4)R² = (3√3/2)R².An equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle has side R√3 (since the circumradius of an equilateral triangle of side s is s/√3, so s = R√3). Its area = (√3/4)(R√3)² = (√3/4)(3R²) = (3√3/4)R².Ratio hexagon : triangle = (3√3/2) : (3√3/4) = 2 : 1.The answer is C.
text: A regular hexagon and an equilateral triangle are both inscribed in the SAME circle. What is the ratio of the area of the hexagon to the area of the triangle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: For a common external tangent to two circles with radii R and r and center distance d, drop a perpendicular: the tangent length is √(d² − (R − r)²).Here R = 8, r = 3, d = 13, so XY = √(13² − (8 − 3)²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12.(A common error is using (R + r), which is the formula for the INTERNAL tangent: √(169 − 121) = √48 = 4√3 ≈ 6.93 — the listed trap.)The answer is C.
text: Two circles, with radii 8 and 3, lie outside each other, and the distance between their centers is 13. A line touches both circles on the same side (a common external tangent), meeting them at points X and Y. Find the length XY of the tangent segment between the two points of tangency.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: Let the radius be r. The perpendicular distance from the center to a chord of length L is √(r² − (L/2)²).For the chord of length 24, half-length = 12, distance from center a = √(r² − 144).For the chord of length 18, half-length = 9, distance from center b = √(r² − 81).Since both chords are on the same side of the center and the shorter (farther) chord is more distant, b − a = 3.Also b² − a² = (r² − 81) − (r² − 144) = 63. Factor: (b − a)(b + a) = 63, so 3(b + a) = 63, giving b + a = 21.Solving b − a = 3 and b + a = 21 gives b = 12, a = 9.From a = 9: r² − 144 = 81, so r² = 225 and r = 15.The answer is C.
text: In a circle, two parallel chords lie on the same side of the center. The longer chord has length 24 and the shorter chord has length 18, and the perpendicular distance between the two chords is 3. Find the radius of the circle.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: The four arcs must total 360°, so arc DA = 360° − (70° + 80° + 60°) = 360° − 210° = 150°.The inscribed angle ∠ABC (vertex at B) intercepts the arc that does NOT contain B, namely arc ADC = arc AD + arc DC = 150° + 60° = 210°.An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc: ∠ABC = 210° / 2 = 105°.Check: the opposite angle ∠ADC intercepts arc ABC = 70° + 80° = 150°, giving 75°, and 105° + 75° = 180° as required for a cyclic quadrilateral.(The value 75° is the opposite angle — a natural trap.)The answer is B.
text: Points A, B, C, D lie in order on a circle, forming cyclic quadrilateral ABCD. The arcs cut off by the sides measure: arc AB = 70°, arc BC = 80°, and arc CD = 60° (each arc taken as the one not containing the other vertices). Find the measure of the interior angle ∠ABC of the quadrilateral.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: By the intersecting chords theorem (power of an interior point), AP × PB = CP × PD.So 8 × 6 = 4 × PD, giving 48 = 4 × PD, so PD = 12.The full chord CD = CP + PD = 4 + 12 = 16.(A common error is to report PD = 12 as the answer, or to forget to add CP.)The answer is D.
text: Two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at an interior point P. Along chord AB, the point divides it so that AP = 8 and PB = 6. Along chord CD, the segment CP = 4. Find the total length of chord CD.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: A regular n-gon inscribed in a circle of radius R can be split into n isosceles triangles, each with two sides of length R and apex angle 360°/n at the center. The area of each is ½R²sin(360°/n), so the polygon's area is ½nR²sin(360°/n).For n = 12: the apex angle is 360°/12 = 30°, and sin 30° = ½.Area = ½ × 12 × R² × ½ = 3R².With R = 10: Area = 3 × 100 = 300.(Note 100π ≈ 314 is the full circle's area — a tempting overshoot; 150√3 ≈ 260 is the inscribed regular hexagon's area.)The answer is D.
text: A regular 12-sided polygon (a regular dodecagon) is inscribed in a circle of radius 10. Find the exact area of the dodecagon.
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: The condition is PA = 2·PB, so PA² = 4·PB². Writing P = (x, y):(x − 3)² + y² = 4[(x − 9)² + y²].Expand: x² − 6x + 9 + y² = 4(x² − 18x + 81 + y²) = 4x² − 72x + 324 + 4y².Bring all terms to one side: 0 = 3x² + 3y² − 66x + 315, i.e. x² + y² − 22x + 105 = 0.Complete the square: (x − 11)² + y² = 121 − 105 = 16.So the radius is √16 = 4. (A common error is to write PA² = 2·PB², which gives radius 6√2.) The answer is B.
text: A point P moves in the plane so that its distance from A(3, 0) is always exactly twice its distance from B(9, 0). The path traced by P is a circle. What is the radius of this circle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Three points are collinear when the area of the triangle they form is zero:x<sub>A</sub>(y<sub>B</sub> − y<sub>C</sub>) + x<sub>B</sub>(y<sub>C</sub> − y<sub>A</sub>) + x<sub>C</sub>(y<sub>A</sub> − y<sub>B</sub>) = 0.Substitute: 4(5 − t) + t(t − 7) + 2(7 − 5) = 0.= 20 − 4t + t² − 7t + 4 = 0 → t² − 11t + 24 = 0.This factors as (t − 3)(t − 8) = 0, giving t = 3 or t = 8.By Vieta's formula the sum of the roots is 11 (also visible directly as the coefficient). The answer is D.
text: The three points A(4, 7), B(t, 5), and C(2, t) are collinear. There are two possible values of t. What is the sum of these two values of t?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Recover B and C from the midpoint relations. Since P is the midpoint of AB, B = 2P − A = (2·2 − 4, 2·5 − 9) = (0, 1). Since Q is the midpoint of AC, C = 2Q − A = (2·7 − 4, 2·6 − 9) = (10, 3).Now compute the area of triangle ABC with A(4, 9), B(0, 1), C(10, 3) using the shoelace formula:Area = ½|x<sub>A</sub>(y<sub>B</sub> − y<sub>C</sub>) + x<sub>B</sub>(y<sub>C</sub> − y<sub>A</sub>) + x<sub>C</sub>(y<sub>A</sub> − y<sub>B</sub>)|= ½|4(1 − 3) + 0(3 − 9) + 10(9 − 1)| = ½|−8 + 0 + 80| = ½(72) = 36.(Using P and Q directly with A gives the medial-triangle area 9, which is only one quarter of the true area.) The answer is D.
text: In triangle ABC, the midpoint of side AB is P(2, 5) and the midpoint of side AC is Q(7, 6). Vertex A is the point (4, 9). What is the area of triangle ABC?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: First find the side lengths. The side opposite a vertex is named with that vertex's lowercase letter.a = BC = √[(12−0)² + (0−5)²] = √169 = 13 (opposite A).b = CA = 5 (opposite B).c = AB = 12 (opposite C).The incenter is the weighted average I = (aA + bB + cC)/(a + b + c):I<sub>x</sub> = (13·0 + 5·12 + 12·0)/(13 + 5 + 12) = 60/30 = 2.I<sub>y</sub> = (13·0 + 5·0 + 12·5)/30 = 60/30 = 2.So I = (2, 2) and the sum of coordinates is 4. (This is consistent with the right angle at A: the inradius is r = Area/s = 30/15 = 2, putting the incenter at (r, r) = (2, 2).) Using the centroid by mistake gives 17/3. The answer is A.
text: Triangle ABC has vertices A(0, 0), B(12, 0), and C(0, 5). Let I be the incenter (the center of the inscribed circle) of this triangle. What is the sum of the coordinates of I?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Put the circle in center-radius form: x² − 4x + y² − 2y = 20 → (x − 2)² + (y − 1)² = 20 + 4 + 1 = 25.So the center is (2, 1) and the radius is r = 5.The perpendicular distance d from the center to the line 3x − 4y − 17 = 0 is:d = |3·2 − 4·1 − 17| / √(3² + 4²) = |6 − 4 − 17| / 5 = 15/5 = 3.Half the chord length is √(r² − d²) = √(25 − 9) = √16 = 4, so the full chord = 2·4 = 8.(Forgetting to double the half-chord gives 4.) The answer is D.
text: A circle has equation x² + y² − 4x − 2y − 20 = 0. The line 3x − 4y = 17 cuts this circle in two points. What is the length of the chord joining these two points?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: For external division of AB in ratio m : n (here m : n = 3 : 1), the section formula is:P = (mB − nA) / (m − n).P<sub>x</sub> = (3·6 − 1·2)/(3 − 1) = (18 − 2)/2 = 16/2 = 8.P<sub>y</sub> = (3·7 − 1·(−1))/(3 − 1) = (21 + 1)/2 = 22/2 = 11.So P = (8, 11) and the sum of its coordinates is 8 + 11 = 19. (Using internal division by mistake gives (5, 5), sum 10.) The answer is E.
text: Point P lies on line AB extended beyond B and divides segment AB externally in the ratio AP : PB = 3 : 1, where A = (2, −1) and B = (6, 7). What is the sum of the coordinates of P?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Since M is parallel to L, it has the form 3x + 4y = c. It passes through (1, 8), so c = 3·1 + 4·8 = 3 + 32 = 35. Thus M is 3x + 4y = 35.The distance between parallel lines 3x + 4y = 15 and 3x + 4y = 35 is:d = |35 − 15| / √(3² + 4²) = 20 / √25 = 20/5 = 4.(Equivalently, the distance from (1, 8) to line L is |3·1 + 4·8 − 15|/5 = 20/5 = 4.) Forgetting to divide by 5 gives 20. The answer is B.
text: Line L has equation 3x + 4y = 15. Line M is parallel to L and passes through the point (1, 8). What is the perpendicular distance between lines L and M?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: A circle tangent to both axes in the first quadrant has its center at (r, r) and radius r. Requiring it to pass through (8, 1):(8 − r)² + (1 − r)² = r².Expand: 64 − 16r + r² + 1 − 2r + r² = r² → r² − 18r + 65 = 0.Factor: (r − 5)(r − 13) = 0, so r = 5 or r = 13. Both are valid (centers (5, 5) and (13, 13), each passing through (8, 1)).By Vieta's, the sum of the radii equals the coefficient 18 (and the product is 65). The answer is C.
text: A circle lies in the first quadrant and is tangent to both the x-axis and the y-axis. It also passes through the point (8, 1). There are exactly two such circles. What is the sum of their radii?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: The largest sphere inside the cube has diameter equal to the cube's edge, so its diameter is 12 cm and its radius is 6 cm. Cube volume = 12³ = 1728 cm³. Sphere volume = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π(6)³ = (4/3)π(216) = 288π cm³. Remaining wood = 1728 − 288π cm³. (Choosing 216π comes from misusing πr³; 144π from halving; 864 from halving the cube.) The answer is A.
text: A solid wooden cube has edge 12 cm. The largest possible sphere that fits entirely inside the cube is carved out and removed, leaving a hollowed wooden block. Find the volume of wood remaining in the block (i.e. the space inside the cube but outside the sphere).
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: For a cube inscribed in a sphere, the cube's space (main) diagonal equals the sphere's diameter. Diameter = 2 × 9 = 18 cm. If the cube has edge a, its space diagonal is a√3, so a√3 = 18, giving a = 18/√3 = 6√3 cm. Volume = a³ = (6√3)³ = 216 × 3√3 = 648√3 cm³. (Using the face diagonal a√2 = 18 gives 1458√2; using a = 18 gives 5832; using the radius instead of diameter gives 81√3.) The answer is B.
text: A solid sphere has radius 9 cm. The largest possible cube that can be cut so as to fit entirely inside the sphere is carved out. Find the volume of that cube.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: The slant height l of a frustum satisfies l = √(h² + (R−r)²) = √(16² + (20−8)²) = √(256 + 144) = √400 = 20 cm. Curved surface area = π(R + r)l = π(20 + 8)(20) = 560π. Add the two circular faces: πR² + πr² = 400π + 64π = 464π. Total = 560π + 464π = 1024π cm². (560π forgets both circles; 960π or 624π forget one circle; 912π uses the height as the slant.) The answer is C.
text: A frustum of a right circular cone has a base of radius 20 cm and a top of radius 8 cm, and the perpendicular (vertical) distance between the two circular faces is 16 cm. Find the total surface area of the frustum (curved surface plus both circular ends).
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: A unit cube has exactly one painted face when it lies on a face of the cuboid but not on any edge, i.e. it is an interior cell of that face. For each pair of opposite faces, the count of such cells per face is (dimension−2)(dimension−2) of that face. Faces 6×5: (6−2)(5−2) = 12 each × 2 = 24. Faces 6×4: (6−2)(4−2) = 8 each × 2 = 16. Faces 5×4: (5−2)(4−2) = 6 each × 2 = 12. Total = 24 + 16 + 12 = 52. (36 counts exactly-two-face edge cubes; 24 counts the fully-unpainted interior; 96 counts cubes with at least one painted face; 120 is the total.) The answer is D.
text: A solid wooden cuboid measuring 6 cm × 5 cm × 4 cm is painted green on all six outer faces and then sliced by cuts parallel to its faces into unit cubes of edge 1 cm. How many of these unit cubes have paint on exactly one face?
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: The exposed surface is the curved surface of the cone plus the curved surface of the hemisphere; the circular base is internal and hidden. Cone slant height l = √(7² + 24²) = √(49 + 576) = √625 = 25 cm. Cone curved area = πrl = π(7)(25) = 175π. Hemisphere curved area = 2πr² = 2π(49) = 98π. Total = 273π = 273 × 22/7 = 858 cm². (1012 wrongly adds the base circle; 1166 uses a full sphere; 704 uses πr² for the dome; 836 uses the height 24 instead of the slant 25.) The answer is E.
text: A toy is in the shape of a right circular cone of base radius 7 cm and vertical height 24 cm, with a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm fixed exactly onto the cone's circular base (so the flat face of the hemisphere coincides with the base of the cone). Find the total exposed surface area of the toy. (Take π = 22/7.)
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Cylinder volume = πr²h = π(9)(10) = 90π cm³. Hemisphere volume = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π(27) = 18π cm³. Removing the hemispherical hollow leaves 90π − 18π = 72π cm³. (54π subtracts a full sphere; 108π adds instead of subtracts; 81π uses (1/3)πr³; 90π ignores the scoop.) The answer is B.
text: A solid right circular cylinder has base radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. A hemispherical hollow of radius 3 cm is scooped out from one of its flat circular ends (the hemisphere's flat face lies on that end). Find the volume of the remaining solid.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Volume is conserved, and sphere volume is proportional to r³, so the new radius R satisfies R³ = 3³ + 4³ + 5³ = 27 + 64 + 125 = 216. Hence R = ∛216 = 6 cm. (12 wrongly adds the radii; 5√2 adds the squares; 5 takes the largest; 4 averages.) The answer is C.
text: Three solid metal spheres of radii 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm are melted together, with no loss of metal, and recast into a single solid sphere. Find the radius of this new sphere.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: When the cone's curved surface is unrolled, it becomes a sector whose radius equals the slant height (24 cm) and whose arc length equals the circumference of the cone's base, 2π(6) = 12π cm. For a sector of radius 24, arc length = (θ/360) × 2π(24). Setting (θ/360) × 48π = 12π gives θ/360 = 12/48 = 1/4, so θ = 90°. Equivalently θ = (r/l) × 360 = (6/24) × 360 = 90°. (1440 inverts the ratio; the others are common guesses.) The answer is D.
text: The curved surface of a right circular cone with base radius 6 cm and slant height 24 cm is cut along a straight line from apex to base and unrolled flat, forming a circular sector. Find the central angle of this sector.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: The submerged cone displaces a volume of water equal to its own volume: V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(7²)(9) = (1/3)π(49)(9) = 147π cm³. This displaced water raises the level in the cylinder, whose base area is π(7²) = 49π cm². Rise = displaced volume / base area = 147π / 49π = 3 cm. (9 forgets the 1/3 factor; 4.5 uses 1/2; 7 and 1 are unrelated guesses.) The answer is E.
text: A cylindrical vessel of base radius 7 cm contains water. A solid right circular cone of base radius 7 cm and height 9 cm is gently lowered, vertex downward, until it is completely submerged, and no water overflows. By how much does the water level in the cylinder rise?
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Let the legs be a = 5, b = 12 and hypotenuse c = 13. The combined shaded area equals (semicircle on a) + (semicircle on b) + (triangle) − (semicircle on c), because the hypotenuse semicircle covers the triangle plus the parts of the leg-semicircles that are not shaded. Semicircle areas are (π/8)a², (π/8)b², (π/8)c². So shaded = (π/8)(a² + b² − c²) + triangle. Since a² + b² = c² (Pythagoras), the π term vanishes, leaving exactly the triangle's area = (1/2)(5)(12) = 30 cm² (the classic lune-of-Hippocrates result). (60 doubles it; 15 halves it; 32.5 and 39 come from mishandling the semicircles.) The answer is A.
text: In a right-angled triangle the two legs measure 5 cm and 12 cm and the hypotenuse measures 13 cm. A semicircle is drawn outward on each of the two legs (each leg as diameter), and a semicircle is drawn on the hypotenuse (hypotenuse as diameter) on the same side as the triangle, so that it overlaps the triangle. The two crescent-shaped regions ('lunes') lying inside the leg-semicircles but outside the hypotenuse-semicircle are shaded. Find the total shaded area.
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: We need 3<sup>1000</sup> mod 1000. Split via CRT into mod 8 and mod 125.Mod 8: 3<sup>2</sup> = 9 ≡ 1, so 3<sup>1000</sup> = (3<sup>2</sup>)<sup>500</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 8).Mod 125: by Euler, φ(125) = 100, and since gcd(3,125)=1 we have 3<sup>100</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 125). Thus 3<sup>1000</sup> = (3<sup>100</sup>)<sup>10</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 125).So 3<sup>1000</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 8) and ≡ 1 (mod 125). The unique residue mod 1000 that is 1 mod 8 and 1 mod 125 is 1 itself.Hence the last three digits are 001. (A common error is to only track the last two digits, giving 01, or to mis-cycle and land on a power of 3 such as 243.) The answer is A.
text: What are the last three digits of 3<sup>1000</sup>?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Use Fermat: since 11 is prime, a<sup>10</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 11) for a not divisible by 11. Reduce the exponent 2019 = 201×10 + 9, so each term equals a<sup>9</sup> (mod 11).3<sup>9</sup>: 3<sup>5</sup> = 243 ≡ 1 (mod 11), so 3<sup>9</sup> = 3<sup>5</sup>·3<sup>4</sup> ≡ 1·81 ≡ 81 − 77 = 4.4<sup>9</sup>: 4<sup>5</sup> = 1024 ≡ 1 (mod 11), so 4<sup>9</sup> = 4<sup>5</sup>·4<sup>4</sup> ≡ 256 ≡ 256 − 253 = 3.5<sup>9</sup>: 5<sup>5</sup> = 3125 ≡ 1 (mod 11), so 5<sup>9</sup> = 5<sup>5</sup>·5<sup>4</sup> ≡ 625 ≡ 625 − 616 = 9.Sum ≡ 4 + 3 + 9 = 16 ≡ 5 (mod 11). The answer is C.
text: What is the remainder when 3<sup>2019</sup> + 4<sup>2019</sup> + 5<sup>2019</sup> is divided by 11?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Every term from 4! onward contains 4! = 24 as a factor, so all of them vanish mod 24. Only 1! + 2! + 3! = 1 + 2 + 6 = 9 survives. The whole 100-term sum collapses to three terms — spotting the stabilisation point is the entire question.
text: What is the remainder when 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 100! is divided by 24?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: The units digit depends only on the units digit of each base, raised to the same exponent (its cyclicity).13<sup>13</sup>: units digit of 3<sup>13</sup>. The cycle of 3 is 3,9,7,1 (period 4); 13 ≡ 1 (mod 4), so units digit = 3.17<sup>17</sup>: units digit of 7<sup>17</sup>. The cycle of 7 is 7,9,3,1 (period 4); 17 ≡ 1 (mod 4), so units digit = 7.19<sup>19</sup>: units digit of 9<sup>19</sup>. The cycle of 9 is 9,1 (period 2); 19 is odd, so units digit = 9.Sum of units digits = 3 + 7 + 9 = 19, whose units digit is 9. The answer is E.
text: What is the units digit of 13<sup>13</sup> + 17<sup>17</sup> + 19<sup>19</sup>?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: The moduli 4, 3, 5 are pairwise coprime with product 60, so by the Chinese Remainder Theorem there is a unique residue mod 60.From N ≡ 4 (mod 5), N ends in candidates 4, 9, 14, 19, 24, 29, … From N ≡ 1 (mod 4), N is odd (since 1 is odd) and one more than a multiple of 4: 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29, …Combine mod 4 and mod 5 (mod 20): need N ≡ 1 (mod 4) and 4 (mod 5). Testing 9: 9 mod 4 = 1, 9 mod 5 = 4, so N ≡ 9 (mod 20): values 9, 29, 49.Now apply N ≡ 2 (mod 3): 9 mod 3 = 0 (fails); 29 mod 3 = 2 (works). So N ≡ 29 (mod 60). The answer is B.
text: A positive integer N leaves remainder 1 when divided by 4, remainder 2 when divided by 3, and remainder 4 when divided by 5. What is the remainder when N is divided by 60?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Build the remainder of a string of k fours mod 7 by appending one digit at a time: r → (10r + 4) mod 7, i.e. r → (3r + 4) mod 7.Starting from 0: 1 four → 4; 2 fours → 3·4+4 = 16 ≡ 2; 3 fours → 3·2+4 = 10 ≡ 3; 4 fours → 3·3+4 = 13 ≡ 6; 5 fours → 3·6+4 = 22 ≡ 1; 6 fours → 3·1+4 = 7 ≡ 0; 7 fours → 3·0+4 = 4. The remainders cycle with period 6: (4, 2, 3, 6, 1, 0).For k = 2024 fours: 2024 mod 6 = 2 (since 2024 = 337×6 + 2). The 2nd entry of the cycle is 2.So the remainder is 2. The answer is B.
text: Let N be the integer formed by writing the digit 4 exactly 2024 times in a row (that is, N = 444…4 with 2024 fours). What is the remainder when N is divided by 7?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Work with units digits. 4343: the digit 3 cycles 3, 9, 7, 1 (period 4); 43 ≡ 3 (mod 4) → units digit 7. 1717: the digit 7 cycles 7, 9, 3, 1; 17 ≡ 1 (mod 4) → units digit 7. The difference ends in 7 − 7 = 0. (4343 is the larger number, so no borrow issues.)
text: What is the remainder when 43<sup>43</sup> − 17<sup>17</sup> is divided by 10?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Reduce each base mod 7 and use negative remainders to simplify.6 ≡ −1 (mod 7), so 6<sup>17</sup> ≡ (−1)<sup>17</sup> = −1 ≡ 6 (mod 7).17 ≡ 3 (mod 7), so 17<sup>6</sup> ≡ 3<sup>6</sup> (mod 7). By Fermat, 3<sup>6</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 7) since 7 is prime and 3 is not divisible by 7.Sum ≡ 6 + 1 = 7 ≡ 0 (mod 7).(Treating 6<sup>17</sup> as +1 instead of −1 gives the trap answer 2.) The answer is A.
text: What is the remainder when 6<sup>17</sup> + 17<sup>6</sup> is divided by 7?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: The last two digits are the sum mod 100. For n ≥ 10, n! contains the factors 2 and 5 at least twice over (indeed 10! already has a factor 100), so n! ≡ 0 (mod 100) for every n ≥ 10. Thus only 1! through 9! contribute.Compute their last two digits: 1!=01, 2!=02, 3!=06, 4!=24, 5!=120→20, 6!=720→20, 7!=5040→40, 8!=40320→20, 9!=362880→80.Sum mod 100: 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 + 20 + 20 + 40 + 20 + 80 = 213 ≡ 13 (mod 100).So the last two digits are 13. (A common slip is to stop at 4! or 5!, or to assume the tail of large factorials wraps to a nonzero value.) The answer is C.
text: What are the last two digits of the sum 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 2024! ?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: We want the multiplicative order of 2 modulo 25 — the least n > 0 with 2<sup>n</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 25). By Euler, φ(25) = 20, so the order must divide 20; the candidate divisors are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20.2<sup>1</sup>=2, 2<sup>2</sup>=4, 2<sup>4</sup>=16, none is 1.2<sup>5</sup> = 32 ≡ 7 (mod 25), not 1.2<sup>10</sup> = (2<sup>5</sup>)<sup>2</sup> ≡ 7<sup>2</sup> = 49 ≡ 24 ≡ −1 (mod 25), not 1.2<sup>20</sup> = (2<sup>10</sup>)<sup>2</sup> ≡ (−1)<sup>2</sup> = 1 (mod 25).Since no smaller divisor of 20 works, the order is 20. (Guessing φ(25)/something, or stopping at 10 where the value is −1, are the usual traps.) The answer is D.
text: What is the smallest positive integer n for which 2<sup>n</sup> leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 25?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Factorise: 540 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3<sup>3</sup> × 5. The number of divisors is d = (2+1)(3+1)(1+1) = 3 × 4 × 2 = 24. The divisors pair up as (e, N/e), and each pair multiplies to N. There are d/2 = 12 such pairs, so the product of all divisors is N<sup>d/2</sup> = 540<sup>12</sup>. (Using 540<sup>24</sup> mistakenly uses d instead of d/2.) The answer is B.
text: Let N = 540. What is the product of all the positive divisors of N? (Express your answer as a power.)
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: A divisor 2<sup>a</sup>3<sup>b</sup>5<sup>c</sup>7<sup>d</sup> is a perfect cube exactly when each of a, b, c, d is a multiple of 3 (including 0). Count the allowed exponents for each prime: for 2<sup>7</sup>, a ∈ {0,3,6} → 3 choices; for 3<sup>9</sup>, b ∈ {0,3,6,9} → 4 choices; for 5<sup>4</sup>, c ∈ {0,3} → 2 choices; for 7<sup>6</sup>, d ∈ {0,3,6} → 3 choices. Multiply: 3 × 4 × 2 × 3 = 72. (2800 = 8×10×5×7 is the total number of divisors; 240 counts perfect-square divisors.) The answer is C.
text: Let M = 2<sup>7</sup> × 3<sup>9</sup> × 5<sup>4</sup> × 7<sup>6</sup>. How many positive divisors of M are perfect cubes?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Factorise: 3600 = 2<sup>4</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>, so the number of divisors is (4+1)(2+1)(2+1) = 45. Since 45 is odd, 3600 is a perfect square (3600 = 60<sup>2</sup>), so one divisor pair is (60, 60) with a = b. Each unordered factorisation pairs a divisor with its complement; the 45 divisors form (45−1)/2 = 22 pairs of distinct factors plus the single repeated pair 60×60 (which is excluded because a ≠ b). Hence there are 22 valid ways. (23 wrongly includes the 60×60 pair.) The answer is D.
text: In how many ways can 3600 be written as a product of two distinct positive integers a × b (where a ≠ b and the order does not matter, so a × b is the same as b × a)?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: By Legendre's formula, the exponent of a prime p in n! is ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p<sup>2</sup>⌋ + ⌊n/p<sup>3</sup>⌋ + …. Here ⌊300/7⌋ = 42, ⌊300/49⌋ = 6, ⌊300/343⌋ = 0. Sum = 42 + 6 = 48. (Stopping at the first term gives the trap 42; it forgets the extra multiples of 49.) The answer is E.
text: What is the exponent of 7 in the prime factorisation of 300! (the product of all integers from 1 to 300)? Equivalently, what is the largest integer k such that 7<sup>k</sup> divides 300! exactly?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Factorise: 1800 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>. The sum of ALL divisors is σ(1800) = (1+2+4+8)(1+3+9)(1+5+25) = 15 × 13 × 31 = 6045. The ODD divisors are exactly the divisors of the odd part 3<sup>2</sup>×5<sup>2</sup> = 225, whose divisor sum is (1+3+9)(1+5+25) = 13 × 31 = 403. The even divisors are all the rest, so their sum is 6045 − 403 = 5642. The answer is B.
text: What is the sum of all the EVEN positive divisors of 1800?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Factorise: 1512 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>3</sup> × 7. For a perfect cube every prime exponent must be a multiple of 3. The exponents of 2 and 3 are already 3 (fine); the exponent of 7 is 1, so it must be raised to 3, requiring two more factors of 7, i.e. multiply by 7<sup>2</sup> = 49. Check: 1512 × 49 = 74088 = 42<sup>3</sup>. (Multiplying by 7 gives 7<sup>2</sup>, still not a cube; 343 = 7<sup>3</sup> overshoots.) The answer is C.
text: What is the smallest positive integer by which 1512 must be multiplied so that the product becomes a perfect cube?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: First convert 2431<sub>5</sub> to base 10: 2×5<sup>3</sup> + 4×5<sup>2</sup> + 3×5 + 1 = 2×125 + 4×25 + 15 + 1 = 250 + 100 + 15 + 1 = 366. Now convert 366 to base 8: 366 = 5×64 + 46, and 46 = 5×8 + 6, so the digits are 5, 5, 6, giving 556<sub>8</sub>. Check: 5×64 + 5×8 + 6 = 320 + 40 + 6 = 366. (366 is the base-10 value, the common trap of not converting.) The answer is A.
text: A number is written as 2431 in base 5 (that is, the base-5 numeral whose digits are 2, 4, 3, 1). What is this same number expressed in base 8?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: All three toll together at multiples of LCM(24, 36, 54). Factorise: 24 = 2<sup>3</sup>×3, 36 = 2<sup>2</sup>×3<sup>2</sup>, 54 = 2×3<sup>3</sup>, so LCM = 2<sup>3</sup>×3<sup>3</sup> = 8×27 = 216 seconds. One hour = 3600 seconds, and ⌊3600/216⌋ = 16 (since 216×16 = 3456 ≤ 3600 < 3672 = 216×17). So after the 8:00:00 start there are 16 further simultaneous tolls (the 16th at 8:57:36; the 17th would come at 3672 s = 61 min 12 s past 8:00, i.e. 9:01:12, beyond the hour). The answer is B.
text: Three bells toll at intervals of 24, 36 and 54 seconds respectively. They all toll together exactly at 8:00:00 AM. How many more times will all three bells toll together during the next one hour (that is, after 8:00:00 AM up to and including 9:00:00 AM)?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: If a divisor d leaves the same remainder for all three numbers, then d divides each pairwise difference. Differences: 4665 − 1305 = 3360, 6905 − 4665 = 2240, 6905 − 1305 = 5600. The largest such d is gcd(3360, 2240, 5600). Now 3360 = 2<sup>5</sup>×3×5×7, 2240 = 2<sup>6</sup>×5×7, 5600 = 2<sup>5</sup>×5<sup>2</sup>×7; the common part is 2<sup>5</sup>×5×7 = 1120. Check: 1305 = 1120 + 185, 4665 = 4×1120 + 185, 6905 = 6×1120 + 185 — each leaves remainder 185. (185 is the common remainder, not the divisor.) The answer is A.
text: What is the largest positive integer that divides each of 1305, 4665 and 6905, leaving the SAME remainder in every case?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Factorise: 7200 = 2<sup>5</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>. Write x = 2<sup>a1</sup>3<sup>b1</sup>5<sup>c1</sup> and y = 2<sup>a2</sup>3<sup>b2</sup>5<sup>c2</sup>. The LCM condition means, for each prime, the larger of the two exponents equals the exponent in 7200. For a prime with exponent e, the number of ordered pairs (i, j) with max(i, j) = e is 2e + 1 (either i = e with j from 0..e, or j = e with i from 0..e−1). So the count is (2×5+1)(2×2+1)(2×2+1) = 11 × 5 × 5 = 275. (138 is the count of UNordered pairs; 54 is the total number of divisors.) The answer is C.
text: How many ordered pairs (x, y) of positive integers satisfy LCM(x, y) = 7200? (Here (a, b) and (b, a) are counted as different ordered pairs.)
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: The letters in alphabetical order are A, E, M, R, S, T. Count how many words come strictly before MASTER, position by position.1st letter M: letters before M are {A, E} = 2 letters. Each fixes the first letter and permutes the remaining 5: 2 × 5! = 2 × 120 = 240.2nd letter A (smallest remaining {A,E,R,S,T}): 0 letters before it: 0 × 4! = 0.3rd letter S, remaining pool {E,R,S,T}: before S are {E,R} = 2: 2 × 3! = 12.4th letter T, remaining pool {E,R,T}: before T are {E,R} = 2: 2 × 2! = 4.5th letter E, remaining pool {E,R}: before E = 0: 0 × 1! = 0.6th letter R, remaining {R}: 0.Words before MASTER = 240 + 0 + 12 + 4 + 0 + 0 = 256. So MASTER is at rank 256 + 1 = 257. (Choice 256 forgets the +1; 720 is the total count.) The answer is B.
text: All 6 letters of the word MASTER (all distinct) are used to form every possible 6-letter "word," and these words are then listed in dictionary (alphabetical) order. What is the rank (position) of the word MASTER in this list?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Seat the men first. Around a circular table, arranging the 5 men in alternating positions fixes a circular pattern; the number of distinct circular arrangements of the 5 men is (5 − 1)! = 4! = 24. Once the men are seated, the 5 gaps between them are now distinguishable (each gap sits between two specific men), so the 5 women can be placed in those 5 gaps in 5! = 120 ways. Total = 24 × 120 = 2880. (Choice 14400 = 5! × 5! double-counts by not removing one rotational degree of freedom; 576 = 4! × 4! wrongly fixes both groups circularly.) The answer is B.
text: Five men and five women are to be seated around a circular table (seats are distinguished only by who sits next to whom) so that the seats strictly alternate between men and women. In how many distinct ways can this be done?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Since no couple may be fully represented, each chosen person must come from a different couple. A 4-person committee with no two people from the same couple must therefore draw exactly one person from each of the 4 couples. From each couple choose 1 of its 2 members: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2<sup>4</sup> = 16.Check by inclusion-exclusion: total C(8,4) = 70; subtract committees containing at least one full couple. Containing a chosen couple: 4 ways to pick that couple × C(6,2) = 15 for the other two seats = 60; add back those containing two full couples: C(4,2) = 6. Bad = 60 − 6 = 54, so good = 70 − 54 = 16. (70 is the unrestricted total; 54 is the count to subtract.) The answer is D.
text: From 4 married couples (8 people in total), a committee of 4 people is to be selected. The committee must NOT contain both members of any single couple. How many such committees are possible?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: First arrange the 7 non-S letters: M, I, I, I, I, P, P. The number of distinct arrangements of these is 7! / (4! × 2!) = 5040 / (24 × 2) = 105. Lining up 7 letters creates 8 gaps (including the two ends) into which S's may go: _ X _ X _ X _ X _ X _ X _ X _. To keep the four S's mutually non-adjacent, choose 4 of these 8 gaps, one S per chosen gap: C(8,4) = 70. Since all four S's are identical, no further factor is needed. Total = 105 × 70 = 7350. (34650 is the total number of arrangements with no restriction.) The answer is B.
text: In how many distinct arrangements of all 11 letters of the word MISSISSIPPI do no two S's stand next to each other? (The word contains one M, four I's, four S's, and two P's.)
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: A path from (0,0) to (5,5) uses 5 E's and 5 N's. The condition y ≤ x at every step means that reading the path left to right, the number of N's never exceeds the number of E's at any prefix — exactly the ballot/Dyck-path condition. The number of such paths is the 5th Catalan number: C<sub>5</sub> = C(10,5) / (5 + 1) = 252 / 6 = 42. (252 = C(10,5) is the count of all monotonic paths; 126 = 252/2 is the naive "half" answer that wrongly assumes symmetry handles the touching/boundary cases; 132 = C<sub>6</sub>.) The answer is C.
text: A token starts at the origin (0,0) and moves to (5,5) on a grid, taking unit steps either one unit East (E) or one unit North (N). How many such monotonic paths never rise above the diagonal line y = x — that is, at every point (x, y) reached along the path, y ≤ x? (The path may touch the diagonal.)
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Remove the lower bounds by substitution. Let y<sub>1</sub> = x<sub>1</sub> − 2 ≥ 0 and y<sub>5</sub> = x<sub>5</sub> − 3 ≥ 0, keeping x<sub>2</sub>, x<sub>3</sub>, x<sub>4</sub> as they are. The equation becomes y<sub>1</sub> + x<sub>2</sub> + x<sub>3</sub> + x<sub>4</sub> + y<sub>5</sub> = 12 − 2 − 3 = 7, with all five new variables ≥ 0. The number of non-negative integer solutions of a 5-variable sum equal to 7 is, by stars and bars, C(7 + 5 − 1, 5 − 1) = C(11, 4) = 330. (1820 = C(16,4) ignores both constraints; 495 = C(12,4) subtracts only one unit somewhere; 210 = C(10,4) over-subtracts.) The answer is C.
text: How many solutions in non-negative integers (x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub>, x<sub>3</sub>, x<sub>4</sub>, x<sub>5</sub>) does the equation x<sub>1</sub> + x<sub>2</sub> + x<sub>3</sub> + x<sub>4</sub> + x<sub>5</sub> = 12 have, subject to x<sub>1</sub> ≥ 2 and x<sub>5</sub> ≥ 3 (the other three variables are unrestricted non-negative integers)?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: A 4-digit number from these digits is greater than 5000 exactly when its thousands digit is in {5, 6, 7} (the smallest such, 5123, already exceeds 5000). It is even when its units digit is in {2, 4, 6}. The digit 6 lies in both sets, so split on whether 6 is used as the thousands or units digit.Case A — units digit = 6: thousands digit from {5, 7} (2 choices); the two middle digits are any distinct choices from the remaining 5 digits in order: 5 × 4 = 20. Subtotal = 2 × 20 = 40.Case B — units digit ∈ {2, 4} (2 choices) and units ≠ 6: thousands digit from {5, 6, 7} (3 choices); middle two from remaining 5: 5 × 4 = 20. Subtotal = 2 × 3 × 20 = 120.Total = 40 + 120 = 160. (180 = 3 × 3 × 20 ignores the conflict over the shared digit 6.) The answer is B.
text: Using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 with no digit repeated, how many 4-digit numbers can be formed that are both even AND greater than 5000?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: If the groups were labeled (Group A, B, C), the count would be the multinomial 12! / (4! × 4! × 4!) = C(12,4) × C(8,4) × C(4,4) = 495 × 70 × 1 = 34650. But the three groups are unlabeled and all have the same size 4, so each distinct partition has been counted 3! = 6 times (once for each way of labeling the three equal-size groups). Divide: 34650 / 6 = 5775. (34650 is the labeled count; 17325 = 34650/2 wrongly divides by 2! instead of 3!.) The answer is C.
text: In how many ways can 12 distinct students be divided into 3 groups of 4 students each, when the groups are unlabeled (interchangeable — only who is grouped with whom matters)?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Any valid East/North route reaches the two checkpoints in the order (3,2) then (4,4), since both coordinates increase. Split the journey into three legs and multiply the path counts.Leg 1 — (0,0) to (3,2): 3 E and 2 N steps, C(5,2) = 10 ways.Leg 2 — (3,2) to (4,4): 1 E and 2 N steps, C(3,1) = 3 ways.Leg 3 — (4,4) to (6,5): 2 E and 1 N steps, C(3,1) = 3 ways.Total = 10 × 3 × 3 = 90. (462 = C(11,5) counts all routes ignoring the stops; 200 counts routes through (3,2) only; 210 counts routes through (4,4) only.) The answer is C.
text: On a city grid, a delivery rider travels from intersection (0,0) to intersection (6,5), at each step moving either one block East or one block North. To make two scheduled stops, the route must pass through BOTH the intersection (3,2) and the intersection (4,4). How many distinct routes satisfy this requirement?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Let x and y be the arrival times in minutes after 5:00, each uniform on [0, 60], so (x, y) is uniform over a 60×60 square of area 3600. They meet exactly when |x − y| ≤ 20. It is easier to find the complement: |x − y| > 20 consists of two right triangles, each with legs of length 60 − 20 = 40. Each triangle has area ½×40×40 = 800, so the 'miss' region has area 1600. Thus P(miss) = 1600/3600 = 4/9, and P(meet) = 1 − 4/9 = 5/9. (Choosing 4/9 forgets to take the complement; 1/3 wrongly uses 20/60.) The answer is C.
text: Anu and Bob each agree to arrive at a cafe at some moment chosen independently and uniformly at random between 5:00 pm and 6:00 pm. Whoever arrives first waits exactly 20 minutes for the other and then leaves. What is the probability that the two actually meet?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Treat all 5 balls as occupying 5 ordered positions, with the 3 red positions equally likely to be any 3 of the 5 slots: there are C(5,3) = 10 equally likely arrangements of the reds. We need the 2nd red to land exactly in position 4, which requires exactly one red among the first three positions and a red in position 4 (the third red then occupies position 5). So the red positions are {one of positions 1-3, position 4, position 5}; there are 3 choices for the single early red, giving 3 favorable arrangements. The probability is 3/10. (2/5 is the maximum, attained at position 3, a tempting wrong pick.) The answer is A.
text: An urn contains 3 red balls and 2 black balls. The balls are drawn one at a time, without replacement, until the urn is empty. What is the probability that the second red ball drawn appears exactly on the 4th draw?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: By symmetry, before any information each key is equally likely to be the correct one, so the lock opens on try k with probability 1/5 for each k from 1 to 5. We are told the correct key is not among the first two tried, which had prior probability 3/5. Then P(opens on 3rd | not in first two) = P(opens on 3rd)/P(not in first two) = (1/5)/(3/5) = 1/3. Equivalently, given the failures, the correct key is equally likely to be any of the 3 untried keys, so the next try succeeds with probability 1/3. (Answer 1/5 ignores the conditioning.) The answer is D.
text: A drawer holds 5 identical-looking keys, exactly one of which opens a certain lock. You try the keys one at a time, without replacement, until the lock opens. Given that the first two keys you tried did NOT open the lock, what is the probability that the third key you try opens it?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: The prior probabilities are P(Box 1) = 1/3 and P(Box 2) = 2/3. The chance of drawing gold from each box is P(gold | Box 1) = 2/5 and P(gold | Box 2) = 4/5. By total probability, P(gold) = (1/3)(2/5) + (2/3)(4/5) = 2/15 + 8/15 = 10/15 = 2/3. By Bayes' rule, P(Box 2 | gold) = [(2/3)(4/5)] / (2/3) = (8/15)/(10/15) = 8/10 = 4/5. (Choosing 2/3 just reuses the prior and ignores the gold evidence; 1/5 is P(Box 1 | gold).) The answer is E.
text: Two boxes sit on a table. Box 1 contains 2 gold coins and 3 silver coins; Box 2 contains 4 gold coins and 1 silver coin. A box is selected at random, but not equally: Box 2 is twice as likely to be chosen as Box 1. One coin is then drawn at random from the chosen box and it turns out to be gold. What is the probability that the coin came from Box 2?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: The number of rolls until the first 6 is geometric with success probability 1/6, so its expectation is 6. Of these, the last roll is the 6, so the expected number of non-6 rolls (each worth $2) is 6 − 1 = 5. Hence the expected gain from non-6 rolls is 2 × 5 = $10, and you always pay the $5 penalty on the terminal six. Net expected value = 10 − 5 = $5. (Using 6 instead of 5 non-six rolls gives the trap value 2×6 − 5 = $7.) The answer is B.
text: You roll a fair six-sided die repeatedly and stop the moment a 6 first appears. For every roll that shows a number other than 6 you earn $2, but on the final roll (the one that shows the 6) you pay a $5 penalty. What is the expected value of your net earnings for the whole game?
