title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: The total number of committees is C(10,4) = 210. 'At least 2 women' means exactly 2 or exactly 3 women (there are only 3 women). Exactly 2 women: C(3,2)×C(7,2) = 3×21 = 63. Exactly 3 women: C(3,3)×C(7,1) = 1×7 = 7. So favorable = 63 + 7 = 70, and the probability is 70/210 = 1/3. (Equivalently, subtract P(0 women)=35/210 and P(1 woman)=105/210 from 1.) The trap 5/6 answers 'at least 1 woman', and 3/10 is 'exactly 2 women'. The answer is C.
text: A committee of 4 people is to be chosen at random from a group of 7 men and 3 women. What is the probability that the committee contains at least 2 women?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: The sum is even exactly when both dice are even or both are odd. Both even: 3×3 = 9 outcomes; both odd: 3×3 = 9 outcomes; so the conditioning event has 18 outcomes. For the product to be divisible by 4: if both numbers are odd, the product is odd, never divisible by 4 (0 of those 9). If both are even, each is a multiple of 2, so the product carries at least 2×2 = 4 and is always divisible by 4 (all 9 of those qualify). Favorable = 9 out of 18, giving 9/18 = 1/2. (5/12 is the unconditional probability that the product is divisible by 4, ignoring the given even-sum condition.) The answer is C.
text: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Given that the sum of the two numbers shown is even, what is the probability that the product of the two numbers is divisible by 4?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Let the two break points be x and y, chosen uniformly and independently on [0, 1]; the point (x, y) is uniform over the unit square. The three pieces can form a triangle exactly when every piece is shorter than 1/2 (if any piece were ≥ 1/2 it would exceed the sum of the other two, violating the triangle inequality). Splitting by which break is on the left, in the region x < y the three pieces are x, y − x, 1 − y, and the conditions x < 1/2, y > 1/2, y − x < 1/2 cut out a triangle of area 1/8; the symmetric region x > y contributes another 1/8. Total favorable area = 1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4. So the probability is 1/4. (1/2 is a common wrong guess from mishandling the inequalities.) The answer is B.
text: A straight stick of length 1 is broken at two points whose positions are chosen independently and uniformly at random along its length, producing three pieces. What is the probability that the three resulting pieces can be arranged to form a triangle?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Let the numbers enrolled in exactly one, exactly two, and exactly three classes be a, b, c. Since everyone takes at least one class, a + b + c = 220. We are told a = 140, so b + c = 80.Now sum the three class sizes. A member in exactly one class is counted once, in exactly two classes is counted twice, and in all three is counted three times:130 + 110 + 85 = a + 2b + 3c, i.e. 325 = 140 + 2b + 3c, so 2b + 3c = 185.Subtract twice the relation b + c = 80 (which gives 2b + 2c = 160) from 2b + 3c = 185:c = 185 − 160 = 25.(Then b = 55, and a + b + c = 140 + 55 + 25 = 220 checks out.) Note 55 is the exactly-two count, not the answer; and (325−220)/2 = 52.5 is the wrong 'two-set' shortcut. The answer is E.
text: Every one of 220 gym members is enrolled in at least one of three classes: Yoga, Pilates, or Spin.• 130 are enrolled in Yoga, 110 in Pilates, and 85 in Spin.• Exactly 140 members are enrolled in exactly one of the three classes.How many members are enrolled in all three classes?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: The number using 'none' is maximized when the number using at least one facility is minimized. The set of users must contain everyone who uses the Library (150), so it has at least 150 students. We can make it exactly 150 by placing all Lab users (120 ≤ 150) and all Gym users (90 ≤ 150) inside that same group of 150 Library users — this is possible because each smaller set fits within the largest.So the minimum possible number of users is max(150, 120, 90) = 150, giving a maximum 'none' count of 200 − 150 = 50.Traps: 200 − (150+120+90) treats the totals as disjoint (impossible here); 200 − 90 = 110 wrongly uses the smallest set. The answer is A.
text: In a group of 200 students, 150 use the Library, 120 use the Lab, and 90 use the Gym during a given week. A student may use any number of these three facilities, including none.What is the largest possible number of students who use none of the three facilities that week?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: Let t be the number who visited all three cities. By inclusion-exclusion, since everyone visited at least one city the union is 300:300 = (180+150+120) − (80+60+50) + t = 450 − 190 + t = 260 + t, so t = 40.The pairwise-overlap counts include those who visited all three. The number who visited exactly two equals the sum of pairwise overlaps minus three times the triple overlap (each all-three tourist is counted in all three pairwise totals):exactly two = 190 − 3(40) = 190 − 120 = 70.(Check: exactly one = 450 − 2×190 + 3×40 = 190; 190 + 70 + 40 = 300.) The trap 190 forgets to remove the triple-counted all-three visitors. The answer is B.
text: Each of 300 tourists visited at least one of three cities: Athens, Berlin, or Cairo.• 180 visited Athens, 150 visited Berlin, 120 visited Cairo.• 80 visited both Athens and Berlin, 60 visited both Berlin and Cairo, 50 visited both Athens and Cairo.How many tourists visited exactly two of the three cities?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: Let x be the total number who play table tennis; then the total who play chess is 2x. The number who play at least one game is 50 − 2 (neither) = 48.By inclusion-exclusion for two sets:(chess) + (table tennis) − (both) = (at least one)2x + x − 12 = 48, so 3x = 60 and x = 20.Therefore chess = 2x = 40. (Check: table tennis = 20, both = 12, so chess-only = 28 and TT-only = 8; 28 + 8 + 12 = 48, valid.)Traps: 20 is the table-tennis total, not chess; 48 is the number playing at least one game; 28 = 40 − 12 subtracts 'both' incorrectly. The answer is C.
text: In a class of 50 students, every student plays chess, table tennis, both, or neither. The total number who play chess is exactly twice the total number who play table tennis. 12 students play both games, and 2 students play neither.How many students play chess?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: From 'at least two = 70' and 'all three = 18', the number reading exactly two is 70 − 18 = 52.The sum of the three pairwise-overlap counts (|A∩B| + |B∩C| + |A∩C|) counts each exactly-two reader once and each all-three reader three times, so it equals 52 + 3(18) = 52 + 54 = 106.By inclusion-exclusion, the number reading at least one magazine is:(120+110+100) − 106 + 18 = 330 − 106 + 18 = 242.Therefore none = 250 − 242 = 8.Traps: using 70 directly as the pairwise-overlap sum, or forgetting to add back the all-three term, both push the union above 250 (giving an impossible negative 'none'). The answer is D.
text: A club of 250 members was surveyed about three magazines: A, B, and C.• 120 read A, 110 read B, 100 read C.• Exactly 18 members read all three magazines.• Exactly 70 members read at least two of the three magazines.How many members read none of the three magazines?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: The number owning at least one pet is 400 − 50 = 350.By inclusion-exclusion: 350 = (220+180+90) − (sum of pairwise overlaps) + 30. With the set-size total 490, this gives:sum of pairwise overlaps = 490 + 30 − 350 = 170.The number owning exactly two pets equals the pairwise-overlap sum minus three times the all-three count: 170 − 3(30) = 170 − 90 = 80.The 350 owners split into exactly-one, exactly-two, and all-three groups:exactly one = 350 − 80 − 30 = 240.Traps: 320 = 350 − 30 forgets the exactly-two group; 80 is the exactly-two count itself. The answer is B.
text: In a neighborhood of 400 people, 220 own a dog, 180 own a cat, and 90 own a bird. Exactly 50 people own none of these pets, and exactly 30 people own all three.How many people own exactly one of the three pets?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: When the motorcycle starts, the car is already 40 × 3 = 120 km ahead. The motorcycle closes this gap at the relative speed 60 − 40 = 20 km/h, so it needs 120 / 20 = 6 hours to catch up. In those 6 hours the motorcycle covers 60 × 6 = 360 km, which is the distance from the depot. (Check: the car's total time is 3 + 6 = 9 h, distance 40 × 9 = 360 km — equal, confirming the meeting point.) The answer is A.
text: A car leaves a depot travelling along a straight highway at a constant 40 km/h. Exactly 3 hours later a motorcycle leaves the same depot along the same highway at a constant 60 km/h, chasing the car. How far from the depot is the point at which the motorcycle draws level with the car?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Let the escalator contribute e steps per second and N be the visible steps. The boy at 1 step/s takes 25 s to make his 25 steps, during which the escalator adds 25e steps, so N = 25 + 25e. The girl at 2 steps/s takes 40/2 = 20 s, so N = 40 + 20e. Equating: 25 + 25e = 40 + 20e ⇒ 5e = 15 ⇒ e = 3. Then N = 25 + 25(3) = 100 (and N = 40 + 20(3) = 100 checks). The answer is D.
text: An escalator moves steadily upward at a constant number of steps per second. A boy who climbs at 1 step per second reaches the top having counted 25 steps under his own feet. A girl who climbs at 2 steps per second reaches the top having counted 40 steps. How many steps are visible on the escalator when it is switched off?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: After three identical draw-and-replace operations the fraction of original milk remaining is (1 − x/64)³. Since milk : water = 27 : 37, milk is 27/(27+37) = 27/64 of the 64 litres. So (1 − x/64)³ = 27/64. Taking cube roots, and using 27/64 = (3/4)³, we get 1 − x/64 = 3/4. Thus x/64 = 1/4 and x = 16. (Check: (1 − 16/64)³ = (3/4)³ = 27/64.) The answer is C.
text: A vessel contains 64 litres of pure milk. The following operation is performed three times in succession: a fixed quantity of x litres is drawn off and replaced by x litres of water, the mixture being stirred uniformly each time. After the three operations the ratio of milk to water in the vessel is 27 : 37. Find x.
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Per 5 kg of mixture there are 3 kg at ₹50 (= ₹150) and 2 kg at ₹75 (= ₹150), a total cost of ₹300 for 5 kg, i.e. a cost price of ₹60 per kg. Selling at 25% profit gives 60 × 1.25 = ₹75 per kg. (The ₹78.75 trap uses the reversed 2 : 3 ratio, giving a cost of ₹63 per kg.) The answer is B.
text: A trader mixes two varieties of rice, one costing ₹50 per kg and the other ₹75 per kg, in the ratio 3 : 2 by weight. He sells the whole mixture at a profit of 25%. At what price per kg does he sell the mixture?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Convert speeds: 54 km/h = 15 m/s, 36 km/h = 10 m/s. Since they move the same way, the relative speed is 15 − 10 = 5 m/s. To overtake completely, the faster train must cover the combined length 180 + 120 = 300 m relative to the slower train. Time = 300 / 5 = 60 seconds. (The 12 s trap uses the opposite-direction relative speed 25 m/s.) The answer is C.
text: A 180-metre-long train running at 54 km/h is on the same track as, and behind, a 120-metre-long train running in the same direction at 36 km/h. How long does the faster train take to completely overtake (pass) the slower one, measured from when its front reaches the slower train's rear until its rear clears the slower train's front?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Arun's daily work is 1/10, Bela's is 1/15. Over each Arun–Bela pair of days they complete 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 of the task. After 5 such pairs (10 days) they have done 5/6, with 1/6 left. Day 11 is Arun's: he does 1/10, leaving 1/6 − 1/10 = 5/30 − 3/30 = 2/30 = 1/15. Day 12 is Bela's: she does exactly 1/15, finishing the job. Total = 12 days. (6 days is the trap from assuming they always work together.) The answer is E.
text: Working alone, Arun can finish a task in 10 days and Bela can finish the same task in 15 days. They work on alternate days — Arun on day 1, Bela on day 2, Arun on day 3, and so on. In how many days is the task completed?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: The last two digits means the value mod 100. Since gcd(23, 100) = 1, exponents can be reduced modulo the Carmichael function λ(100) = lcm(λ(4), λ(25)) = lcm(2, 20) = 20 (Euler's totient φ(100) = 40 also works here). So we need the exponent 23<sup>23</sup> mod 20.Compute 23<sup>23</sup> mod 20: 23 ≡ 3 (mod 20). The powers of 3 mod 20 cycle with period 4: 3<sup>1</sup> = 3, 3<sup>2</sup> = 9, 3<sup>3</sup> = 27 ≡ 7, 3<sup>4</sup> = 81 ≡ 1. Since 23 ≡ 3 (mod 4), 3<sup>23</sup> ≡ 3<sup>3</sup> ≡ 7 (mod 20). So the exponent is ≡ 7 (mod 20).Therefore 23<sup>(23<sup>23</sup>)</sup> ≡ 23<sup>7</sup> (mod 100). Reduce step by step: 23<sup>2</sup> = 529 ≡ 29; 23<sup>4</sup> ≡ 29<sup>2</sup> = 841 ≡ 41; 23<sup>7</sup> = 23<sup>4</sup> · 23<sup>2</sup> · 23 ≡ 41 × 29 × 23. Now 41 × 29 = 1189 ≡ 89, and 89 × 23 = 2047 ≡ 47 (mod 100). So the last two digits are 47.(A common trap is to compute only the single level 23<sup>23</sup> mod 100 = 67, ignoring the tower.) The answer is 47.
text: What are the last two digits of the power tower 23<sup>(23<sup>23</sup>)</sup> ?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: The four moduli 5, 7, 9, 11 are pairwise coprime, so by the Chinese Remainder Theorem there is a unique solution modulo 5 × 7 × 9 × 11 = 3465. Solve in stages.Start with N ≡ 2 (mod 5) and N ≡ 3 (mod 7). Write N = 5k + 2; then 5k + 2 ≡ 3 (mod 7), so 5k ≡ 1 (mod 7). Since 5<sup>−1</sup> ≡ 3 (mod 7) (because 5 × 3 = 15 ≡ 1), k ≡ 3 (mod 7). Thus N ≡ 5(3) + 2 = 17 (mod 35).Combine with N ≡ 4 (mod 9). Write N = 35m + 17; then 35m + 17 ≡ 4 (mod 9), i.e. 8m + 8 ≡ 4, so 8m ≡ −4 ≡ 5 (mod 9). Since 8 ≡ −1, this is −m ≡ 5, so m ≡ 4 (mod 9). Then N ≡ 35(4) + 17 = 157 (mod 315).Combine with N ≡ 5 (mod 11). Write N = 315t + 157; then 315t + 157 ≡ 5 (mod 11). Now 315 = 28·11 + 7 so 315 ≡ 7, and 157 = 14·11 + 3 so 157 ≡ 3. Thus 7t + 3 ≡ 5, so 7t ≡ 2 (mod 11). Since 7<sup>−1</sup> ≡ 8 (mod 11) (7 × 8 = 56 ≡ 1), t ≡ 16 ≡ 5 (mod 11). The smallest non-negative t is 5, giving N = 315(5) + 157 = 1575 + 157 = 1732.Check: 1732 = 5·346 + 2, = 7·247 + 3, = 9·192 + 4, = 11·157 + 5. The answer is 1732.
text: What is the smallest positive integer N that simultaneously leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5, remainder 3 when divided by 7, remainder 4 when divided by 9, and remainder 5 when divided by 11?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: By the power of a point P, the square of the tangent length equals the product of the two secant segments measured from P: PT<sup>2</sup> = PA · PB.We are told PB = 4 · PA, so substitute: PT<sup>2</sup> = PA · (4 · PA) = 4 · PA<sup>2</sup>. With PT = 10 this gives 100 = 4 · PA<sup>2</sup>, so PA<sup>2</sup> = 25 and PA = 5.Then PB = 4 × 5 = 20. Since A lies between P and B on the secant, the chord AB = PB − PA = 20 − 5 = 15.Verify the power relation: PA · PB = 5 × 20 = 100 = 10<sup>2</sup> = PT<sup>2</sup>. (Common traps: stopping at PA = 5, reporting the far distance PB = 20, or copying PT = 10.) The answer is 15.
text: From an external point P, a tangent line touches a circle at T with PT = 10. A secant line from P cuts the circle at A (the nearer point) and B (the farther point). It is given that PB = 4 × PA. What is the length of the chord AB?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: Because AC is a diameter, every angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle, so ∠ABC = 90° and ∠ADC = 90°. Thus triangles ABC and ADC are right-angled at B and D respectively, with AC as common hypotenuse.From right triangle ABC: AC = √(AB<sup>2</sup> + BC<sup>2</sup>) = √(7<sup>2</sup> + 24<sup>2</sup>) = √(49 + 576) = √625 = 25 (the 7−24−25 triple). So the diameter AC = 25.From right triangle ADC: DC = √(AC<sup>2</sup> − AD<sup>2</sup>) = √(625 − 225) = √400 = 20 (the 15−20−25 triple).Now apply Ptolemy's theorem to cyclic quadrilateral ABCD: the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides:AC · BD = AB · CD + BC · AD.So 25 · BD = 7 × 20 + 24 × 15 = 140 + 360 = 500, giving BD = 500 ÷ 25 = 20.(Traps: forgetting the diameter forces right angles, or reusing a side length such as 15 or 24.) The answer is 20.
text: Cyclic quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in a circle, and its diagonal AC is a diameter of the circle. The sides satisfy AB = 7, BC = 24, and AD = 15. What is the length of the other diagonal, BD?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: Split the task into two independent choices. First, choose which 2 of the 5 distinct boxes are the empty ones: this can be done in C(5, 2) = 10 ways.Second, the remaining 3 boxes must together hold all 12 identical balls with each of these 3 boxes receiving at least 1 ball (otherwise more than two boxes would be empty). The number of positive-integer solutions of y<sub>1</sub> + y<sub>2</sub> + y<sub>3</sub> = 12 with every y<sub>i</sub> ≥ 1 is, by stars and bars, C(12 − 1, 3 − 1) = C(11, 2) = 55.Since the two choices are independent, multiply: 10 × 55 = 550.(Traps: forgetting the 'at least 1' surjection requirement and using C(13, 2) = 78 per choice, giving 780; or omitting the box-selection factor and reporting just 55.) The answer is 550.
text: In how many ways can 12 identical balls be distributed among 5 distinct boxes so that exactly two of the boxes end up empty?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Use inclusion-exclusion on the three 'bad' events, where event E<sub>i</sub> is 'the i-th feuding pair sits together'. Total unrestricted arrangements of 8 distinct people: 8! = 40320.For a chosen set of k pairs forced together, glue each such pair into a single block (the two people inside can be ordered in 2! ways), leaving 8 − k objects to arrange: (8 − k)! × 2<sup>k</sup> arrangements, and there are C(3, k) ways to choose which pairs are glued.k = 1: C(3,1) · 2<sup>1</sup> · 7! = 3 × 2 × 5040 = 30240.k = 2: C(3,2) · 2<sup>2</sup> · 6! = 3 × 4 × 720 = 8640.k = 3: C(3,3) · 2<sup>3</sup> · 5! = 1 × 8 × 120 = 960.By inclusion-exclusion, the number with no feuding pair adjacent is8! − 30240 + 8640 − 960 = 40320 − 30240 + 8640 − 960 = 17760.(Traps: stopping after one subtraction gives 40320 − 30240 = 10080; mis-signing the terms or dropping the 2<sup>k</sup> block factor gives 25200 or 30240.) The answer is 17760.
text: Eight distinct people are to be seated in a single row of 8 chairs. Among them there are three particular pairs of feuding people: (P<sub>1</sub>, P<sub>2</sub>), (P<sub>3</sub>, P<sub>4</sub>), and (P<sub>5</sub>, P<sub>6</sub>) — six distinct individuals forming three disjoint pairs. In how many arrangements is it true that no feuding pair sits in two adjacent chairs?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Multiply both sides by the conjugate: (√(x+15) − √x)(√(x+15) + √x) = (x+15) − x = 15. Since the sum equals 15, the difference must equal 15/15 = 1, so √(x+15) − √x = 1. Adding this to the original equation: 2√(x+15) = 16, so √(x+15) = 8 and x + 15 = 64, giving x = 49. Check: √64 + √49 = 8 + 7 = 15. (Choosing 64 is the classic slip of solving for x + 15 instead of x.) The answer is D.
text: A real number x satisfies √(x + 15) + √x = 15. What is the value of x?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Let s = x + y and p = xy. The first equation gives p + s = 23. The second is xy(x + y) = ps = 120. So s and p are roots of t² − 23t + 120 = 0, i.e. (t − 8)(t − 15) = 0, giving {s, p} = {8, 15}. If s = 15, p = 8, then x and y solve t² − 15t + 8 = 0, which has no integer roots. So s = 8, p = 15, giving integers x = 3, y = 5. Then x² + y² = s² − 2p = 64 − 30 = 34. (209 comes from wrongly taking s = 15, p = 8.) The answer is A.
text: Positive integers x and y satisfy xy + x + y = 23 and x<sup>2</sup>y + xy<sup>2</sup> = 120. What is the value of x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup>?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Let the speed be v and distance D. Faster case: D/v − D/(v+10) = 1, so 10D = v(v+10). Slower case: D/(v−10) − D/v = 1.5, so 10D = 1.5·v(v−10). Setting them equal: v + 10 = 1.5(v − 10), so v + 10 = 1.5v − 15, giving 0.5v = 25 and v = 50 km/h. Then 10D = 50 × 60 = 3000, so D = 300 km. Check: at 50 km/h the trip takes 6 h; at 60 km/h it takes 5 h (1 less); at 40 km/h it takes 7.5 h (1.5 more). The answer is C.
text: A train covers a fixed route at a constant speed. If its speed were 10 km/h greater, it would take 1 hour less; if its speed were 10 km/h smaller, it would take 1.5 hours more. What is the length of the route, in km?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: If the integer roots are p and q, then pq = 72 and b = −(p + q). Since 72 > 0, the roots have the same sign. Positive factor pairs of 72: (1,72), (2,36), (3,24), (4,18), (6,12), (8,9), giving sums 73, 38, 27, 22, 18, 17 — six distinct values, hence six negative values of b. The negative pairs give the same six sums with opposite sign, hence six positive values of b. No pair has equal roots (72 is not a perfect square), and no overlap occurs, so there are 6 + 6 = 12 values. (Answering 6 forgets the negative-root pairs; 24 double-counts ordered pairs.) The answer is E.
text: The quadratic equation x<sup>2</sup> + bx + 72 = 0 has two integer roots (not necessarily distinct). How many different integer values of b are possible?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: From x² = x + 1, reduce powers step by step. x³ = x·x² = x² + x = (x + 1) + x = 2x + 1. x⁴ = x·x³ = 2x² + x = 2(x + 1) + x = 3x + 2. x⁵ = x·x⁴ = 3x² + 2x = 3(x + 1) + 2x = 5x + 3. So a = 5, b = 3 and a + b = 8. (The coefficients are Fibonacci numbers; picking 7 or 13 comes from stopping one power too early or going one too far.) The answer is B.
text: Let x be the positive root of x<sup>2</sup> − x − 1 = 0. Then x<sup>5</sup> can be written as ax + b, where a and b are integers. What is a + b?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Take each candle's initial length as 1. After t hours the first has length 1 − t/4 and the second 1 − t/3. Require 1 − t/4 = 2(1 − t/3), i.e. 1 − t/4 = 2 − 2t/3. Then 2t/3 − t/4 = 1, so (8t − 3t)/12 = 1, giving 5t/12 = 1 and t = 12/5 hours = 2.4 hours = 2 hours 24 minutes. Check: at t = 2.4, lengths are 1 − 0.6 = 0.4 and 1 − 0.8 = 0.2, and 0.4 = 2 × 0.2. The answer is C.
text: Two candles of equal length are lit at the same moment. The first burns down completely in 4 hours and the second in 3 hours, each at its own constant rate. After how much time will the first candle be exactly twice as long as the second?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-equations

solution: Rewrite so the two variable parts have constant product: 4x + 9/(x − 1) = 4(x − 1) + 9/(x − 1) + 4. For x > 1 both terms are positive, so by AM–GM, 4(x − 1) + 9/(x − 1) ≥ 2√(4 × 9) = 12, with equality when 4(x − 1)² = 9, i.e. x − 1 = 3/2, x = 5/2. Hence the minimum is 12 + 4 = 16. Check at x = 5/2: 4(2.5) + 9/(1.5) = 10 + 6 = 16. (Answering 12 forgets to add back the constant 4.) The answer is A.
text: For x > 1, what is the minimum value of4x + 9/(x − 1) ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Rearrange: n² − 3n − 40 < 0, which factors as (n − 8)(n + 5) < 0. The product of the two factors is negative exactly when n lies strictly between the roots: −5 < n < 8. The integers in this range are −4, −3, …, 7, which is 7 − (−4) + 1 = 12 values. Note the endpoints fail: n = −5 gives 25 = 25 and n = 8 gives 64 = 64, and the inequality is strict. (Answering 13 or 14 comes from wrongly including one or both endpoints.) The answer is D.
text: How many integer values of n satisfyn<sup>2</sup> < 3n + 40 ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Apply AM–GM to the two terms 2x and 5y: (2x + 5y)/2 ≥ √(2x · 5y), so 20 ≥ √(10xy). Squaring: 400 ≥ 10xy, hence xy ≤ 40. Equality holds when 2x = 5y = 20, i.e. x = 10, y = 4, which indeed satisfies the constraint and gives xy = 40. (Answering 400 forgets to divide by the coefficient product 10; 20 comes from halving the correct answer.) The answer is B.
text: Positive real numbers x and y satisfy 2x + 5y = 40. What is the maximum possible value of the product xy?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Both sides are non-negative, so squaring preserves the inequality: (x − 3)² > 4x², i.e. x² − 6x + 9 > 4x², so 3x² + 6x − 9 < 0. Dividing by 3: x² + 2x − 3 < 0, which factors as (x + 3)(x − 1) < 0, giving −3 < x < 1. The integers are −2, −1, 0: three values. Check x = 0: 3 > 0 true; x = −3: 6 > 6 false (correctly excluded); x = 1: 2 > 2 false. (Answering 4 or 5 comes from including an endpoint.) The answer is E.
text: How many integer values of x satisfy|x − 3| > 2|x| ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Pair the outer and inner factors: (x + 1)(x + 4) = x² + 5x + 4 and (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 5x + 6. Let u = x² + 5x + 5, so the product is (u − 1)(u + 1) = u² − 1 ≥ −1. The minimum −1 is attained when u = 0, i.e. x² + 5x + 5 = 0, which has real solutions x = (−5 ± √5)/2, so the bound is achieved. (Answering 0 assumes the product of four factors can't go negative; it can, when exactly one or three factors are negative.) The answer is B.
text: Over all real numbers x, what is the minimum value of(x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 3)(x + 4) ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-inequalities

solution: Iterate directly: f(1) = 5; f(5) = 13; f(13) = 29; f(29) = 61; f(61) = 125. So f<sup>(5)</sup>(1) = 125. Alternatively, note f<sup>(n)</sup>(x) = 2<sup>n</sup>x + 3(2<sup>n</sup> − 1) (each iteration doubles and adds 3), so f<sup>(5)</sup>(1) = 32 · 1 + 3 · 31 = 32 + 93 = 125. (Answering 61 stops one iteration early; 93 is only the constant part 3(2⁵ − 1).) The answer is D.
text: Let f(x) = 2x + 3, and let f<sup>(n)</sup> denote f composed with itself n times, so f<sup>(2)</sup>(x) = f(f(x)). What is the value of f<sup>(5)</sup>(1)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Find f explicitly. Let t = 2x + 1, so x = (t − 1)/2. Then f(t) = 4·[(t − 1)/2]² + 6·(t − 1)/2 + 5 = (t − 1)² + 3(t − 1) + 5 = t² + t + 3. As x runs over all reals, t = 2x + 1 also covers all reals, so we minimise t² + t + 3: the vertex is at t = −1/2, giving 1/4 − 1/2 + 3 = 11/4. (Answering 3 comes from minimising the original expression in x at x = 0 without completing the square: the true minimum of 4x² + 6x + 5 is at x = −3/4.) The answer is C.
text: A function f satisfies f(2x + 1) = 4x<sup>2</sup> + 6x + 5 for every real number x. What is the minimum value of f over all real inputs?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Write everything in terms of t = 3<sup>x</sup>. Since 9<sup>x</sup> = (3<sup>x</sup>)² = t² and 3<sup>x+1</sup> = 3t, the equation becomes t² − 3t − 54 = 0, which factors as (t − 9)(t + 6) = 0. Since t = 3<sup>x</sup> > 0, we must have t = 9 (the root t = −6 is rejected). Then 3<sup>x</sup> = 9 gives x = 2. Check: 9² − 3³ = 81 − 27 = 54. The answer is B.
text: What is the value of x that satisfies9<sup>x</sup> − 3<sup>x+1</sup> = 54 ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Telescope from 0 up to 10: f(10) − f(0) = [f(10) − f(9)] + [f(9) − f(8)] + … + [f(1) − f(0)] = 4·10 + 4·9 + … + 4·1 = 4(1 + 2 + … + 10) = 4 · 55 = 220. Hence f(10) = 3 + 220 = 223. (Answering 220 forgets to add f(0) = 3; 203 comes from using 4·(1 + … + 10) = 200 via the wrong sum 50.) The answer is E.
text: A function f, defined for all real numbers, satisfies f(x) − f(x − 1) = 4x for every real x, and f(0) = 3. What is the value of f(10)?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: Key identity: f(x) + f(1 − x) = 1. Indeed f(1 − x) = 4<sup>1−x</sup>/(4<sup>1−x</sup> + 2) = 4/(4 + 2·4<sup>x</sup>) = 2/(4<sup>x</sup> + 2), so f(x) + f(1 − x) = (4<sup>x</sup> + 2)/(4<sup>x</sup> + 2) = 1. The four arguments pair up as (1/5, 4/5) and (2/5, 3/5), each pair summing to 1, so the total is 1 + 1 = 2. (Answering 4 treats every term as roughly 1; answering 1 pairs all four terms into a single unit.) The answer is A.
text: Let f(x) = 4<sup>x</sup> / (4<sup>x</sup> + 2). What is the value off(1/5) + f(2/5) + f(3/5) + f(4/5) ?
title: Quant advanced: algebra-functions

solution: The common difference is d = (a<sub>31</sub> − a<sub>5</sub>)/(31 − 5) = (5 − 31)/26 = −1. Then a<sub>n</sub> = a<sub>5</sub> + (n − 5)d = 31 − (n − 5) = 36 − n. So a<sub>36</sub> = 36 − 36 = 0. (This is the general fact: if the pth term is q and the qth term is p, the (p + q)th term is 0. Answering −1 overshoots by one step, a classic off-by-one.) The answer is C.
text: In an arithmetic progression, the 5th term is 31 and the 31st term is 5. What is the 36th term?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: In a GP the middle term squared equals the product of its neighbours: (x + 9)² = x(x + 45). Expanding: x² + 18x + 81 = x² + 45x, so 81 = 27x and x = 3. The terms are 3, 12, 48, and the common ratio is 12/3 = 4. Check: 48/12 = 4 as well. (Answering 12 confuses the second term with the ratio; answering 3 confuses x itself with the ratio.) The answer is D.
text: The three numbers x, x + 9, and x + 45 form a geometric progression (in that order). What is the common ratio of the progression?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Rationalise each term: 1/(√k + √(k+1)) = (√(k+1) − √k)/[(k+1) − k] = √(k+1) − √k. The sum telescopes: (√2 − √1) + (√3 − √2) + … + (√100 − √99) = √100 − √1 = 10 − 1 = 9. (Answering 10 forgets to subtract √1; 99 terms does not mean the answer relates to 99.) The answer is A.
text: Evaluate the sum1/(√1 + √2) + 1/(√2 + √3) + 1/(√3 + √4) + … + 1/(√99 + √100).
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Write the terms as a/r, a, ar. Their sum is a(1/r + 1 + r) = 21. The reciprocals 1/(a/r), 1/a, 1/(ar) sum to (1/a)(r + 1 + 1/r) = 7/12 — the same bracket appears in both. Dividing the equations: a² = 21 ÷ (7/12) = 36, so a = 6 (terms are positive). Then 6(1/r + 1 + r) = 21 gives r + 1/r = 5/2, so r = 2 or r = 1/2. Either way the terms are 3, 6, 12, and the largest is 12. Check: 3 + 6 + 12 = 21; 1/3 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 7/12. (Answering 6 gives the middle term, not the largest.) The answer is E.
text: Three positive numbers in geometric progression have sum 21, and the sum of their reciprocals is 7/12. What is the largest of the three numbers?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: The monthly savings form an AP with first term 200 and common difference 40. The total after n months is S<sub>n</sub> = (n/2)[2·200 + (n − 1)·40] = n(200 + 20(n − 1)) = 20n² + 180n. Set 20n² + 180n = 5040 and divide by 20: n² + 9n − 252 = 0, which factors as (n − 12)(n + 21) = 0. Since n > 0, n = 12. Check: S<sub>12</sub> = 20·144 + 180·12 = 2880 + 2160 = 5040. The answer is B.
text: A worker saves $200 in the first month and in each subsequent month saves $40 more than in the previous month. After how many months will her total savings first reach exactly $5040?
title: Quant advanced: progressions

solution: Use the Law of Cosines on the angle at P: QR² = PQ² + PR² − 2·PQ·PR·cos(120°). Since cos(120°) = −1/2, the subtraction becomes an addition: QR² = 49 + 64 − 2(7)(8)(−1/2) = 113 + 56 = 169, so QR = 13. The trap answer √57 comes from wrongly using cos(120°) = +1/2 and computing 113 − 56 = 57. The answer is D.
text: In triangle PQR, PQ = 7, PR = 8, and the angle at P measures 120°. What is the length of side QR?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Key fact: the area of a triangle equals 4/3 times the area of the triangle formed by its three medians. Here the medians 9, 12, 15 themselves form a right triangle, because 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225 = 15². The median triangle's area is (1/2)(9)(12) = 54. So the original triangle's area is (4/3)(54) = 72. Choosing 54 means you stopped at the median triangle; choosing 40.5 means you multiplied by 3/4 instead of 4/3. The answer is C.
text: The three medians of a triangle have lengths 9, 12, and 15. What is the area of the triangle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Viviani's theorem: for any interior point of an equilateral triangle, the sum of the perpendicular distances to the three sides equals the altitude of the triangle. So the altitude h = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. For side length s, h = (s√3)/2, so s = 24/√3 = 8√3. Area = (√3/4)s² = (√3/4)(192) = 48√3. (Check: connecting the point to the vertices splits the triangle into three pieces of total area (1/2)s(3 + 4 + 5) = (1/2)(8√3)(12) = 48√3.) Using 12 as the side length instead of the altitude gives the trap 36√3. The answer is B.
text: A point lies inside an equilateral triangle. The perpendicular distances from this point to the three sides of the triangle are 3, 4, and 5. What is the area of the triangle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: In a right triangle the hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumscribed circle, so c = 2(14.5) = 29. For a right triangle with legs a, b: inradius r = (a + b − c)/2, so 6 = (a + b − 29)/2, giving a + b = 41. The semiperimeter is s = (41 + 29)/2 = 35, and area = r·s = 6 × 35 = 210. (Indeed the triangle is 20-21-29: 20 + 21 − 29 = 12 = 2r, and (1/2)(20)(21) = 210.) Choosing 420 means you forgot the 1/2 in the leg product; 105 is halving 210 a second time. The answer is E.
text: A right triangle has an inscribed circle of radius 6 and a circumscribed circle of radius 14.5. What is the area of the triangle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Let the base be 2x and each equal side be a, so 2a + 2x = 32, i.e. a = 16 − x. The altitude to the base bisects it, so a² = 8² + x²: (16 − x)² = 64 + x², which gives 256 − 32x = 64, so x = 6. The base is 12 and the legs are 10 (check: 10 + 10 + 12 = 32). Area = (1/2)(12)(8) = 48. Choosing 96 means you forgot the 1/2; 60 comes from wrongly using a leg (10) with the altitude. The answer is A.
text: An isosceles triangle has perimeter 32, and the altitude drawn to its base (the unequal side) has length 8. What is the area of the triangle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: Apollonius' theorem: if m is the median to side a, and b, c are the other two sides, then b² + c² = 2m² + a²/2. Substituting: 7² + 9² = 2(7²) + a²/2, so 130 = 98 + a²/2, giving a²/2 = 32, a² = 64, a = 8. Dropping the factor 2 on the median term gives a² = 162 (the trap 9√2); writing 2a² instead of a²/2 gives a = 4. The answer is C.
text: In a triangle, two of the sides have lengths 7 and 9, and the median drawn to the third side has length 7. What is the length of the third side?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-triangles

solution: The perpendicular from the center O to the chord meets it at its midpoint M. Half the chord is 8, so OM = √(10² − 8²) = √36 = 6. The nearest point of the circle to M lies along ray OM extended past M to the circle: its distance from M is (radius) − OM = 10 − 6 = 4. Answering 6 means you stopped at the center-to-chord distance instead of continuing to the circle. The answer is A.
text: A chord of length 16 is drawn in a circle of radius 10. M is the midpoint of the chord. What is the distance from M to the nearest point on the circle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: For a common internal tangent, the tangent length is √(d² − (r₁ + r₂)²), because shifting one radius across creates a right triangle whose legs are the tangent length and r₁ + r₂ = 8, with hypotenuse d = 17. Length = √(17² − 8²) = √(289 − 64) = √225 = 15. Using the difference of radii (r₁ − r₂ = 2) is the external-tangent formula and gives the trap √285. The answer is B.
text: Two circles with radii 5 and 3 lie completely outside each other, and the distance between their centers is 17. A common internal tangent is drawn (a line tangent to both circles that crosses the segment joining the centers). What is the length of this tangent segment between its two points of tangency?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: Segment area = sector area − triangle area. Sector: (120/360)π(12²) = (1/3)(144π) = 48π. Triangle formed by the two radii and the chord: (1/2)r²sin(120°) = (1/2)(144)(√3/2) = 36√3. So the minor segment has area 48π − 36√3. Forgetting the 1/2 in the triangle formula gives 48π − 72√3; adding instead of subtracting gives 48π + 36√3. The answer is D.
text: A chord of a circle of radius 12 subtends an angle of 120° at the center. What is the area of the minor segment, the region enclosed between the chord and the minor arc?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: Let O be the center and T a point of tangency. OT is perpendicular to the tangent PT, and the line PO bisects the 60° angle, so angle OPT = 30°. In right triangle OTP: tan(30°) = OT/PT, so r = 12·tan(30°) = 12/√3 = 4√3. Using tan(60°) instead of the half-angle gives the trap 12√3; answering 6 comes from wrongly treating r as 12·sin(30°) with 12 as a hypotenuse. The answer is C.
text: From an external point P, two tangent segments are drawn to a circle, each of length 12, and the angle between the two tangents at P is 60°. What is the radius of the circle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: When two circles are externally tangent, the distance between their centers equals the sum of their radii. Call the radii a, b, c with a + b = 6, a + c = 8, b + c = 10. Adding all three: 2(a + b + c) = 24, so a + b + c = 12. Then c = 12 − 6 = 6, b = 12 − 8 = 4, a = 12 − 10 = 2. The smallest radius is 2. Answering 3 comes from just halving the smallest center distance, which would only be right if that pair had equal radii. The answer is E.
text: Three circles are mutually tangent externally (each pair touches at exactly one point, with the circles outside one another). The distances between the three pairs of centers are 6, 8, and 10. What is the radius of the smallest circle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-circles

solution: Use the shoelace formula on the vertices in order. Down-products: (1)(2) + (7)(6) + (8)(5) + (2)(1) = 2 + 42 + 40 + 2 = 86. Up-products: (1)(7) + (2)(8) + (6)(2) + (5)(1) = 7 + 16 + 12 + 5 = 40. Area = |86 − 40|/2 = 46/2 = 23. Forgetting to halve at the end gives the trap 46. The answer is A.
text: A quadrilateral has vertices, taken in order, at (1, 1), (7, 2), (8, 6), and (2, 5). What is its area?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Write the line in intercept form x/a + y/b = 1 with a, b > 0. Passing through (2, 3) means 2/a + 3/b = 1. By AM-GM, 1 = 2/a + 3/b ≥ 2√(6/(ab)), so √(6/(ab)) ≤ 1/2, giving ab ≥ 24. The triangle's area is ab/2 ≥ 12, with equality when 2/a = 3/b = 1/2, i.e. a = 4, b = 6 (check: 2/4 + 3/6 = 1). Minimum area = 12. Answering 6 is the common error of taking the product of the coordinates (2)(3) as the area. The answer is D.
text: A line with negative slope passes through the point (2, 3) and, together with the positive x-axis and positive y-axis, encloses a triangle. What is the least possible area of this triangle?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: A 90° counterclockwise rotation about the origin sends (x, y) to (−y, x), so P′ = (−4, 3). Distance PP′ = √((3 − (−4))² + (4 − 3)²) = √(49 + 1) = √50 = 5√2. Shortcut: P and P′ both lie on a circle of radius 5 about the origin, separated by a 90° central angle, so PP′ is the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle with legs 5, i.e. 5√2. Answering 5 confuses the distance from the origin with the distance moved; 10 would be a 180° rotation. The answer is B.
text: The point P(3, 4) is rotated 90° counterclockwise about the origin to give the point P′. What is the distance between P and P′?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: Let the vertices be O(0, 0), A(a, 0), and B(0, b). The centroid is the average of the vertices: ((a + 0 + 0)/3, (0 + b + 0)/3) = (a/3, b/3). So a/3 = 8 and b/3 = 6, giving a = 24 and b = 18. Hypotenuse AB = √(24² + 18²) = √(576 + 324) = √900 = 30. Answering 10 = √(8² + 6²) means you forgot to scale the centroid coordinates up by 3. The answer is E.
text: A right triangle has its two legs along the positive x-axis and positive y-axis, with the right angle at the origin. The centroid of the triangle is the point (8, 6). What is the length of the hypotenuse?
title: Quant advanced: geometry-coordinate

solution: The circumference of the base is 44, so 2πr = 44 gives r = 44 × 7/(2 × 22) = 7 cm, and the height is h = 20 cm. Volume = πr²h = (22/7)(49)(20) = 22 × 7 × 20 = 3080 cm³. Rolling along the shorter side instead (20 as circumference) gives the trap 1400; treating 44 as the radius-related diameter leads to other wrong values. The answer is D.
text: A rectangular sheet of paper measures 44 cm by 20 cm. It is rolled up along its longer side to form a hollow cylinder (so the 44 cm edge becomes the circumference of the base, and the height is 20 cm). Taking π = 22/7, what is the volume enclosed by the cylinder, in cubic centimeters?
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: The metal is the region between the two cylinders: V = π(R² − r²)h = (22/7)(5² − 3²)(21) = (22/7)(16)(21) = 22 × 16 × 3 = 1056 cm³. The classic mistake is computing π(R − r)²h = (22/7)(4)(21) = 264: you must subtract the squares, not square the difference. Choosing 1650 means you took the full outer cylinder and forgot to remove the hollow; 594 is the inner (hollow) volume itself. The answer is A.
text: A metal pipe is a hollow cylinder of length 21 cm. Its outer radius is 5 cm and its inner radius is 3 cm. Taking π = 22/7, what is the volume of the metal in the pipe, in cubic centimeters?
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: The sector's radius becomes the cone's slant height: l = 15. The arc length becomes the base circumference: arc = (216/360)(2π)(15) = (3/5)(30π) = 18π, so 2πr = 18π and r = 9. The vertical height is h = √(l² − r²) = √(225 − 81) = 12. Volume = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(81)(12) = 324π cm³. Using the slant height 15 in place of the vertical height gives the trap 405π; forgetting the 1/3 gives 972π. The answer is E.
text: A sector of a circle has radius 15 cm and central angle 216°. The two straight edges of the sector are brought together and joined so that it forms a right circular cone (the sector's arc becomes the cone's base circle). What is the volume of the cone, in cubic centimeters?
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Rotating a right triangle about one leg produces a cone whose height is that leg and whose base radius is the other leg. Here h = 15 and r = 8, so V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(64)(15) = 320π cm³. Rotating about the 8 cm leg instead would give (1/3)π(225)(8) = 600π, the main trap; forgetting the 1/3 gives 960π. The answer is B.
text: A right triangle has legs of length 8 cm and 15 cm. It is rotated one full turn about its 15 cm leg, sweeping out a solid of revolution. What is the volume of this solid, in cubic centimeters?
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Surface area scales as r², so the new-to-old area ratio is 1.44, which means the radius scales by √1.44 = 1.2 (a 20% increase). Volume scales as r³, so the volume ratio is 1.2³ = 1.728, i.e. a 72.8% increase. Answering 172.8% confuses the ratio (the new volume is 172.8% OF the old) with the increase; 44% wrongly carries the area change straight over to volume; 20% stops at the radius. The answer is C.
text: The surface area of a solid sphere increases by 44%. By what percentage does the volume of the sphere increase?
title: Quant advanced: mensuration

solution: Only the last two digits of the base matter: 2026 ≡ 26 (mod 100). Powers of 26: 26² = 676 ≡ 76, and 76 is idempotent (76 × 76 = 5776 ≡ 76), while 76 × 26 = 1976 ≡ 76. So 26n ≡ 76 for every n ≥ 2. Numbers ending in 76 absorb everything — recognising the idempotent pair 25/76 kills this instantly.
text: When 2026<sup>2026</sup> is written out in full, what are its final two digits?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: n(n − 1) must be divisible by 4 and by 25. Since n and n − 1 are coprime, each prime power must divide one of them: n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4) AND n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 25). CRT gives 2 × 2 = 4 residues mod 100: n ≡ 0, 1, 25, 76. In 1…100 these are 1, 25, 76, 100 — 4 integers (the “automorphic” endings).
text: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 satisfy n² ≡ n (mod 100)?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: We need n ≡ 3 (mod 7) and n ≡ 4 (mod 9). Write n = 7k + 3 and require 7k + 3 ≡ 4 (mod 9), i.e. 7k ≡ 1 (mod 9). Since 7 × 4 = 28 ≡ 1 (mod 9), the inverse of 7 is 4, so k ≡ 4 (mod 9). Then n = 7(9m + 4) + 3 = 63m + 31. The solutions in range are 31, 94, 157, 220, 283, 346, 409, 472 — we need 63m + 31 ≤ 500, i.e. m ≤ 7.44, so m = 0, 1, …, 7. That is 8 values. Answering 7 is the classic off-by-one (forgetting m = 0). The answer is C.
text: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 500 leave a remainder of 3 when divided by 7 AND a remainder of 4 when divided by 9?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: gcd(2, 100) ≠ 1, so Euler cannot be applied directly — split by CRT. Mod 4: 22026 ≡ 0. Mod 25: φ(25) = 20 and 2026 ≡ 6 (mod 20), so 22026 ≡ 26 = 64 ≡ 14 (mod 25). Seek x ≡ 0 (mod 4), x ≡ 14 (mod 25): x = 64. Applying φ(100) = 40 blindly to a non-coprime base is the trap.
text: Let N = 2<sup>2026</sup>. What is the remainder when N is divided by 100?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Key fact: 111 = 3 × 37, so any block of three consecutive 1s is divisible by 37 — and more generally the 30-digit repunit (ten blocks of 111 spaced by powers of 1000) is divisible by 37. Write N = R<sub>30</sub> × 10<sup>2</sup> + 11, where R<sub>30</sub> is the repunit with 30 ones. Since 37 divides R<sub>30</sub>, we get N ≡ 11 (mod 37). Verification of the block argument: R<sub>30</sub> = 111 × (10<sup>27</sup> + 10<sup>24</sup> + … + 1). Answering 0 assumes 37 divides all repunits; answering 1 comes from miscounting 32 as 31 = 30 + 1. The answer is B.
text: Let N be the integer formed by writing the digit 1 exactly 32 times in a row (N = 111…1 with 32 ones). What is the remainder when N is divided by 37?
title: Quant advanced: number-remainders

solution: Prime-factorise 10!: exponent of 2 is ⌊10/2⌋ + ⌊10/4⌋ + ⌊10/8⌋ = 5 + 2 + 1 = 8; exponent of 3 is 3 + 1 = 4; exponent of 5 is 2; exponent of 7 is 1. So 10! = 2<sup>8</sup> × 3<sup>4</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup> × 7. An odd divisor uses no factor of 2, so count divisors of the odd part 3<sup>4</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup> × 7: (4+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 30. Answering 270 counts ALL divisors (9 × 5 × 3 × 2); 240 counts the even ones. The answer is C.
text: How many positive divisors of 10! (the product of all integers from 1 to 10) are odd?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Factorise: 8400 = 84 × 100 = (2<sup>2</sup> × 3 × 7) × (2<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>) = 2<sup>4</sup> × 3 × 5<sup>2</sup> × 7. A divisor 2<sup>a</sup>3<sup>b</sup>5<sup>c</sup>7<sup>d</sup> is a multiple of 12 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3 exactly when a ≥ 2 and b ≥ 1. Count the choices: a ∈ {2, 3, 4} gives 3 options; b must be 1 (only 1 option since the exponent of 3 in 8400 is 1); c ∈ {0, 1, 2} gives 3; d ∈ {0, 1} gives 2. Total: 3 × 1 × 3 × 2 = 18. Equivalently, these are the divisors of 8400/12 = 700 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup> × 7, which has 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 divisors. Answering 60 counts all divisors of 8400. The answer is E.
text: How many positive divisors of 8400 are multiples of 12?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: If gcd(a, b) = 1 and ab = N, then for each prime, its ENTIRE prime power must go wholly to a or wholly to b (splitting a prime between them would make it a common factor). N has exactly 5 distinct primes (2, 3, 5, 7, 11), so there are 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 ordered assignments, giving 32 ordered pairs (a, b). Since N is not a perfect square, no pair has a = b, so the number of unordered pairs is 32 ÷ 2 = 16. (Note the pair 1 × N is legitimately coprime and IS counted.) Answering 32 forgets to halve; 15 wrongly excludes the pair (1, N); 8 miscounts the distinct primes as 4. The answer is B.
text: Let N = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5 × 7 × 11. In how many ways can N be written as a product a × b of two positive integers with gcd(a, b) = 1, where the order of the factors does not matter?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: Factor out 5 from each of the 20 terms: P = 5<sup>20</sup> × (1 × 2 × … × 20) = 5<sup>20</sup> × 20!. Trailing zeros = min(exponent of 2, exponent of 5). Exponent of 5: 20 (factored out) + exponent of 5 in 20! = 20 + (⌊20/5⌋ + ⌊20/25⌋) = 20 + 4 = 24. Exponent of 2: only from 20!, namely ⌊20/2⌋ + ⌊20/4⌋ + ⌊20/8⌋ + ⌊20/16⌋ = 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 18. Here the 2s are scarcer than the 5s (the reverse of the usual factorial situation!), so the number of trailing zeros is min(18, 24) = 18. Answering 24 counts only the fives — the classic trap. The answer is D.
text: Let P = 5 × 10 × 15 × … × 100 (the product of all multiples of 5 from 5 to 100). How many consecutive zeros are there at the right-hand end of P?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: If n = p<sup>a</sup>q<sup>b</sup>…, the divisor count is (a+1)(b+1)… = 28. Factorisations of 28: 28; 14 × 2; 7 × 4; 7 × 2 × 2. These give exponent patterns (27), (13, 1), (6, 3), (6, 1, 1). Assign the largest exponents to the smallest primes and compare: 2<sup>27</sup> (huge); 2<sup>13</sup> × 3 = 24576; 2<sup>6</sup> × 3<sup>3</sup> = 64 × 27 = 1728; 2<sup>6</sup> × 3 × 5 = 64 × 15 = 960. The smallest is 960. Check: 960 = 2<sup>6</sup> × 3 × 5 has (6+1)(1+1)(1+1) = 28 divisors. Note 720 has 30 divisors and 840 has 32 — small numbers with MANY divisors, but not exactly 28. The answer is A.
text: What is the smallest positive integer that has exactly 28 positive divisors?
title: Quant advanced: number-factors

solution: For 3 years at rate r, CI − SI = P[(1 + r)<sup>3</sup> − 1 − 3r] = P(3r<sup>2</sup> + r<sup>3</sup>). With r = 0.1: 3(0.01) + 0.001 = 0.031. So 0.031P = 620, giving P = 620 ÷ 0.031 = 20,000. Verify: CI on 20,000 at 10% for 3 years = 20,000(1.331 − 1) = 6,620; SI = 20,000 × 0.10 × 3 = 6,000; difference = 620. Answering ₹62,000 comes from using the 2-year formula Pr<sup>2</sup> = 620 by mistake. The answer is B.
text: The difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on a certain sum for 3 years at 10% per annum is ₹620. What is the sum?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Total work = 24 men × 30 days × 8 h/day = 5,760 man-hours. Work done in the first 12 days = 24 × 12 × 8 = 2,304 man-hours, leaving 5,760 − 2,304 = 3,456 man-hours. The remaining 16 men have 30 − 12 = 18 days, so the required hours per day = 3,456 ÷ (16 × 18) = 3,456 ÷ 288 = 12. Sanity check: the workforce dropped by a factor 16/24 = 2/3, so daily hours must rise by 3/2: 8 × 3/2 = 12. The answer is D.
text: A contractor plans to build a wall in 30 days using 24 men working 8 hours a day. After 12 days (work having proceeded exactly on schedule), 8 men leave the site. How many hours per day must the remaining men work so that the wall is still finished on day 30?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Let the train's length be L and speed v. Passing the pole: L = 12v. Passing the platform: L + 360 = 30v. Subtracting: 360 = 18v, so v = 20 m/s and L = 240 m. The oncoming train: 36 km/h = 10 m/s, length 240 m. For opposite directions the relative speed is 20 + 10 = 30 m/s, and the distance to cover is the sum of the lengths, 240 + 240 = 480 m. Time = 480 ÷ 30 = 16 seconds. Answering 48 comes from subtracting the speeds (same-direction formula); 24 comes from forgetting to add the other train's speed (480 ÷ 20); 12 uses only one train's length. The answer is A.
text: A train passes a signal pole in 12 seconds and a 360-metre-long platform in 30 seconds, travelling at a constant speed. How long will the same train take to completely cross a 240-metre-long train travelling in the opposite direction at 36 km/h?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Suppose x litres of solution are removed and replaced with pure acid. The removed solution carries away 0.3x litres of acid, and x litres of pure acid come in. Final acid = 0.3(60 − x) + x = 18 + 0.7x litres. Setting this equal to 44% of 60 litres = 26.4: 18 + 0.7x = 26.4, so 0.7x = 8.4 and x = 12. Verify: remove 12 L (leaving 14.4 L acid in 48 L), add 12 L pure acid: 26.4/60 = 44%. Answering 8.4 treats the needed 14-percentage-point rise as litres directly; 14 comes from dropping the 0.7 factor incorrectly. The answer is C.
text: A tank contains 60 litres of a solution that is 30% acid. How many litres of the solution must be drawn off and replaced with pure acid so that the tank contains a 44% acid solution?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Let the distance be d km. The time difference between the slow trip and the fast trip is 6 + 10 = 16 minutes = 16/60 hours (late by 6 versus early by 10 spans the FULL 16-minute gap). So d/4 − d/6 = 16/60. The left side is d(3 − 2)/12 = d/12, hence d/12 = 4/15, giving d = 48/15 = 3.2 km. Verify: at 4 km/h the trip takes 48 min; at 6 km/h it takes 32 min; difference = 16 min, consistent with 6 late/10 early around a 42-minute deadline. The classic error is using only 6 (or only 10) minutes as the gap instead of their sum. The answer is E.
text: Walking from home to school at 4 km/h, a student arrives 6 minutes late. Walking the same route at 6 km/h, she arrives 10 minutes early. What is the distance from her home to school?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: Let the incomes be 5x and 4x, and the expenditures be 3y and 2y. Savings = income − expenditure, so 5x − 3y = 6,000 and 4x − 2y = 6,000. From the second equation: 2x − y = 3,000, so y = 2x − 3,000. Substitute into the first: 5x − 3(2x − 3,000) = 6,000, i.e. 5x − 6x + 9,000 = 6,000, so x = 3,000 (and y = 3,000). Aditi's income = 5x = ₹15,000. Verify: Aditi 15,000 − 9,000 = 6,000 saved; Bala 12,000 − 6,000 = 6,000 saved. Answering ₹12,000 gives Bala's income instead of Aditi's. The answer is C.
text: The monthly incomes of Aditi and Bala are in the ratio 5 : 4, and their monthly expenditures are in the ratio 3 : 2. If each of them saves ₹6,000 per month, what is Aditi's monthly income?
title: Quant advanced: arithmetic-advanced

solution: For choosing k non-adjacent positions from n in a CIRCLE, the count is [n/(n−k)] × C(n−k, k). Here n = 12, k = 4: (12/8) × C(8,4) = 1.5 × 70 = 105. Sanity check via cases: fix chair 1 as chosen or not. If chair 1 is chosen, chairs 2 and 12 are forbidden, and we need 3 non-adjacent chairs from the 9 chairs 3–11 in a LINE: C(9−3+1, 3) = C(7,3) = 35. If chair 1 is not chosen, we need 4 non-adjacent chairs from chairs 2–12 in a line: C(11−4+1, 4) = C(8,4) = 70. Total = 35 + 70 = 105. Trap answers: C(9,4) = 126 uses the straight-line formula and ignores that the first and last chairs are neighbors in a circle; C(8,4) = 70 drops the circular correction factor; C(12,4) = 495 ignores the adjacency restriction entirely. The answer is C.
text: A round table has 12 chairs equally spaced around it. In how many ways can 4 of the 12 chairs be selected so that no two selected chairs are adjacent to each other?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Split by how many of each letter the 4-letter word uses, writing (p, e, r) for the counts of P, E, R with p ≤ 3, e ≤ 2, r ≤ 1 and p + e + r = 4. The possibilities and their arrangement counts: (3,1,0): 4!/3! = 4; (3,0,1): 4!/3! = 4; (2,2,0): 4!/(2!·2!) = 6; (2,1,1): 4!/2! = 12; (1,2,1): 4!/2! = 12. Total = 4 + 4 + 6 + 12 + 12 = 38. Note (0,2,1) and similar fail because e + r can contribute at most 3 letters, so at least one P is forced except when p ≥ 1 anyway. Trap answers: 360 = 6P4 treats all six letters as distinct; 180 divides 360 by 2! correcting only for the E's; 60 = 6!/(3!2!) counts arrangements of the FULL 6-letter word, not 4-letter ones. The answer is A.
text: Using the letters of the word PEPPER (which contains three P's, two E's, and one R), how many distinct 4-letter arrangements can be formed? Each letter may be used no more times than it appears in PEPPER.
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Count all assignments, then subtract the forbidden ones. Total with no restriction: 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 ordered choices. Forbidden = both Arjun and Bela hold offices: choose which 2 of the 3 offices they occupy and in what order (3 × 2 = 6 ways), then fill the remaining office from the other 7 members (7 ways): 6 × 7 = 42. Valid = 504 − 42 = 462. Trap answers: 504 ignores the restriction; 498 = 504 − 6 forgets to multiply by the 7 choices for the third officer; 420 = 504 − 84 double-counts the forbidden cases; 336 = 8 × 7 × 6 wrongly bans Bela from serving at all. The answer is D.
text: A club of 9 members must elect a president, a treasurer, and a secretary (three different people, one per office). Two particular members, Arjun and Bela, refuse to serve as officers at the same time (either may serve alone). How many valid ways are there to fill the three offices?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: First count ALL positive solutions of x + y + z = 20: C(19,2) = 171. Next remove solutions with a repeated value. Solutions with x = y: 2x + z = 20 forces x = 1, ..., 9 (z must stay positive), giving 9 solutions; by symmetry y = z and x = z also give 9 each; x = y = z would need 3x = 20, impossible. No solution is counted twice among these (that would require all three equal), so ordered solutions with all values DISTINCT = 171 − 27 = 144. Each set of three distinct values appears in 3! = 6 orders, but exactly one of those orders has x < y < z, so the count is 144/6 = 24. Trap answers: 171 forgets both the distinctness and ordering conditions; 144 counts all distinct-value orderings without imposing x < y < z; 27 is the number of repeated-value solutions; 18 comes from subtracting the 27 before dividing incorrectly. The answer is B.
text: How many ordered triples of positive integers (x, y, z) satisfy x + y + z = 20 with the strict inequalities x < y < z?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Use inclusion–exclusion on the letters that are missing. Total strings: 3<sup>5</sup> = 243. Subtract strings missing at least one specific letter: 3 choices of missing letter, each leaving 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 strings, total 96. But strings using only ONE letter were subtracted twice, so add them back: 3 strings (AAAAA, BBBBB, CCCCC). Count = 243 − 96 + 3 = 150. Trap answers: 243 ignores the requirement; 147 = 243 − 96 forgets the add-back term; 96 is the subtracted quantity itself; 90 comes from a wrong surjection shortcut. The answer is E.
text: How many 5-character strings can be formed using the letters A, B, and C (repetition allowed) if each of the three letters must appear at least once in the string?
title: Quant advanced: permutations-combinations

solution: Use the complement: P(at least one repeat) = 1 − P(all four rolls distinct). All distinct: the first roll can be anything, then 5/6, 4/6, 3/6 for the next three, so P = (6 × 5 × 4 × 3)/6<sup>4</sup> = 360/1296 = 5/18. Therefore P(at least two match) = 1 − 5/18 = 13/18. Trap answers: 5/18 stops at the complement and forgets to subtract from 1; 671/1296 = 1 − (5/6)<sup>4</sup> wrongly demands only that rolls 2–4 differ from the first roll; 91/216 = 1 − (5/6)(4/6)(3/6)·… is the 3-roll version of the problem. The answer is A.
text: A fair six-sided die is rolled 4 times. What is the probability that at least two of the four rolls show the same number?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Classify 1–20 by remainder mod 3: remainder 0: {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18} — 6 numbers; remainder 1: {1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19} — 7 numbers; remainder 2: {2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20} — 7 numbers. A sum is divisible by 3 when both numbers have remainder 0, or one has remainder 1 and the other remainder 2. Favorable pairs: C(6,2) + 7 × 7 = 15 + 49 = 64. Total pairs: C(20,2) = 190. Probability = 64/190 = 32/95. Trap answers: 49/190 forgets the both-remainder-0 pairs; 3/10 = 57/190 wrongly pairs remainder-1 with remainder-1 and remainder-2 with remainder-2 instead; 1/3 assumes divisibility by 3 is uniform, which fails because the remainder classes are unequal in size. The answer is C.
text: Two distinct integers are chosen at random from the integers 1 through 20 inclusive. What is the probability that their sum is divisible by 3?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Count length-n sequences of H/T with no HH. Let a<sub>n</sub> be that count. A valid sequence ends in T (append T to any valid sequence of length n−1) or ends in TH (append TH to any valid sequence of length n−2), so a<sub>n</sub> = a<sub>n−1</sub> + a<sub>n−2</sub> with a<sub>1</sub> = 2, a<sub>2</sub> = 3. Then a<sub>3</sub> = 5, a<sub>4</sub> = 8, a<sub>5</sub> = 13, a<sub>6</sub> = 21. Probability = 21/2<sup>6</sup> = 21/64. Trap answers: 13/64 uses a<sub>5</sub> (off-by-one in the Fibonacci ladder); 17/32 = 34/64 overshoots to a<sub>7</sub>; 5/16 = 20/64 and 33/64 are near-miss miscounts from trying to subtract HH-containing strings position by position, which double-counts overlaps. The answer is E.
text: A fair coin is flipped 6 times in a row. What is the probability that heads never comes up on two consecutive flips?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Ria wins the match either 2–0 or 2–1. Win 2–0: she wins games 1 and 2: (2/3)<sup>2</sup> = 4/9. Win 2–1: games 1–2 split 1–1 (two orders: WL or LW), then she wins game 3: 2 × (2/3)(1/3)(2/3) = 8/27. Total = 4/9 + 8/27 = 12/27 + 8/27 = 20/27. Note this exceeds her single-game probability 2/3 = 18/27, as it should — a longer series favors the stronger player. Trap answers: 4/9 counts only the straight 2–0 win; 2/3 assumes the match probability equals the single-game probability; 16/27 forgets one of the two orders in the 2–1 path; 22/27 adds (2/3)(1/3)(2/3) twice plus 4/9 with an arithmetic slip. The answer is B.
text: Ria and Sam play a table-tennis match that ends as soon as one of them has won 2 games (no game can be tied). Ria wins each game independently with probability 2/3. What is the probability that Ria wins the match?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: For the median to be 5, one drawn number must be 5 itself, one must be smaller, and one must be larger. Numbers smaller than 5: {1, 2, 3, 4} — 4 choices. Numbers larger than 5: {6, 7, 8} — 3 choices. Favorable selections: 1 × 4 × 3 = 12. Total selections: C(8,3) = 56. Probability = 12/56 = 3/14. Trap answers: 1/8 assumes each of the 8 values is equally likely to be the median (they are not — extreme values can rarely be the middle); 15/56 uses 5 numbers below instead of 4; 9/28 = 18/56 miscounts by including 5 among the smaller values; 5/28 = 10/56 drops two of the favorable pairs. The answer is D.
text: A hat contains 8 slips of paper numbered 1 through 8. Three slips are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that the median (middle value) of the three numbers drawn is exactly 5?
title: Quant advanced: probability

solution: Let e<sub>1</sub>, e<sub>2</sub>, e<sub>3</sub> be the numbers who drank exactly one, exactly two, and exactly three beverages. Two facts: (1) everyone drank something, so e<sub>1</sub> + e<sub>2</sub> + e<sub>3</sub> = 180; (2) summing the individual beverage counts counts each exactly-two person twice and each exactly-three person three times, so e<sub>1</sub> + 2e<sub>2</sub> + 3e<sub>3</sub> = 100 + 90 + 75 = 265. Subtracting (1) from (2): e<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sub>3</sub> = 85. With e<sub>2</sub> = 55: 2e<sub>3</sub> = 30, so e<sub>3</sub> = 15. Trap answers: 30 is 2e<sub>3</sub>, forgetting the final division by 2; 25 and 10 come from treating the 55 as the sum of pairwise intersections |A∩B| + |B∩C| + |A∩C| (which actually equals 55 + 3 × 15 = 100); 45 is 3e<sub>3</sub>. The answer is A.
text: At a conference, each of the 180 attendees drank at least one of coffee, tea, or juice during the breakfast break. Exactly 100 drank coffee, 90 drank tea, and 75 drank juice. Exactly 55 attendees drank exactly two of the three beverages. How many attendees drank all three beverages?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: Let b = number who like both brands. Then those who like ONLY A number 90 − b, and only B number 75 − b, so exactly-one = (90 − b) + (75 − b) = 165 − 2b. Setting 165 − 2b = 95 gives b = 35. People who like at least one brand = exactly-one + both = 95 + 35 = 130. Neither = 150 − 130 = 20. Trap answers: 35 is the both-brands count, not what was asked; 55 = 150 − 95 forgets to remove the both group from the remainder; 15 = 90 + 75 − 150 wrongly assumes every shopper likes at least one brand; 30 halves the exactly-one deficit incorrectly. The answer is C.
text: A market-research firm surveyed 150 shoppers about two snack brands. Exactly 90 shoppers like brand A and exactly 75 like brand B (these counts include anyone who likes both). Exactly 95 shoppers like exactly one of the two brands. How many of the 150 shoppers like neither brand?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: Work region by region. Users of exactly two tools: P&Q only = 18 − 7 = 11; Q&R only = 17 − 7 = 10; P&R only = 16 − 7 = 9; total exactly-two = 30. Only P = 48 − 11 − 9 − 7 = 21; only Q = 45 − 11 − 10 − 7 = 17; only R = 42 − 10 − 9 − 7 = 16. Exactly one = 21 + 17 + 16 = 54. (Check: union = 54 + 30 + 7 = 91, matching 48 + 45 + 42 − 18 − 17 − 16 + 7 = 91, so 9 freelancers use none — consistent.) Trap answers: 91 is the union (at least one tool); 61 = 91 − 30 forgets to also remove the all-three group; 33 = 135 − 2(51) applies the exactly-one formula but drops the +3 × 7 correction term; 44 miscounts one of the pairwise-only regions. The answer is E.
text: In a survey of 100 freelancers about three tools — P, Q, and R — the results were:• 48 use P, 45 use Q, 42 use R.• 18 use both P and Q, 17 use both Q and R, 16 use both P and R (each of these counts includes those who use all three).• 7 use all three tools.How many of the 100 freelancers use exactly one of the three tools?
title: Quant advanced: set-theory

solution: SD ignores shifts and sign, and scales by |coefficient|: new SD = |−3/5| × 15 = 9. The “35” and the minus sign are decoys — adding a constant never changes SD, and reflecting the data flips signs of deviations but not their squares.
text: A data set has standard deviation 15. Every value x is replaced by (35 − 3x)/5. What is the standard deviation of the new data set?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: The new value sits on the mean, so the mean is unchanged and it contributes zero squared deviation. Sum of squared deviations stays 15 × 48 = 720, now divided by 16: variance = 720/16 = 45. Rule: appending a value equal to the mean always shrinks variance by the factor n/(n+1).
text: A list of 15 observations has (population) variance 48. A 16th observation, exactly equal to the mean of the original 15, is appended. What is the variance of the 16 observations?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: Combined mean = (20·30 + 30·40)/50 = 36. Combined variance = weighted mean of (variance + squared distance of group mean from combined mean): [20(25 + 36) + 30(100 + 16)]/50 = (1220 + 3480)/50 = 94. Averaging the two variances (62.5) ignores the between-group spread — the classic error.
text: Group P has 20 observations with mean 30 and standard deviation 5. Group Q has 30 observations with mean 40 and standard deviation 10. What is the variance of the combined group of 50 observations?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: Sum = 140, and the 4th value in sorted order is 25, forcing the 5th and 6th to be at least 25. To maximise the largest, minimise everything else: 1, 1, 1, 25, 25, 25 leaves 140 − 78 = 62. Forgetting that the two values above the median must also be ≥ 25 gives the trap answer 68.
text: Seven positive integers (not necessarily distinct) have mean 20 and median 25. What is the greatest possible value of the largest integer?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: Sum = 270. Median is the 5th of 9 sorted values. Minimise the bottom four as 1, 2, 3, 4 (sum 10). If the median is m, distinctness forces the top five to total at least m + (m+1) + (m+2) + (m+3) + (m+4) = 5m + 10. So 5m + 20 ≤ 270 ⇒ m ≤ 50, achieved by {1,2,3,4,50,51,52,53,54}. Answer: 50.
text: Nine distinct positive integers have mean 30. What is the greatest possible value of the median?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: Sum = 120; the four 7s are the smallest values (28), so the 5th and 6th values must average 9. Take them as 9, 9. To free up budget, make the 7th–9th values as small as possible without creating a rival mode: 9 can appear once more (three 9s < four 7s), then 10, 10. That uses 28 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 10 + 10 = 75, leaving 45. Any attempt with 8, 10 as the middle pair wastes more (checking: max 43). Constructed list: {7,7,7,7,9,9,9,10,10,45}.
text: A list of 10 positive integers has a unique mode of 7 occurring exactly 4 times, median 9, and mean 12. What is the greatest possible value of the largest element?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: I: the mean stays μ (the two new values are symmetric), and they add exactly σ² + σ² to the squared-deviation total: new variance = (25σ² + 2σ²)/27 = σ² — unchanged. II: adds zero spread but increases n, so SD shrinks. III: every deviation flips sign but squares identically — unchanged. Answer: I and III.
text: A data set D of 25 values has mean μ and standard deviation σ > 0. Which of the following operations leave the standard deviation exactly unchanged?I. Appending the two values μ + σ and μ − σII. Appending the value μ twiceIII. Multiplying every value by −1
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: 46 and 78 are exactly 2 standard deviations from the mean. By Chebyshev’s inequality, at most 1/k² = 1/4 of any distribution lies k = 2 or more SDs from the mean, so at least 3/4 of 200 = 150 lie strictly inside. 190 (the 95% empirical rule) is the trap — that requires a normal distribution, which is not given.
text: 200 students took a test. The mean score is 62 and the standard deviation is 8. No assumption is made about the shape of the distribution. At least how many students must have scored strictly between 46 and 78?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: Σ(x+5)² = Σx² + 10Σx + 25n = 1000 + 600 + 250 = 1850. Dropping the cross term 2·5·Σx gives the trap 1250. (Bonus check: the SD is √(1000/10 − 6²) = 8 before and after the shift.)
text: Ten numbers have Σx = 60 and Σx² = 1000. Each number is increased by 5. What is the sum of the squares of the new numbers?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: Let A have a students, so C has 2a and B has 60 − 3a. Total score: 62a + 74(60 − 3a) + 170a = 4500 ⇒ 10a + 4440 = 4500 ⇒ a = 6. So B = 60 − 18 = 42. Check: (372 + 3108 + 1020)/60 = 75. ✓
text: A school has sections A, B and C with average scores 62, 74 and 85. Section C has twice as many students as section A, the three sections total 60 students, and the overall average is exactly 75. How many students are in section B?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: The median is the average of the 20th and 21st smallest. Count of elements ≤ t is ⌊t/3⌋ + ⌊t/4⌋ (common multiples like 12, 24, 36 are counted twice — it is a multiset). At t = 35 the count is 11 + 8 = 19; at t = 36 it jumps by two (36 is both a multiple of 3 and of 4) to 21. So the 20th and 21st values are both 36: median = 36.
text: M is the combined multiset (duplicates kept) of all multiples of 3 from 3 to 60 and all multiples of 4 from 4 to 80 — 40 numbers in total. What is the median of M?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: With range 20 the values live in an interval [m, m+20]. Spread is maximised by pushing values to the endpoints; keeping the mean at 50 forces the endpoints to be symmetric: 40 and 60, three values each. Variance = 10² = 100, SD = 10. Any asymmetric split (e.g. endpoints 45/65) puts unequal weights on the endpoints and yields less. SD can never exceed half the range.
text: Six numbers have mean 50 and range exactly 20. What is the maximum possible standard deviation?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: n = 20 + x. Cumulative counts: ≤2 is 8, ≤3 is 8 + x. The median position(s) must fall inside the block of 3s. For x = 4 (n = 24) the 12th value is 3 but the 13th is 4 → median 3.5. For x = 5 (n = 25) the 13th value is the last 3 → median exactly 3. Answer: 5.
text: Scores 1–5 have frequencies: score 1 → 3, score 2 → 5, score 3 → x, score 4 → 7, score 5 → 5, where x is a positive integer. What is the smallest x for which the median score is exactly 3?
title: Quant advanced: statistics

solution: Total = 25 × 48 = 1200. Remove the tails: 1200 − 5·20 − 5·70 = 1200 − 100 − 350 = 750, over 15 scores = 50. Note the middle mean exceeds the overall mean because the low tail is more extreme than the high tail.

So x could be negative (e.g., x = −0.5) or positive (e.g., x = 2). Not sufficient.Statement (2): x² > x means x(x − 1) > 0, giving x < 0 OR x > 1. Again x can be negative or positive. The interval (−1, 0) still contains negative values (x = −0.5 satisfies both: (−0.5)³ = −0.125 > −0.5 and 0.25 > −0.5), while x = 2 is positive and satisfies both. So even together the sign is not determined. The trap is assuming the two inequalities pin down x > 1; they don't eliminate the negative sliver. The answer is E.

solution: Write n in prime-factored form with exponents eₐ. n is a perfect cube exactly when every eₐ is a multiple of 3.Statement (1): n<sup>2</sup> is a perfect cube. The exponents of n<sup>2</sup> are 2eₐ, and these must each be divisible by 3. Since gcd(2, 3) = 1, 3 | 2eₐ forces 3 | eₐ for every prime. So every exponent of n is a multiple of 3, meaning n itself is a perfect cube. A definite YES. The trap is thinking 'n<sup>2</sup> cube' only weakly constrains n; in fact the coprimality of 2 and 3 transfers the cube property all the way down to n. SUFFICIENT.Statement (2): n is a perfect square. Then n = 64 = 4<sup>3</sup> is a perfect cube (YES), but n = 9 = 3<sup>2</sup> is not a perfect cube (NO). Both outcomes occur. NOT sufficient.Since (1) alone settles it and (2) alone does not, the answer is A.

Hence x has a factor of 2 and a factor of 3, so 6 | x. The even-exponent rule for squares is what upgrades the lone factor of 3 in 12 into a guaranteed factor of 3 in x. A definite YES. solution: Recall ab = gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b).Statement (1): gcd = 4 and lcm = 60. Write a = 4m, b = 4n with gcd(m, n) = 1; then lcm = 4mn = 60, so mn = 15. The coprime factor pairs of 15 are (1, 15) and (3, 5), giving (a, b) = (4, 60) with a + b = 64, or (a, b) = (12, 20) with a + b = 32. Two different sums. NOT sufficient.Statement (2): ab = 240 with a < b allows (1, 240), (2, 120), (3, 80), (4, 60), (12, 20), ... — many different sums. NOT sufficient.Together: note ab = gcd × lcm = 4 × 60 = 240, so statement (2)'s product is automatically consistent and adds no real constraint beyond a < b. Both surviving pairs from (1) already satisfy a < b: (4, 60) and (12, 20), with sums 64 and 32. The C-trap is recalling that ab is fixed at 240 and assuming a + b must follow; but two distinct coprime splits of 15 remain, so a + b is still not unique. NOT sufficient even together. The answer is E.

solution: If n = p₁<sup>e₁</sup>p₂<sup>e₂</sup>···, the divisor count is (e₁ + 1)(e₂ + 1)···, and n<sup>2</sup> has divisor count (2e₁ + 1)(2e₂ + 1)···.Statement (1): n<sup>2</sup> has 15 divisors, so (2e₁ + 1)(2e₂ + 1)··· = 15. Two cases: 15 = 15 means a single prime with 2e + 1 = 15, so e = 7 and n = p<sup>7</sup>, giving n the divisor count 7 + 1 = 8; or 15 = 3 × 5 means two primes with 2e + 1 = 3 and 2f + 1 = 5, so e = 1, f = 2 and n = p·q<sup>2</sup>, giving (1 + 1)(2 + 1) = 6 divisors. So n has either 8 or 6 divisors. solution: The units digit of a power depends only on the units digit of x.Statement (1): the units digit of x<sup>2</sup> is 6. Squaring each digit 0–9 gives units digits 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1; the value 6 arises from a units digit of 4 (4<sup>2</sup> = 16) or 6 (6<sup>2</sup> = 36).
