Could-be-false.D directly contradicts the premise that supporters were a majority among car commuters.A is far too strong and is contradicted by the derivation, which shows opponents exist among non-car commuters.
text: In a municipal survey, every resident either commutes by car or does not, and supporters and opponents of a new transit levy were each counted. Among residents who commute by car, supporters of the levy were a majority. Across all residents, opponents of the levy outnumbered supporters.Which of the following must be true?
title: Verbal: cr-inference

answer: The retailer offered free two-day shipping in no week last quarter.
options: Last quarter's abandonment rate was always exactly 20%.
Every promotional week last quarter had an abandonment rate below 20%.
No week last quarter was a promotional week.
Free two-day shipping is the only way to push abandonment below 20%.
The retailer offered free two-day shipping in no week last quarter.
solution: Premise: offering free two-day shipping ⇒ abandonment below 20%. Last quarter, abandonment was NEVER below 20%. By contraposition (modus tollens), free two-day shipping was offered in no week last quarter — exactly choice E.Why the others fail:C overreaches. We learned shipping was not offered, but the retailer offers free shipping ONLY during promotional weeks — that means free shipping implies a promotional week, not that every promotional week has free shipping. Promotional weeks could exist without the offer, so we cannot conclude there were none. Could-be-false.B is contradicted: if any promotional week occurred, its abandonment rate was at or above 20% (the rate was never below 20% all quarter), so 'below 20%' is false for it.D 'the only way' is too strong; the premise gives a sufficient condition (shipping ⇒ low abandonment), not a necessary one. Other causes of low abandonment are not excluded.A 'exactly 20%' is unsupported; 'never below 20%' permits rates above 20%, not only equal to 20%. Could-be-false.
text: An online retailer reports that whenever it offers free two-day shipping, its cart-abandonment rate falls below 20%. Last quarter, the abandonment rate never fell below 20% in any week. The retailer offers free two-day shipping only during promotional weeks.Which of the following can be properly concluded from the statements above?
title: Verbal: cr-inference

answer: Some enterprise-software startups in the portfolio raised a Series B within 18 months of their Series A.
options: Founders with prior exits cause their startups to survive longer.
Some enterprise-software startups in the portfolio raised a Series B within 18 months of their Series A.
First-time founders in the portfolio had lower five-year survival rates than founders with prior exits.
Most startups in the portfolio that survived five years raised a Series B within 18 months.
Every enterprise-software startup in the portfolio was led by a founder with a prior exit.
solution: Chain the categorical claims. Prior-exit founders raised a Series B within 18 months at a rate greater than zero, so at least one prior-exit-led startup did raise a Series B within 18 months. Every prior-exit founder led an enterprise-software startup. Therefore at least one enterprise-software startup raised a Series B within 18 months — choice B is supported.Why the others fail:A asserts causation ('cause ... survive longer'); the data are observational correlations (survival linked to fast Series B; prior exits linked to fast Series B), which cannot establish that prior exits CAUSE survival. Too strong.C chains two correlations into a survival comparison between founder types, but the survival statistic was tied to Series-B timing, not directly to founder experience; first-time founders who happened to raise a fast Series B could survive at the higher rate. Not forced.D reverses the conditional: a higher survival rate AMONG fast-Series-B startups does not imply that most SURVIVORS were fast-Series-B startups (that depends on group sizes and the survival rate of the other group). Could-be-false.E reverses premise 3: all prior-exit founders led enterprise-software startups, but enterprise-software startups could also be led by first-time founders. Could-be-false.
text: A venture fund's analysis of its portfolio showed that startups that raised a Series B within 18 months of their Series A had a higher five-year survival rate than those that did not. It also found that startups led by founders with prior exits raised a Series B within 18 months at a higher rate than startups led by first-time founders, and that rate was greater than zero. Every founder with a prior exit in the portfolio led a startup in enterprise software.Which of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?
title: Verbal: cr-inference

answer: Whether sales of Veraline's other soups, which were not reformulated or advertised, rose by a similar percentage over the same six months
options: Whether sales of Veraline's other soups, which were not reformulated or advertised, rose by a similar percentage over the same six months
Whether the natural preservative costs more per unit than the artificial one it replaced
Whether consumers can taste any difference between soup made with the natural preservative and soup made with the artificial one
Whether the natural preservative keeps the soup fresh for as long as the artificial preservative did
Whether Veraline's competitors also use natural preservatives in their comparable soups
solution: The conclusion is that the preservative switch caused the 14% rise. To evaluate a causal claim like this, the most useful move is to check for an alternative explanation that would have raised sales anyway. Option (A) does exactly that: if Veraline's other, unchanged-and-unadvertised soups also rose ~14% over the same period, some general factor (a market-wide demand bump, a pricing or distribution change, seasonality) is the more likely cause, and the conclusion is weakened; if those other soups were flat, the conclusion is strengthened. The answer to (A) swings the conclusion, which is the hallmark of the right evaluate answer.(E) is irrelevant: what competitors do does not tell us why Veraline's own sales moved. (B) Cost per unit bears on profitability, not on whether the switch drove the sales increase — sales could rise regardless of cost. (C) Whether consumers can taste a difference does not address the cause of the sales change; the ad campaign touted the change as 'natural,' not as better-tasting, so a taste difference is beside the point. (D) Shelf life affects spoilage and returns, not the stated 14% sales rise. Only (A)'s answer can change the conclusion either way.
text: Last year, Veraline Foods replaced the artificial preservative in its flagship soup with a natural one and prominently advertised the change. Over the following six months, unit sales of that soup rose 14%. Veraline's marketing director concludes that the switch to the natural preservative was responsible for the sales increase.Which of the following would be most useful to investigate in order to evaluate the marketing director's conclusion?
title: Verbal: cr-evaluate

answer: Over the same year, did recorded fare-evasion incidents at the 60 stations that kept human collectors rise, fall, or stay the same?
options: Are the 40 automated stations located in neighborhoods with higher average incomes than the 60 staffed stations?
Did the number of human collectors employed by the authority decline after the automated gates were installed?
Do automated gates allow passengers to board more quickly during peak hours than human collectors do?
Did the cost of installing and maintaining the automated gates exceed the overtime savings the authority achieved?
Over the same year, did recorded fare-evasion incidents at the 60 stations that kept human collectors rise, fall, or stay the same?
solution: The conclusion is a comparative causal claim: automated gates reduce evasion more effectively than human collectors. The before-after drop at automated stations alone cannot establish that, because evasion might have fallen everywhere for some independent reason (more enforcement campaigns, a fare cut, better signage, a downturn in ridership of the evading demographic). Option (E) supplies the missing comparison group. If evasion at the human-staffed stations also fell ~22%, the automation gets no special credit and the conclusion collapses; if it stayed flat or rose while automated stations dropped, the conclusion is supported. The answer swings the conclusion, so (E) is the test that evaluates it.(A) is the tempting trap: income could correlate with evasion. But it does not address the conclusion as stated, because we are told the automated stations' evasion fell year over year — a stable neighborhood-income difference was already present in the baseline year and cannot explain a year-over-year change. (D) and (B) concern cost and staffing, not the effectiveness comparison. (C) Boarding speed is a different benefit entirely and says nothing about evasion. Only (E)'s answer can move the conclusion either way.
text: To cut overtime costs, the city transit authority installed automated fare gates at its 40 busiest stations; the remaining 60 stations kept human fare collectors. In the year after installation, the 40 automated stations together recorded 22% fewer fare-evasion incidents than they had the year before. The authority's analyst concludes that automated gates reduce fare evasion more effectively than human collectors do.The answer to which of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the analyst's conclusion?
title: Verbal: cr-evaluate

answer: Whether patients given an inactive placebo in the same trial also reported a substantial drop in migraine days
options: Whether the patients in the trial had been correctly diagnosed with chronic migraines before enrolling
Whether the drug is more expensive to manufacture than competing migraine medications
Whether the 30% reduction was sustained for the full duration of the trial or concentrated in its first week
Whether patients given an inactive placebo in the same trial also reported a substantial drop in migraine days
Whether the drug produces side effects more severe than those of migraine treatments already on the market
solution: The argument infers drug efficacy from a 30% before-versus-after drop in migraine days. The central vulnerability is that self-reported symptom counts often fall in trials regardless of the active ingredient — the placebo effect, regression to the mean, and reporting bias all push the same way. Option (D) tests precisely this: if placebo patients showed a similar drop, the 30% cannot be credited to the drug and the argument fails; if placebo patients did not improve, the drug's effect stands out and the argument is strengthened. That swing is what an evaluate answer must produce.(E) Side-effect severity bears on the risk-benefit and on whether it should be preferred, but not on whether the drug works; even a drug with bad side effects can be efficacious. (C) is tempting, but a drop concentrated early versus spread evenly would still be a real reduction relative to baseline; without a control it tells us nothing about cause. (A) Confirming the diagnosis matters for generalizability but does not bear on whether the observed change was caused by the drug. (B) Manufacturing cost is irrelevant to efficacy. Only (D) can change the conclusion either way.
text: A pharmaceutical startup reports that in its trial, patients who took its new drug for migraines reported, on average, 30% fewer migraine days per month than they had before the trial. The company argues that the drug is an effective treatment for chronic migraines and should be approved.Which of the following would it be most useful to determine in order to evaluate the company's argument?
title: Verbal: cr-evaluate

answer: In the same three-year period, did Aldoria also enact a separate ban on single-use plastics or a major recycling expansion that would independently reduce landfill tonnage?
options: Has the cost of waste disposal for the average Aldorian household risen or fallen since the composting mandate took effect?
Do a majority of our state's residents say they would support a mandatory composting program?
Does our state currently send more total tonnage to landfills each year than Aldoria did before its mandate?
In the same three-year period, did Aldoria also enact a separate ban on single-use plastics or a major recycling expansion that would independently reduce landfill tonnage?
Is the climate in our state similar enough to Aldoria's that food waste would decompose at comparable rates in compost facilities?
solution: The editorial credits Aldoria's composting mandate with the 35% landfill drop, then recommends copying it. The reasoning is vulnerable if some other policy enacted in the same window did the heavy lifting. Option (D) targets exactly that confound: if Aldoria simultaneously banned single-use plastics or expanded recycling, those measures could account for much of the 35%, and attributing the drop to composting — and recommending composting alone — is unwarranted; if no such measures existed, the composting attribution is much stronger. The answer swings the conclusion, which is what an evaluate question requires.(C) Whether our state landfills more tonnage than Aldoria did is about scale, not about whether composting caused the drop. (B) Resident support bears on political feasibility, not on whether the mandate works. (E) Climate-driven decomposition rates are a tempting 'will it transfer?' concern, but the editorial's inference rests on whether composting caused Aldoria's drop, and decomposition speed does not address that causal link or the alternative-cause problem. (A) Household cost is a side issue. Only (D) can change the conclusion either way.
text: Editorial: Our state should adopt mandatory composting, as the neighboring state of Aldoria did three years ago. Since Aldoria's mandate took effect, the total tonnage of waste its residents send to landfills has dropped by 35%. Clearly, a composting mandate is the way to achieve a large reduction in landfill waste.The answer to which of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the editorial's reasoning?
title: Verbal: cr-evaluate

answer: Whether the average market price of gasoline during the year after the switch was roughly the same as it had been the year before
options: Whether the firm's drivers found the electric vans easier to operate than the gasoline vans
Whether the electric vans require less frequent routine maintenance than the gasoline vans did
Whether the average market price of gasoline during the year after the switch was roughly the same as it had been the year before
Whether the price of electricity is expected to rise over the next several years
Whether competing logistics firms have also begun adopting electric delivery vans
solution: Management attributes the entire 42% drop in energy spending to the switch to electric. But spending is price times quantity, and a confound lurks in price. Option (C) isolates it: if gasoline prices had crashed in the year after the switch, then even the firm's old gasoline fleet would have cost much less to run, so part of the 42% reflects cheaper fuel rather than the technology change — weakening the conclusion. Conversely, if gas prices were roughly flat, the saving is attributable to the switch, strengthening it. Because the answer can move the conclusion either way, (C) is the right evaluate choice. (A tempting subtlety: one might think a comparison of old gas prices versus new electricity prices matters, but the conclusion is about whether the switch produced the realized saving relative to staying on gas, so the relevant counterfactual is what running the gas fleet would have cost in the new year — i.e., gasoline prices in that year.)(D) Future electricity prices do not bear on a saving already realized this past year. (B) Maintenance frequency is a separate cost category, not the fuel-and-energy spending the projection covered. (E) Competitor adoption is irrelevant to this firm's realized savings. (A) Driver ease of operation says nothing about cost. Only (C) can change the conclusion.
text: A logistics firm switched its delivery fleet from gasoline vans to electric vans, projecting that it would cut its annual fuel-and-energy spending by at least 40%. After the switch, the firm found that its combined annual spending on vehicle energy had indeed fallen by 42% compared with the previous year. Management concludes that the switch to electric vans achieved the projected savings.Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating management's conclusion?
title: Verbal: cr-evaluate

answer: Were the students who chose to participate in the peer-tutoring program already earning higher grades than non-participants before the program began?
options: Do students at other universities with similar peer-tutoring programs report being satisfied with them?
Does the university have enough trained peer tutors to serve every student if the program is made mandatory?
Are the final grades in the courses covered by the program assigned on a curve relative to all students in the course?
Were the students who chose to participate in the peer-tutoring program already earning higher grades than non-participants before the program began?
Did participating students spend more total hours studying than non-participating students during the term?
solution: The program was voluntary, so the comparison is between self-selected participants and everyone else — a textbook selection-bias setup. The dean's causal conclusion ('the program improves performance') is only warranted if the two groups were comparable to start. Option (D) tests this directly: if participants were already stronger students before the program, their higher final grades may reflect pre-existing ability rather than any effect of tutoring, gutting the conclusion; if the groups started equal, the grade gap is better attributed to the program, supporting it. The answer swings the conclusion, so (D) is the evaluate answer.(E) is the trap. More study hours among participants seems to undercut the program — but it does not change the conclusion either way as cleanly as (D), because tutoring sessions are a form of study, and the program could be exactly what induced the extra studying; extra hours could be the mechanism through which the program works rather than a rival cause. (C) Curving could complicate interpreting absolute grades, but with the same curve applied to both groups the comparison still reflects relative performance. (B) Tutor capacity bears on feasibility of the mandate, not on whether tutoring causes improvement. (A) Satisfaction elsewhere is irrelevant to this causal claim. Only (D) decisively moves the conclusion.
text: A university found that students who participated in its new peer-tutoring program earned higher final grades, on average, than students who did not participate. The dean concludes that the peer-tutoring program improves students' academic performance and plans to make it mandatory for all students.The answer to which of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the dean's conclusion?
title: Verbal: cr-evaluate

answer: Scanning and bagging items oneself at a kiosk takes most customers noticeably longer than it took a trained cashier to do the same work.
options: Scanning and bagging items oneself at a kiosk takes most customers noticeably longer than it took a trained cashier to do the same work.
The chain installed fewer total checkout points than before, so that during peak hours all kiosks were frequently occupied at once.
Customers who use self-service kiosks tend to purchase fewer items per visit than those who used the old standard lanes.
A competing grocery chain in the same region kept its staffed checkout lanes and advertised them heavily.
The kiosks were programmed to display promotional offers on screen while customers waited for an attendant to clear errors.
solution: The paradox: waiting in line dropped 40%, yet dissatisfaction with checkout speed rose. Resolution must reconcile less line-waiting with a worse perception of overall speed. (A) does exactly this: "checkout speed" as the customer experiences it includes the time spent at the register, not just the time waiting to reach it. If self-scanning is slower than a cashier, the total time from joining the line to finishing can rise even though the queue itself is shorter — so customers feel checkout got slower. (B) is the strongest trap: fewer checkout points would tend to lengthen wait times, contradicting the stated 40% drop, so it deepens rather than resolves the paradox. (C) fewer items would make checkout faster, deepening the paradox. (D) and (E) are irrelevant to why these shoppers, with shorter lines, feel speed worsened.
text: After a regional grocery chain replaced its standard checkout lanes with self-service kiosks, the average time a customer spent waiting in line fell by nearly 40%. Yet over the same period, the proportion of shoppers who reported being dissatisfied with the speed of checkout actually rose sharply.Which of the following, if true, best explains the apparent discrepancy between the shorter wait times and the increased dissatisfaction with checkout speed?
title: Verbal: cr-paradox

answer: The drug must be taken daily without interruption to lower cholesterol, and trial participants — unlike most prescribed patients — were monitored to ensure they never missed a dose.
options: Patients in the general population who were prescribed the drug had, on average, higher baseline cholesterol than the trial participants.
The placebo group in the trial was larger than the group that received the active drug.
Heart attacks have many causes besides high cholesterol, several of which the drug does not address.
The drug also produces a modest reduction in blood pressure as a side effect.
The drug must be taken daily without interruption to lower cholesterol, and trial participants — unlike most prescribed patients — were monitored to ensure they never missed a dose.
solution: The discrepancy is between a strong trial effect and a null real-world effect for the same drug. The resolver must identify a difference between trial conditions and ordinary prescribing. (E) supplies it: efficacy depends on perfect adherence, which the trial enforced through monitoring but the general population does not achieve — so in practice the drug's effect washes out. (C) is the classic trap: it's true and tempting, but it applies equally to the trial and the general population, so it cannot explain why the drug worked in one setting and not the other. (B) group size differences don't bias the rate comparison and don't differ between settings. (D) a blood-pressure benefit would, if anything, make the drug look more effective in the population, deepening the paradox. (A) higher baseline cholesterol would, if anything, leave more room for benefit, not explain a null result.
text: A pharmaceutical firm ran a year-long trial of a new cholesterol drug. Among trial participants, those taking the drug had a 30% lower rate of heart attacks than those taking a placebo. When the same drug was later approved and prescribed to the general population, however, patients taking it showed no measurable reduction in heart-attack rates compared with similar untreated patients.Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the discrepancy between the trial result and the general-population result?
title: Verbal: cr-paradox

answer: Faster initial travel times led many commuters who had previously used side streets or commuted at off-peak hours to begin driving the highway during rush hour.
options: The construction work required to widen the highway took longer to complete than the planners had originally estimated.
Faster initial travel times led many commuters who had previously used side streets or commuted at off-peak hours to begin driving the highway during rush hour.
Some commuters switched from driving to a newly expanded commuter rail line that runs parallel to the highway.
The cost of widening the highway exceeded the budget the city had allocated for the project.
The widened highway required more frequent resurfacing than the original four-lane road had.
solution: Paradox: extra capacity gave a temporary improvement that fully evaporated. The resolution is the well-known "induced demand" mechanism. (B) names it: the initial speed gain attracted new rush-hour drivers (from side streets and off-peak times) until congestion rebuilt to the old equilibrium — precisely why times returned to baseline. (C) is the key trap: commuters leaving the highway for rail would reduce highway traffic and help preserve the improvement, so it deepens the paradox. (A) construction delay doesn't bear on why times rose after the road opened and initially improved. (D) cost overrun is irrelevant to travel time. (E) resurfacing frequency, by itself, doesn't explain a steady return to the exact prior travel time during normal operation.
text: City planners widened a heavily congested commuter highway from four lanes to six, expecting average rush-hour travel times along the corridor to fall. For the first month after the wider road opened, travel times did drop. But within a year, average rush-hour travel times along the same corridor had returned to exactly what they were before the widening.Which of the following, if true, does most to explain why the travel-time improvement disappeared?
title: Verbal: cr-paradox

answer: Before the bonus existed, employees referred only candidates they personally judged to be strong fits, whereas the bonus led them to refer many acquaintances regardless of suitability, lowering the share of referrals the company chose to hire.
options: The cash bonus was paid only after a referred hire completed six months of employment with the company.
The company's total number of new hires from all sources increased substantially during the year the bonus was offered.
Several competing firms launched similar referral-bonus programs during the same year.
Employees who referred candidates were, on average, more experienced than employees who did not.

Before the bonus existed, employees referred only candidates they personally judged to be strong fits, whereas the bonus led them to refer many acquaintances regardless of suitability, lowering the share of referrals the company chose to hire.
solution: Three times as many referrals but fewer referral hires means the hire rate per referral collapsed. (E) explains the mechanism directly: the bonus changed referrer behavior from selective (strong fits) to indiscriminate, so even though referrals tripled, the fraction actually hired fell far enough that absolute hires dipped. That reconciles a surge in volume with a drop in output. (B) is the trap: more total hires from all sources would, if anything, predict more referral hires too, so it deepens the paradox. (A) a delayed payout affects when bonuses are paid, not how many referrals convert to hires. (D) the experience of referrers doesn't bear on hire conversion of the referrals. (C) competitors' programs might affect the candidate pool generally but don't explain why this company's tripled referrals yielded fewer hires.
text: A software company introduced a generous referral bonus: any employee who referred a candidate who was hired received a large cash payment. In the year after the program launched, the number of candidates referred by employees roughly tripled. Yet the number of new hires who came through employee referrals was slightly lower than it had been the year before the bonus existed.Which of the following, if true, best explains the surprising drop in referral hires despite the surge in referrals?
title: Verbal: cr-paradox

answer: The reservation system allowed visitors to choose any available entry time slot, and the great majority chose the mid-morning slots, concentrating arrivals at the popular trailheads into a few hours.
options: The park raised its entrance fee at the same time it introduced the reservation system.
The reservation system allowed visitors to choose any available entry time slot, and the great majority chose the mid-morning slots, concentrating arrivals at the popular trailheads into a few hours.
Visitors with reservations spent on average more total time inside the park than visitors had before.
The reservation website occasionally crashed during the first weeks of the season, frustrating some prospective visitors.
Many casual visitors who previously wandered to quieter trailheads were deterred by the reservation requirement and stopped visiting the park entirely.
solution: Fewer visitors overall, yet worse peak crowding at the popular trailheads, means the timing or distribution of visits shifted. (B) resolves it: by letting everyone self-select slots, the system funneled most arrivals into the same mid-morning window at the same popular spots, so peak-time density rose even as the daily total fell. (E) is the strongest distractor — it explains the 15% drop in total visitation, but if those lost visitors used quieter trailheads, their departure would relieve pressure elsewhere, not increase crowding at the popular ones; it deepens rather than resolves the paradox. (A) higher fees would tend to reduce crowding everywhere. (C) longer stays could add some crowding but doesn't explain concentration at peak times at the popular sites specifically. (D) website crashes reduce visitors, deepening the paradox.
text: A national park introduced an online reservation system requiring all visitors to book an entry time slot in advance, intending to reduce overcrowding at the most popular trailheads. In the first season under the new system, the total number of visitors to the park fell by about 15%. Even so, park rangers reported that the most popular trailheads were more crowded at peak times than they had been before reservations were required.Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the popular trailheads became more crowded even as overall visitation fell?
title: Verbal: cr-paradox

answer: Because the newer aircraft are quieter and more comfortable, the airline was able to add many additional flights on the route and fill them, so total miles flown rose by more than 20%.
options: Because the newer aircraft are quieter and more comfortable, the airline was able to add many additional flights on the route and fill them, so total miles flown rose by more than 20%.
The newer aircraft require a different grade of jet fuel than the older planes did.
Maintenance costs for the newer aircraft were lower than for the older planes.
The newer aircraft were more expensive to purchase and finance than the older planes they replaced.
A competing airline reduced its fares on the same route during the year.
solution: Fuel per mile dropped 20% and the per-gallon price was flat, yet total fuel cost rose. Total fuel cost = (fuel per mile) × (miles flown) × (price per gallon). With the first and third factors not increasing, only a rise in miles flown can push the total up. (A) supplies exactly that: the airline expanded flights enough that total miles rose by more than 20%, overwhelming the per-mile efficiency gain. (D) and (C) concern purchase, financing, or maintenance costs — not fuel costs, so they're outside the scope of the contradiction. (B) the grade of fuel doesn't change cost if the per-gallon price is stated as unchanged. (E) a competitor's fares affect demand and revenue but, without telling us flights or miles increased, do not explain higher fuel consumption.
text: An airline replaced the older planes on its busiest route with newer aircraft that burn 20% less fuel per mile flown. Fuel is the airline's single largest operating cost on that route. Over the following year, however, the airline's total fuel costs on that route increased compared with the year before, even though fuel prices per gallon were unchanged.Which of the following, if true, best resolves the apparent contradiction?
title: Verbal: cr-paradox

answer: By more accurately identifying genuinely high-risk patients, the new protocol moved many borderline patients — who were previously labeled high-risk but usually survived — into the low-risk category, leaving the high-risk group composed of sicker patients on average.
options: The total number of patients arriving at the hospital's emergency department increased over the two-year period.

By more accurately identifying genuinely high-risk patients, the new protocol moved many borderline patients — who were previously labeled high-risk but usually survived — into the low-risk category, leaving the high-risk group composed of sicker patients on average.
Some patients classified as low-risk under the new protocol chose to seek care at other hospitals.
The new protocol takes slightly longer for staff to administer than the old protocol did.
The hospital hired additional emergency physicians during the same two-year period.
solution: This is a classification-mix (stage-migration) paradox: each group's death rate can change purely because who is in each group changed, even if treatment quality is constant or improved. (B) gives the mechanism: a more accurate protocol strips relatively healthy borderline patients out of the high-risk bucket (raising that bucket's average severity, hence its death rate) and adds those likely-survivors to the low-risk bucket (lowering its death rate). Both shifts follow from better classification — satisfying the requirement that the protocol not be worse. (D) longer administration time doesn't explain divergent rate changes between groups. (A) more patients overall doesn't change the composition logic. (E) more physicians would tend to lower death rates in both groups, not raise one. (C) low-risk patients leaving wouldn't raise the high-risk death rate and isn't tied to severity.
text: A hospital introduced a new triage protocol that, according to several controlled studies, correctly identifies high-risk emergency patients more accurately than the protocol it replaced. In the two years since adopting it, the hospital has documented that the death rate among patients its triage system classifies as "high-risk" has risen, while the death rate among those classified as "low-risk" has fallen.Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain these changes in death rates without implying that the new protocol performs worse than the old one?
title: Verbal: cr-paradox

answer: The first characterizes the reasoning the author goes on to challenge; the second is the author's own conclusion.
options: The first identifies the pattern of reasoning the author endorses; the second states the conclusion that follows from that pattern.
The first is an objection the author rejects; the second restates the position of the critics in different terms.
The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is evidence offered in support of that conclusion.
The first is a premise the author accepts; the second is a competing prediction the author dismisses.
The first characterizes the reasoning the author goes on to challenge; the second is the author's own conclusion.
solution: Map the structure. The critics' argument is described in the first sentence. The first boldface ("This reasoning treats the fate of the car-sharing ventures as a reliable guide...") characterizes the critics' inference — and the very next word, "But," signals that the author is about to attack it. So the first boldface is the reasoning the author challenges, not endorses. The author then gives a disanalogy (different cost, regulation, users) and closes with the second boldface ("may well succeed"), which is the author's own conclusion. That is exactly choice E.Why the traps fail: (A) says the author endorses the first portion's pattern — but the "But" shows the author rejects it, so A inverts the author's stance. (B) calls the second boldface a restatement of the critics' position; in fact it is the opposite of the critics' position (they predict failure, the author predicts possible success). (C) mislabels the first boldface as the main conclusion, but it is a description of someone else's reasoning, and the author's conclusion is the second boldface, not the first. (D) wrongly says the author accepts the first portion as a premise, when the author's whole point is to undermine it. The answer is E.
text: Critics of the new municipal bike-share program argue that it will fail because the city's three earlier attempts at car-sharing all collapsed within two years. This reasoning treats the fate of the car-sharing ventures as a reliable guide to what will happen to bike-sharing. But car-sharing and bike-sharing differ in cost, regulatory burden, and the demographics of likely users; the earlier failures therefore tell us little about the prospects of the current program. The bike-share program may well succeed despite its predecessors' record.In the argument above, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
title: Verbal: cr-boldface

answer: The first is a finding that the analysts cite in support of their recommendation and that the author concedes; the second is the consideration the author uses to undercut that recommendation.
options: The first is an assumption on which the analysts' recommendation depends; the second identifies a flaw in that assumption.
The first is evidence the author rejects as inaccurate; the second is the author's reason for rejecting it.
The first is the recommendation the author opposes; the second is the reason the analysts give for it.
The first is a finding that the analysts cite in support of their recommendation and that the author concedes; the second is the consideration the author uses to undercut that recommendation.
The first states the author's main conclusion; the second provides evidence for that conclusion.
solution: Trace the moves. The analysts recommend a price increase, citing past insensitivity of demand. The first boldface ("previous increases did not measurably reduce the number of units sold") is that very factual finding — and the author signals agreement with "It is true that...," i.e., the author concedes it. Then "However" introduces a changed condition (a substitute is coming), and the second boldface states the upshot the author uses to undercut the recommendation. That is precisely choice D: a conceded supporting finding, then the consideration that weighs against the recommendation.Why the traps fail: (C) calls the first boldface the recommendation; the recommendation is to raise the price, which is stated in the first sentence, not the boldface — the first boldface is a piece of evidence the analysts rely on. (E) says the first boldface is the author's main conclusion, but the author's position is critical of the price increase, and that critical point lives in the second boldface, not the first. (A) mislabels the first boldface as an "assumption"; it is an observed fact the author grants, not an unstated assumption. (B) is the most tempting trap: it claims the author rejects the first boldface as inaccurate — but "It is true that" shows the author accepts it; what the author disputes is the inference drawn from it, not its accuracy. The answer is D.
text: A pharmaceutical firm's analysts recommend raising the price of its only patented drug, reasoning that because demand for the drug has been insensitive to past price increases, a further increase will boost revenue. It is true that previous increases did not measurably reduce the number of units sold. However, those increases all occurred before any therapeutic substitute existed; a rival's substitute is now expected to reach the market within the year. Once that substitute is available, even a modest price increase could drive a substantial share of patients to switch.In the argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
title: Verbal: cr-boldface

answer: The first is a fact the economist accepts and that the commentators take as decisive; the second is the economist's conclusion that this fact is not decisive.
options: The first is evidence the economist offers for the main conclusion; the second is that main conclusion.
The first is a claim the economist disputes; the second is an alternative explanation that, if true, would establish the commentators' position.
The first is the conclusion the commentators draw; the second is the economist's main conclusion, which contradicts it.
The first is a fact the economist accepts and that the commentators take as decisive; the second is the economist's conclusion that this fact is not decisive.
The first is the economist's main conclusion; the second is a concession the economist makes to the opposing view.
solution: Identify the parties. The commentators conclude that the credit is working, treating the timing coincidence as proof. The first boldface ("The surge did indeed begin in the same quarter the credit took effect") is that coincidence stated as a fact — "did indeed" shows the economist accepts it, and it is the very thing the commentators treat as decisive. The economist then supplies a rival cause (necessity-driven start-ups from layoffs) and reaches the second boldface: the credit need not be the cause. That is the economist's conclusion that the conceded fact is not decisive — choice D.Why the traps fail: (C) says the first boldface is the commentators' conclusion; it is not — the commentators' conclusion is that the credit is working, whereas the boldface is just the timing fact both sides accept. (A) calls the first boldface the economist's own supporting evidence for his conclusion; but the timing fact actually supports the commentators' view — the economist's real evidence is the layoff explanation, which is not boldfaced. (B) wrongly says the second boldface, if true, would establish the commentators' position; it does the reverse — it weakens their causal claim. (E) inverts roles by calling the first boldface the main conclusion; the main conclusion is the second boldface. The answer is D.
text: Economist: Some commentators claim that the recent surge in start-up formation proves the new tax credit for entrepreneurs is working. The surge did indeed begin in the same quarter the credit took effect. Yet that same quarter also saw a sharp, unrelated drop in corporate hiring, which pushed many laid-off workers to start their own ventures out of necessity. The tax credit, then, need not be the cause of the increase in start-ups, even granting that the two coincided in time.In the economist's argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
title: Verbal: cr-boldface

answer: The first acknowledges a general tendency that favors the competitor's claim; the second is the conclusion the spokesperson draws against that claim.
options: The first is the spokesperson's primary evidence; the second is the competitor's response to that evidence.
The first is the spokesperson's main conclusion; the second is a restatement of it.
The first acknowledges a general tendency that favors the competitor's claim; the second is the conclusion the spokesperson draws against that claim.
The first is the competitor's conclusion; the second is the spokesperson's evidence against it.
The first is an assumption the spokesperson rejects; the second explains why it should be rejected.
solution: Lay out the structure. The competitor argues: more warehouses ⇒ faster. The first boldface ("Greater warehouse count does tend to shorten the average distance") concedes a general tendency that supports the competitor — "does tend to" marks acknowledgment, not endorsement of the full claim. The spokesperson then introduces a counter-factor (real-time routing) and concludes in the second boldface that warehouse count alone does not settle which network is faster. That matches choice C: a concession favoring the opponent, then the author's contrary conclusion.Why the traps fail: (D) labels the first boldface the competitor's conclusion, but the competitor's conclusion is "our network is faster"; the boldface is only a general tendency the spokesperson grants. (B) says the first boldface is the main conclusion and the second merely restates it — but the two say different things (one concedes a tendency, the other denies that tendency is decisive), and only the second is the author's conclusion. (E) calls the first boldface an assumption the spokesperson rejects; the spokesperson accepts it as true, disputing only its decisiveness. (A) treats the second boldface as the competitor's reply, but it is plainly the spokesperson's own closing conclusion ("therefore"). The answer is C.
text: Spokesperson: Our competitor asserts that its delivery network is faster than ours because it operates more regional warehouses. Greater warehouse count does tend to shorten the average distance a package must travel. But our routing software re-optimizes every shipment in real time, which more than offsets the distance disadvantage, so our average delivery time is in fact the lower of the two. Warehouse count alone, therefore, does not determine which network is faster.In the spokesperson's argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
title: Verbal: cr-boldface

answer: The first is a fact consistent with the prevailing view that the biologist does not contest; the second is the rival explanation the biologist concludes is superior.
options: The first is the biologist's main conclusion; the second is a concession to the prevailing view.
The first is the evidence the biologist relies on most heavily; the second is the conclusion that evidence supports.
The first is a fact consistent with the prevailing view that the biologist does not contest; the second is the rival explanation the biologist concludes is superior.
The first is the prevailing view's conclusion; the second is the biologist's evidence against it.
The first is a finding the biologist shows to be false; the second is the conclusion that follows once it is discarded.
solution: Sort the claims. The prevailing view: predator spread is causing the decline. The first boldface ("The predator's range has indeed expanded") is a fact that fits that view — "indeed" signals the biologist does not contest it. The biologist then presents a competing cause (the blight wiping out the food source, with declines worst where the blight was worst) and concludes in the second boldface that the food-loss explanation is superior. That is choice C.Why the traps fail: (D) calls the first boldface the prevailing view's conclusion; the conclusion is "the predator is shrinking the population," whereas the boldface is only the range-expansion fact, which both sides accept. (A) inverts the roles, naming the first boldface the main conclusion; the biologist's conclusion is the second boldface. (B) says the first boldface is the evidence the biologist relies on most; in fact the biologist's load-bearing evidence is the blight correlation, and the first boldface supports the opposing view. (E) is the strongest trap: it claims the biologist shows the first boldface to be false — but "indeed" concedes its truth; the biologist disputes only whether it is the best explanation, not whether the range actually expanded. The answer is C.
text: Biologist: A widely held view holds that the songbird population in the valley is shrinking because of the spread of a nonnative predator. The predator's range has indeed expanded across the valley over the past decade. But over that same decade, a fungal blight destroyed most of the berry shrubs the songbirds feed on, and population declines have been steepest precisely where the blight, not the predator, hit hardest. The loss of the food source is a better explanation of the decline than the spread of the predator is.In the biologist's argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
title: Verbal: cr-boldface

answer: The first states a condition under which the proposal would achieve its aim; the second is the analyst's conclusion that the condition is unlikely to be met in the relevant way.
options: The first states a condition under which the proposal would achieve its aim; the second is the analyst's conclusion that the condition is unlikely to be met in the relevant way.
The first is an objection to the proposal; the second is the analyst's reply defending the proposal.
The first is the analyst's main conclusion; the second is the evidence supporting it.
The first is a prediction the analyst endorses; the second is a competing prediction the analyst rejects.
The first is the proposal's stated goal; the second is the means proposed to achieve that goal.
solution: Read the logic. The proposal aims to relieve congestion via a fare cut. The first boldface is conditional: "If lower fares drew a large number of current drivers onto buses, highway traffic would ease." It states the condition under which the proposal would work — the analyst does not assert the condition holds, only what would follow if it did. The survey evidence then shows the switchers are pedestrians and cyclists, not drivers, so the condition is not met in the way that matters; the second boldface concludes the cut is unlikely to relieve congestion. That is choice A.Why the traps fail: (C) names the first boldface the main conclusion, but it is a hypothetical, and the actual conclusion is the second boldface. (E) misreads the first boldface as the goal and the second as the means; the goal (relieve congestion) and means (cut fares) are both in the first sentence, not the boldface. (D) calls the first boldface a prediction the analyst endorses; but it is conditional — the analyst neither asserts the antecedent nor predicts the consequent will occur, and in fact argues the trigger fails. (B) reverses the analyst's stance: the second boldface attacks the proposal, it does not defend it. The answer is A.
text: Policy analyst: A proposal would cut the city bus fare in half to relieve highway congestion. If lower fares drew a large number of current drivers onto buses, highway traffic would ease noticeably. However, surveys consistently show that the people most likely to switch to buses in response to a fare cut are not drivers but current pedestrians and cyclists, who add nothing to highway traffic in the first place. The fare cut, then, is unlikely to relieve highway congestion to any meaningful degree.In the policy analyst's argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
title: Verbal: cr-boldface

answer: The first describes what the cited result would indicate if a certain interpretation held; the second is the conclusion the author reaches after casting doubt on that interpretation.
options: The first is evidence the author uses to support adopting the policy; the second is the author's endorsement of the policy.
The first describes what the cited result would indicate if a certain interpretation held; the second is the conclusion the author reaches after casting doubt on that interpretation.
The first is the position the author ultimately defends; the second is an objection the author overcomes.
The first is the conclusion of the argument; the second is a premise supporting it.
The first is an assumption the author shows to be true; the second is the consequence of that assumption.
solution: Follow the reasoning. Someone proposes the four-day week, citing the pilot team's higher satisfaction. The first boldface ("Higher satisfaction... is exactly what we would expect if the shorter week were genuinely beneficial") lays out what the result would indicate under the rosy interpretation — it does not assert that interpretation is correct. The author then undermines it: the team self-selected (volunteers who lobbied), so their enthusiasm may be confounded. The second boldface concludes the results are weak grounds for a company-wide rollout. That is choice B.Why the traps fail: (D) and (C) both call the first boldface the conclusion or the author's defended position, but the author's actual conclusion is the second boldface, which is skeptical of the policy. (A) says the author uses the first boldface to support adopting the policy and that the second is an endorsement; in fact the author casts doubt on the result and the second boldface argues against a full rollout, the opposite of endorsement. options: explaining how a revived theoretical model and supporting evidence have unsettled the long-standing default view of how wages and minimum wages operate

tracing the historical reasons that the theory of monopsony was marginalized for most of the twentieth century

solution: The passage opens with the competitive “textbook” default (para 1), introduces monopsony as a long-marginalized alternative that complicates it (para 2), and reviews recent empirical work that has “revived interest” in it, closing with the author’s stance that the competitive model can no longer be treated as the natural default (para 3). text: For much of the twentieth century, the textbook account of how wages are set treated the labor market as effectively competitive: many employers bid for workers who could costlessly move between jobs, so any firm that tried to pay below the prevailing wage would lose its entire workforce, and each worker was paid a wage equal to the value of what an additional hour of their labor produced. Within this framework, a legally imposed minimum wage above the competitive level could only reduce employment, because firms confronted with a wage floor would hire fewer workers than the market would otherwise sustain.An older but long-marginalized alternative, the theory of monopsony, complicates this picture. A monopsonistic employer faces an upward-sloping supply of labor: to attract more workers it must raise the wage it offers, and—absent the ability to pay each worker a different rate—it must raise the wage paid to existing workers as well. The marginal cost of an additional hire therefore exceeds that worker’s wage. A profit-maximizing monopsonist responds by hiring fewer workers and paying a lower wage than a competitive market would. Crucially, within a band, a minimum wage can compel such an employer to pay more and employ more, because it severs the link between the wage and the marginal cost of hiring.Recent empirical work has revived interest in this once-peripheral model. Studies exploiting regional variation in minimum-wage increases have frequently found employment effects far smaller than the competitive model predicts, and sometimes none at all. Proponents read these results as evidence that frictions—search costs, geographic immobility, imperfect information—confer monopsony power on many ordinary employers, not merely the isolated company town of textbook caricature. Skeptics counter that null employment effects are also consistent with firms absorbing higher labor costs through reduced profits, higher prices, or slower future hiring that conventional studies fail to detect. What seems increasingly difficult to defend, however, is the once-reflexive assumption that the competitive model is the natural default and monopsony the exotic exception. solution: The passage moves from the textbook image of mutualism, to the hidden complexity (the oxygen paradox and leghemoglobin), to the practical upshot that the legume's contribution is an integrated, costly physiology rather than a transferable gene—which is why engineering fixation into cereals is hard. Choice A captures that arc.B is too extreme and distorts the text: the author presents cereal engineering as a tempting but problematic aspiration, never as 'the only sustainable path.' E overstates: the passage says fixation in legumes occurs in nodules but never claims fixation is impossible outside nodules—other free-living diazotrophs exist (the broader category 'diazotrophs' is introduced). text:
<div style="background:#f7f9fd;border-left:4px solid #4759bd;padding:12px 16px;margin:0 0 14px;border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;line-height:1.55">Atmospheric nitrogen is abundant—it constitutes roughly 78% of the air—yet most organisms cannot use it, because the triple bond joining the two nitrogen atoms in N₂ is among the most stable in chemistry. Only certain prokaryotes, the diazotrophs, possess nitrogenase, the enzyme that cleaves this bond and reduces N₂ to ammonia. Among the most studied diazotrophs are rhizobia, soil bacteria that infect the roots of legumes and inhabit specialized swellings called nodules. There the bacterium trades fixed nitrogen for carbon compounds supplied by the plant, a reciprocity long offered as a textbook emblem of mutualism.Yet the relationship is less placid than that emblem suggests. Nitrogenase is irreversibly poisoned by oxygen, while the bacterium's own respiration—needed to power the energy-hungry reaction—demands oxygen. The legume resolves this contradiction by synthesizing leghemoglobin, a pigment that binds oxygen tightly enough to keep the enzyme's surroundings nearly anoxic, yet releases it fast enough to sustain respiration. The plant, in other words, does not merely host the bacterium; it actively engineers a chemical environment without which fixation would be impossible.This dependence has tempted some agronomists to imagine transferring nitrogen-fixing capacity to cereals such as wheat and rice, which would lessen reliance on the synthetic fertilizers whose manufacture consumes vast quantities of fossil fuel. The difficulty is that the legume's contribution is not a single transferable gene but an integrated physiology—nodule formation, oxygen regulation, and a carbon subsidy so large that fixation can cost the plant a fifth of its photosynthetic output. A cereal endowed with nitrogenase but lacking these supports might fix little nitrogen while paying a steep metabolic toll. The symbiosis endures, this analysis suggests, not because it is effortless but because each partner has evolved to absorb costs the other cannot.
Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
title: Verbal: rc-main-idea

answer: It binds oxygen tightly enough to keep nitrogenase's surroundings nearly anoxic while still releasing oxygen quickly enough to support the bacterium's respiration.
options: It triggers the formation of nodules on the legume's roots, allowing rhizobia to infect the plant.
It supplies the carbon compounds that the bacterium requires in exchange for fixed nitrogen.
It binds oxygen tightly enough to keep nitrogenase's surroundings nearly anoxic while still releasing oxygen quickly enough to support the bacterium's respiration.
It directly cleaves the triple bond in N₂, a reaction that the bacterium's nitrogenase cannot complete alone.
It permanently removes oxygen from the nodule, eliminating the bacterium's need to respire.
solution: Paragraph 2 states leghemoglobin 'binds oxygen tightly enough to keep the enzyme's surroundings nearly anoxic, yet releases it fast enough to sustain respiration.' That dual action is exactly choice C.A confuses leghemoglobin with the plant's carbon subsidy (a separate contribution described in paragraph 1 and 3). D is wrong because nitrogenase—not leghemoglobin—cleaves the N₂ bond; leghemoglobin manages oxygen, it does not perform the reduction. E is a too-extreme misreading: the pigment does NOT eliminate respiration; the whole point is that respiration must continue (it 'releases [oxygen] fast enough to sustain respiration'). A pulls in nodule formation, which the passage lists as a separate part of the integrated physiology (paragraph 3), not a function of leghemoglobin.
text:
<div style="background:#f7f9fd;border-left:4px solid #4759bd;padding:12px 16px;margin:0 0 14px;border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;line-height:1.55">Atmospheric nitrogen is abundant—it constitutes roughly 78% of the air—yet most organisms cannot use it, because the triple bond joining the two nitrogen atoms in N₂ is among the most stable in chemistry. Only certain prokaryotes, the diazotrophs, possess nitrogenase, the enzyme that cleaves this bond and reduces N₂ to ammonia. Among the most studied diazotrophs are rhizobia, soil bacteria that infect the roots of legumes and inhabit specialized swellings called nodules. There the bacterium trades fixed nitrogen for carbon compounds supplied by the plant, a reciprocity long offered as a textbook emblem of mutualism.Yet the relationship is less placid than that emblem suggests. Nitrogenase is irreversibly poisoned by oxygen, while the bacterium's own respiration—needed to power the energy-hungry reaction—demands oxygen. The legume resolves this contradiction by synthesizing leghemoglobin, a pigment that binds oxygen tightly enough to keep the enzyme's surroundings nearly anoxic, yet releases it fast enough to sustain respiration. The plant, in other words, does not merely host the bacterium; it actively engineers a chemical environment without which fixation would be impossible.This dependence has tempted some agronomists to imagine transferring nitrogen-fixing capacity to cereals such as wheat and rice, which would lessen reliance on the synthetic fertilizers whose manufacture consumes vast quantities of fossil fuel. The difficulty is that the legume's contribution is not a single transferable gene but an integrated physiology—nodule formation, oxygen regulation, and a carbon subsidy so large that fixation can cost the plant a fifth of its photosynthetic output. A cereal endowed with nitrogenase but lacking these supports might fix little nitrogen while paying a steep metabolic toll. The symbiosis endures, this analysis suggests, not because it is effortless but because each partner has evolved to absorb costs the other cannot.
According to the passage, leghemoglobin contributes to nitrogen fixation by performing which of the following functions?
title: Verbal: rc-detail

answer: fix relatively little nitrogen while still incurring a substantial metabolic cost, because it would lack the oxygen regulation and carbon-supply systems that legumes provide.
options: fix nitrogen as efficiently as a legume, because nitrogenase is the only component strictly required for the reduction of N₂ to ammonia.
fix relatively little nitrogen while still incurring a substantial metabolic cost, because it would lack the oxygen regulation and carbon-supply systems that legumes provide.
be unable to fix any nitrogen at all, since nitrogenase cannot function in the presence of the oxygen produced by photosynthesis.
outperform legumes in nitrogen fixation, because cereals devote a smaller share of their photosynthetic output to the process.
immediately lose its nitrogenase to oxygen poisoning, rendering the modification permanently useless across all subsequent generations.
solution: Paragraph 3 says directly that 'a cereal endowed with nitrogenase but lacking these supports might fix little nitrogen while paying a steep metabolic toll.' The inference simply tracks that sentence and its reasoning—the missing supports are the oxygen regulation (leghemoglobin) and the carbon subsidy. Choice B states exactly this.A contradicts the passage's central argument that fixation requires an integrated physiology, not nitrogenase alone. C is too absolute ('any nitrogen at all'): the text says 'little,' not zero, and the harm comes from lacking supports, not from an inescapable oxygen block in cereals specifically. D inverts the logic: the smaller photosynthetic devotion is precisely what would be missing (legumes spend up to a fifth of their output to make fixation work), so a cereal that does not pay that cost would fix less, not more. E overstates with 'immediately... permanently... all subsequent generations'—the passage discusses inefficiency and cost, not a guaranteed total, heritable failure.

answer: complicate the 'textbook emblem of mutualism' by showing that the symbiosis rests on an active chemical intervention by the plant.
options: complicate the 'textbook emblem of mutualism' by showing that the symbiosis rests on an active chemical intervention by the plant.
prove that leghemoglobin is chemically identical to the hemoglobin found in animal blood, establishing a shared evolutionary origin.
argue that the rhizobia–legume relationship is not truly mutualistic but is instead a form of parasitism by the bacterium.

solution: Paragraph 1 ends by calling the relationship 'a textbook emblem of mutualism.' C is too extreme: the author complicates the mutualism but never reclassifies it as parasitism—indeed the closing line affirms it endures as a reciprocal, evolved arrangement.

answer: sober skepticism about its feasibility, grounded in the recognition that the legume's contribution is an integrated physiology rather than a single transferable trait.
options: outright dismissal, on the grounds that nitrogen fixation in cereals is biologically impossible and the proposal is therefore not worth pursuing.

solution: The author treats the proposal as understandable ('has tempted some agronomists') and worthwhile in motivation (reducing fossil-fuel-intensive fertilizer), but then devotes the rest of paragraph 3 to 'the difficulty'—the integrated physiology, the carbon cost, the likely 'little nitrogen... steep metabolic toll.' answer: trace how scholarly understanding of the informal economy shifted from a developmentalist view to a revisionist one, and argue that the category itself is too heterogeneous for a single evaluation
options: demonstrate that the informal economy is growing rather than shrinking in cities of the developing world
trace how scholarly understanding of the informal economy shifted from a developmentalist view to a revisionist one, and argue that the category itself is too heterogeneous for a single evaluation
defend the developmentalist position that informality is a transitional residue destined to disappear as states modernize
refute the revisionist claim that informality is structurally embedded in modern economies
argue that romanticizing the informal economy obscures the precarity experienced by its most vulnerable participants
solution: The passage moves through three stages — the developmentalist view (para 1), the revisionist challenge and its celebratory offshoot (para 2), and the critical backlash (para 3) — and closes with the author's own thesis that ‘informality’ lumps together unlike phenomena, so no single verdict fits. Option B captures both the historical arc and the author's concluding stance, so it is correct.Option A states one empirical claim made by the revisionists, but the passage uses that claim as a step, not its purpose; the author's own point is evaluative, not a defense of the growth thesis. Option D is wrong because the author explicitly says critics ‘rarely dispute’ the embeddedness claim — the passage does not refute it. Option E restates only the critics' point from paragraph 3, a sub-argument the author reports rather than the overall purpose. Option C inverts the author's view: the passage presents the developmentalist position as the outdated thesis that revisionism overturned, not as something the author defends.
text: For most of the twentieth century, sociologists treated the so-called informal economy — unregistered, untaxed, and largely unregulated economic activity — as a transitional residue, a holdover destined to shrink as states modernized and formal labor markets expanded. On this developmentalist view, street vending, off-the-books domestic work, and unlicensed manufacture were symptoms of incomplete industrialization; their persistence signaled a failure of policy rather than a stable feature of economic life.Beginning in the 1980s, a revisionist current challenged this premise. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in Latin American and South Asian cities, these scholars argued that informality was not vanishing but in many places growing, and that it was frequently interwoven with, rather than separate from, the formal sector: registered firms routinely subcontracted to unregistered workshops to cut costs. Informality, on this account, was less a sign of underdevelopment than a strategy — for firms seeking flexibility and for workers excluded from formal protections. Some revisionists went further, celebrating the informal economy as a site of grassroots entrepreneurial vigor unencumbered by bureaucratic friction.That celebratory turn, however, has drawn pointed criticism. Critics note that romanticizing informality obscures the precarity it entails: the absence of legal recourse, pensions, and workplace safety falls hardest on those with the least bargaining power. Yet these same critics rarely dispute the revisionists' central empirical claim — that informality is durable and structurally embedded. The disagreement, properly understood, is not about whether informality persists but about how to evaluate it. I would suggest that this evaluative split is itself instructive: it reveals that ‘informality’ bundles together phenomena — survival labor and tax-avoiding subcontracting — that share a legal status but little else, and that no single normative verdict can do justice to so heterogeneous a category. answer: Successive schools have reinterpreted Rome’s end, and the latest, materialist correction is valuable yet at risk of restoring the abrupt-collapse narrative it set out to replace.
options: The transformationist school erred chiefly in relying on Christian institutions rather than on legal and linguistic continuities.
Gibbon’s moralizing explanation of decline has been revived by historians who study coin finds and pottery distributions.
Successive schools have reinterpreted Rome’s end, and the latest, materialist correction is valuable yet at risk of restoring the abrupt-collapse narrative it set out to replace.
The debate over Rome’s fall is ultimately unresolvable because textual and archaeological evidence can never be reconciled.
Archaeological evidence has conclusively refuted the transformationist school and vindicated the catastrophist account of Rome’s fall.
solution: The passage traces three successive schools (catastrophist, transformationist, materialist) and closes with the author’s own qualified stance: the materialist correction is “salutary,” but “risks reintroducing… the very narrative of abrupt collapse.” Choice 2 captures both the survey-of-interpretations structure and that final authorial caveat.Why the others fail: Choice 1 is too extreme — the author calls the materialist case salutary but never says it “conclusively refuted” anyone, and the materialists explicitly do not revive catastrophism wholesale. Choice 3 invents an “unresolvable” thesis the author never asserts; the author takes a side (finds the correction salutary). Choice 4 misreads the materialists, who “reject its moralizing causes” — i.e., they do not revive Gibbon’s moral explanation. Choice 5 is a fabricated detail; the passage lists law, language, and Christian institutions together as transformationist evidence and never claims one was an error.
text:
<div style="background:#f7f9fd;border-left:4px solid #4759bd;padding:12px 16px;margin:0 0 14px;border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;line-height:1.55">For much of the twentieth century, the collapse of the Western Roman Empire was narrated as a story of decline and fall: a once-vigorous civilization, sapped by moral decay, fiscal exhaustion, and barbarian violence, simply ceased to function. This “catastrophist” reading, inherited from Gibbon and sharpened by mid-century scholars, treated the fifth century as a rupture — the lights of urban, literate, monetized life going dark across the West.Beginning in the 1970s, a revisionist school recast the period as one of “transformation” rather than collapse. Drawing on continuities in law, language, and Christian institutions, these historians argued that Rome did not so much fall as gradually metamorphose into the early medieval world, with Germanic elites accommodating themselves to Roman administrative forms rather than demolishing them. On this view, the very word “barbarian” obscures how thoroughly the newcomers had been Romanized before they ever held power.More recently, a third group of scholars has pushed back against the transformationists, marshalling archaeological evidence — coin finds, pottery distributions, skeletal data, the shrinking of cattle — to argue that material living standards did, in fact, decline sharply and rapidly. Yet these archaeologically minded historians do not simply revive the old catastrophism; they reject its moralizing causes while accepting its claim of genuine rupture. The disappearance of mass-produced goods, they contend, is not a matter of interpretive emphasis but a measurable fact, and one that the transformationist emphasis on elite cultural continuity conveniently overlooks.The dispute is therefore not merely about evidence but about which evidence counts. Where transformationists read texts produced by a surviving literate elite, the materialists read the silent residue of ordinary life. answer: draws its conclusions disproportionately from sources reflecting the experience of a literate elite
options: accepts the catastrophists’ moral explanations while rejecting their chronology
relies on archaeological data that the materialists have since shown to be unreliable
concerns itself only with the fifth century and ignores the early medieval world
denies that Germanic elites had been Romanized before coming to power
draws its conclusions disproportionately from sources reflecting the experience of a literate elite
solution: This requires combining paragraph 3 and paragraph 4. answer: arguing that competing explanations of technology diffusion are better treated as complementary than as rivals, and faulting the field for not doing so
options: tracing the historical development of diffusion models from the epidemic account to more sophisticated successors
refuting the epidemic model of technology diffusion by showing that ignorance is rarely the true barrier to adoption
establishing that the speed of technology diffusion depends chiefly on how quickly information about an innovation spreads among potential adopters
demonstrating that the rank and stock accounts together provide a complete explanation of why technologies diffuse along an S-shaped curve

text:
<div style="background:#f7f9fd;border-left:4px solid #4759bd;padding:12px 16px;margin:0 0 14px;border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;line-height:1.55">Economists have long modeled the diffusion of a new technology as an S-shaped curve: adoption begins slowly among a few pioneers, accelerates as the technology proves itself and information spreads, and finally plateaus once the pool of potential users is saturated. The standard “epidemic” account attributes this shape to the spread of information—potential adopters learn of the innovation by contact with those who have already adopted it, much as a contagion propagates through a population. On this view, the chief barrier to diffusion is ignorance, and the chief remedy is communication.Yet the epidemic model struggles to explain why some technologies of demonstrable superiority diffuse over decades rather than months, long after knowledge of them has become universal. A competing “rank” account holds that firms differ in the benefit they would derive from adopting, so that diffusion reflects not the spread of awareness but the gradual arrival of conditions under which adoption becomes profitable for successively less-suited firms. A third, “stock” account emphasizes that the return to adopting often falls as more firms adopt—because, say, the cost advantage of a new process erodes once competitors share it—so that later adopters face weaker incentives than pioneers did.These accounts are frequently presented as rivals, and empirical studies have sometimes pitted them against one another, asking which best fits a given diffusion path. That framing, however, mistakes the question. The mechanisms are not mutually exclusive; a single episode of diffusion may be governed by information spread early on, by heterogeneity in firm benefit throughout, and by erosion of returns near the end. The persistent search for a single dominant mechanism has, if anything, obscured the more useful task of specifying the conditions under which each becomes salient. Until diffusion research embraces that compositional view, its models will continue to fit curves while explaining little.
The passage is primarily concerned with
title: Verbal: rc-main-idea

answer: attributes the weakening of later adopters’ incentives to the prior adoption decisions of other firms
options: predicts that diffusion will accelerate, rather than plateau, as the number of adopters grows
applies only to process technologies that lower production costs, whereas the rank account applies to all innovations
locates the cause of slow diffusion in firms’ ignorance of an innovation rather than in the economics of adoption
attributes the weakening of later adopters’ incentives to the prior adoption decisions of other firms
holds that the benefit a firm derives from a technology depends on inherent differences among firms rather than on how many firms have already adopted
solution: The passage says the stock account emphasizes that “the return to adopting often falls as more firms adopt,” so that later adopters face weaker incentives than pioneers—i.e., the decline in incentive is caused by other firms’ prior adoption. The rank account, by contrast, rests on firms differing in intrinsic benefit. So D correctly isolates the stock account’s distinguishing feature: incentive erosion driven by how many others have adopted.Why the others fail: E describes the rank account (benefit from inherent differences), not the stock account—a classic swap trap. C describes the epidemic account (ignorance), not the stock account. A contradicts the text: the stock mechanism weakens incentives over time, consistent with a plateau, not acceleration. B overreaches—the cost-advantage erosion is given only as an example (“because, say”), and the passage never restricts the stock account to process technologies or claims the rank account covers “all innovations.”
